I do not see why it is mentioned here, because it has nothing to do with this particular charter, and because in the Bill before us, the charter is surrounded by some very stringent conditions. There is a little amendment which I could suggest to clause 11 when we come to it, and which is in one or two other charters, and it is one to which I am sure the promoters of the Bill will agree to. Everything else is so surrounded by conditions that I think hon. gentlemen opposite should be satisfied to let the Bill go through. I do not 3ee how the country runs any risk, nor do I see how it ran any risk when the Burrard Inlet charter went through. As to the contention that the promoters of the Burrard Inlet charter were acting as trustees for the municipalities, we had nothing to show that they were. If they had been, they should have incorporated the trust deeds in their charter, and that would have been absolute proof. Now, this matter was fully discussed in the Railway Committee, and passed that committee, and I hope hon. members opposite will withdraw their opposition. I ask them in all fairness to do so.

The only water-powers available to this company are those owned by the Dominion, and I cannot see why the government, before they convey any water-powers to this company, should not declare that they will ' consider the whole Question and lay down some definite policy.' The House should have the power to pronounce whether the waterpower will be alienated or not. There are no people out there now and no market for the water, and the individuals who are seeking this Act of incorporation do not live in the territory. One of them is from Campbellton, New Brunswick, another from Montreal, and another from London. England. They have no personal interest in the .locality and are simply company promoters.

Does the hon. gentleman forget that we are giving them simply the right to acquire water-power in connection with their undertaking and not for general purposes, and the undertaking is to build a certain railway? When they come to build it and want water-power, the Minister of the Interior can deal out justice to them, and at the same time, protect the public interest.

I have had something to do with water-powers for the last 25 or 30 years, and the question to me is whether it is in the best interests of the people in general that water-powers, at the disposal of the government, should be acquired by either railway companies or canal companies, or whether it is not better that they should be left for the general use of the public. Take as an illustration this whole Ottawa valley, from the town of Brockville to Pembroke, where there are some ten or twelve towns and villages, and several streams that afford from one to ten water-powers in each town or village, I have never known that a railway company or a canal company had any control over those water-powers, and as a consequence they are developed by private parties for manufacturing purposes. The question to me is this, whether it would not be better in these towns, where these railways are going through, to have the water-powers under the control of the government, either Dominion or provincial, than under the control of a railway or canal company. From my experience, I believe it would be

in the interest of the development of this country that 'whatever water-powers the government control should be retained by the government, because people would much prefer going to the government to get the franchise of a water-power than to a railway or canal company.

I would like to ask whether this Bill is not intended to give the incorporators the right to control water-powers under clause 15 of the Railway Act? That clause provides:
Enter into and upon any Crown lands without previous license therefor, or into or upon the lands of any person whomsoever, lying in the intended route or line of the railway, and make surveys, examinations or other necessary arrangements.

Admitting that there is a water-fall, if the company ran its line within a few feet of that water-fall-and I think they have the right to take 100 feet for right of way-if in that 100 feet is included that fall, would not this company thereby get control' of the water-power, and actually, if it was not necessary to put -a dam there to raise the *water, get the beneficent effects of the stream and convert it into a power on their own property? It seems to me they could by that very means take possession of numerous valuable water-powers. If the minister has passed through Kenora in daylight, he must have noticed that the Canadian Pacific railway passes right by the edge of a water-fall, close to the Lake of the Woods Milling Company, where the fall is on the right of way of the railway, and the railway would have the right to go on that property and utilize that power. Notwithstanding the fact that that power is in the province, the province would be deprived of the right and the beneficial interest which they have in the stream because of the fact that this special company acquired the right to expropriate the land for the purpose of running its railway. Could not this company, by the same means, * get control of valuable water-powers?

My hon. friend is entirely right if the water-power happens to be on the right of way of the railway. The railway would then be the owner of the water-power because it is the owner of the property. But it would have that right irrespective altogether of section 13. If my hon. friend imagines that a railway company will be allowed to go zig-zagging here and there to cross a water-power, of course, that might possibly occur, but it is a most improbable supposition. Under section 13, the company could not erect a dam without coming to the Minister of Public Works for the approval of the Governor in Council. It could not flood back the water without authority. And I think my hon. friend Mr. THOBTJRN.
will agree with me that there are very few water powers in this country that can be utilized to advantage without the building of a dam, or without going to a large expense to sink flumes to carry the water from above the dam to the foot of the falls, which, in the great majority of cases, would carry a considerable distance beyond the right of way which the company is authorized to take. But the point to which I draw my hon. friend's attention is that it would not affect the case he refers to even if section 13 was struck out.

What I object to is giving a railway corporation the right to take over water-powers. I think they should have no such rights and have thought so for a long time. The minister said they would not zig-zag their railway to reach water-powers. But they may run a line straight to reach a valuable water-power, and their engineer would probably take good care of that. The minister knows that on the Canadian Pacific railway in the west are several water-powers under the control of the railway company. There are instances where there are substantial water-powers that could be used without erecting a dam at all.

The conditions at Kenora to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) refers are against his own argument. It is true the Canadian Pacific railway runs over the water-power at that point-and not one but four water-powers, for the Lake of the Woods has three different outlets discharging into Winnipeg river. The railway crosses each of these at the head of the falls. But that does not give the Canadian Pacific railway the right to these water-powers. All four water-powers are developed, but they are in the hands of private corporations. The Lake of the Woods Milling Company was not a pow'er development by reason of the falls, but by reason of the narrow strip of land between the river and the lake, and they tunnelled underneath across the railway. At the other outlets they made their power at Keewatin. The railway company got no control. At Keewatin, they have a 300-foot right of way, because they have sidings, but even that did not give them control of the waterpower, because the water could not be taken from the head and vented in that space. They cross the Wabigon river where there is a water-power and, though the railway crosses right over the falls, that power is developed by a private company, and for the same reason. It is inconceivable that a narrow strip of right of way under any circumstances could give a railway control of a water-power. The best evidence that this cannot be done is the fact that there is not a single case that can be pointed out. I have travelled a good deal in this country and I do not know of

one such case. I do not believe that any hon. member can point to a case where the railway right of way gave control of a water-power.

The hon. member (Mr. Conmee) has cited instances where, although this power was within the right of way of the railway, the railway companies never used the water-powers they reached. It is for that reason that I say we should not put it in the Bill.

What I said was that not only the railway company did not control, but that other private companies have developed and used the water-power and are using it to-day. The power to which he has referred is all developed and is running great establishments.
I understand that some of them at least were by negotiation with the railway company.
Not at all.
Perhaps the hon. member is better informed than I am, but I am not always disposed to take what he says without further evidence than his mere statement.

Suppose that there are valuable undeveloped water-powers in that country, would it not be desirable, seeing that they are at a long distance from coal supply, to operate the railway by electricity? And, in that case, would it not be well for the railway to have authority to utilize water-power for that purpose? It seems to me the very thing the development of which we ought to facilitate if we are giving the company a charter.

We are roid that they have millions of tons of coal in that country. But is there good reason to provide, now by the incorporation of a company for what may happen a hundred years 1 once, tieing up, in the meantime, valuable assets of the country in the interest of private corporations? I do not think there is.

If it would pay the railway company to develop and use the water-power, would it not pay the government to develop it, then let the railway come to the government for what power it needs? The government could sell to the railway company what they want and get a reasonable return on the capital, and they could supply -any municipality or others at favourable rates.

My hon. friend (Mr. S. Sharpe) is opening up a very broad question of government ownership. I would not like to say that it would not be wise for the government to do it, but I do not think the country is, at the present moment, prepared to approve of the government going into a large scheme of developing water-powers all over the country.
On section 11:
11. The company may purchase, lease, or otherwise acquire, hold, enjoy and manage such lands, water-lots, wharfs, docks, dockyards, slips, warehouses, elevators, offices and other building's as it finds necessary and convenient for its purpose, and may construct any of such works or buildings, and sell or otherwise dispose thereof for the purposes of the company, and may carry on the business of warehousemen and wharfingers, and charge wharfage and other dues for the use of any such property, and may enter into any agreements with any such company respecting the use of any of the property of such company.

My hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) has placed in my hands an amendment which he has asked me to .suggest to the committee. The amendment is to strike out the words after the word 'property' in the third line from the bottom, and insert the words, 'but no such wharfage or other dues shall be charged or taken until they have been approved of by the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, who may also revise such wharfage and other dues from time to time.' I think that is a very good provision.
I would ask the minister whether, in this section, the words ' or otherwise acquired ' would cover acquisition by expropriation?
No, that would mean by purchase, lease or otherwise acquired. It must be by some voluntary arrangement. It would not give power to expropriate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am not prepared offhand to say that this amendment would be in order, as rule 111 provides that it must have one day's notice.

I would not press it unless it had the unanimous approval of the committee. But it is limiting the powers of the company, it is making a charge of wharfage and other dues subject to the approval of the Railway Commission. I submit the amendment revised as follows:
But no such wharfage or other dues shall be charged or taken until they have been approved bv the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, who may also revise such wharfage and other dues from time to time.

It seems to me there is an anomaly here. Nearly all wharfages dues imposed by the government are imposed through the Marine and Fisheries Department, but we are transferring them now to the Railway Commission.

These are- dues upon a private wharf owned by a railway company. But the wharf would be owned in

connection with terminal railway facilities, and it seems appropriate that the Railway Commission should have charge of these dues.

There will probably be a mix-up. You can imagine that this railway reaches several towns where there is much shipping, and private wharfs exist alongside the company's wharf. In one case control of rates would be vested in the Marine and Fisheries Department, and in the other case in the Railway Commission.
On section 13,
I understand this section in connection with section 4 will give them no right to sell to the municipality without a by-law on the part of the municipality.
That is clear.
Later on, by the amendment, it gives them express power .to sell and distribute in a municipality.

That will be subject to
the provisions of section 247.

I doubt whether it goes that far. Ini the general clause at the beginning of the section, we make it subject to section 247 of the Railway Act, and then, apparently contradicting that, we give them power to sell and distribute to the municipality.
Suppose we put in the seventh line on page 3 the words ' may subject to the like provisions ' ?
Yes.

Subclause 8 of section 247 of the Railway Act has this provision:
Nothing contained in this section shall be deemed to authorize the company to exercise the powers therein mentioned for the purpose of selling or distributing light, heat, power or electricity in cities, towns or villages, without the company having first obtained consent therefor by a by-law of the municipality.
That requires them to get a by-law of consent from the municipality?

Yes. I would move:
That immediately after the word ' may ' where it occurs in line 7, on page 3, there shall be inserted the words 'subject also to the provisions of said section 247 of the Railway Act '.

If they get this: power subject to that section, and having regard to the subsection that 1 have just read providing that they may sell power after getting the authority of the municipality, would they not then have the power to sell without coming under the clause which provides that the Board of Railway Commissioners may approve of the tariff?

No, the last clause covers that. There is a double security. There is the consent of the municipality under section 247 of the Railway Act, and then the rates must be approved by the Board of Railway Commissioners under the last clause.
Amendment (Mr. Pugsiey) agreed to.
On section 16, issue of securities other than railway.

Should not the Minister of Public Works or some other responsible minister have some supervision over the amount of the securities to be issued under section 16? Suppose the company acquired a water-poweT, they could issue bonds away beyond what is necessary to construct a dam or other works, and then when they came to fix the rates the Railway Commission would not have in mind the cost of the construction so much as the amount of capitalization. The company would want a revenue upon the amount of the capitalization, and not upon the cost of construction.
The board is not bound to do that.

I know, but they always look at that for stock is transferred to widows and orphans, and the protection of vested rights comes in, and they say that we must give an income on the amount of capitalization, and not on the cost of construction.

There is a great deal in what my hon. friend says, but the objection to doing that is that you would have the Minister of Public Works certifying to the value of the property, investors would rely upon the certificate of a responsible officer of the government that the value would fairly represent their security, and it might do more harm than good. The investor usually looks out as to these things where the securities are issued upon floating property. They are simply upon the security of vessels, and other works which may be undertaken.

They would include
water-powers.
I think it would be better to leave it to the investor.
We limit the amount of securities that may be issued with respect to the railway. Why not with respect to the other works of the company?

In regard to the railway you limit it to so much per mile, but I have never known it to be limited in cases where railway companies are authorized to build steamers or other works. You cannot say that >a company should not issue beyond $200,000 or $300,000, and

if you say they cannot issue bonds beyond their value it means that the Minister of Public "Works fixes the value and makes these bonds good. The idea is given to the public by the issue of a certificate of a reponsible officer of the government that the value is equal to the amount of the securities issued. If investors, relying upon that certificate instead of making an examination for themselves, were to suffer loss they would feel that the government had done them a very great wrong, and I think it would be very objectionable to attempt to make any provision in regard to that rather than to leave it to the investor to make the examination for himself.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

House in committee on Bill (No. 115) to incorporate the St. Lawrence Power Transmission Company Limited.-Mr. Pardee.

This Bill has many objectionable features even with all the amendments made to it in the Private Bills Committee. In its original form it had many objectionable provisions, some of which were removed after many days' discussion in the committee. When the Bill came up for discussion in the Private Bills Committee, I moved that it be referred to the Committee on the Conservation of the National Resources of Canada for report. The promoters naturally objected and asked, in somewhat querulous tones, what the Conservation Commission had to do with a transmission line? On a division, however, the Bill was referred to the commission and we had a report from the chairman. In that report he objected to 9 clauses out of 19. I have his letter here, which I think ought to be placed on 'Hansard'.
Referring to the letter of your clerk on the subject of Bill (No. 115), I beg to state that the Bill has been examined as carefully as time and information permits.
The St. Lawrence Power Company is at present seeking authority to develop a power scheme by damming the St. Lawrence river at Long Sault. This project is being opposed by the Commission of Conservation for reasons. some of which have already been made public.
An examination of Bill (No. 115) indicates clearly that the introduction of this Bill is a portion of the St. Lawrence Power Company's plans. It is to be noted that the president of the power company and one of its engineers
are the first named among the proposed incorporators, and the powers asked for are of an unusual and very sweeping character.
The passage of the Bill as it stands would give parliamentary sanction to an important portion of the St. Lawrence Power Company's proposals, and would complicate the situation unnecessarily.
On the other hand it is urged that some of the towns affected, particularly Prescott and Broekville, are without a supply of power, and that a transmission line is necessary in their interest. There does not appear to be any reason why authority for the construction of a transmission line, simply, should not be given, and if Bill (No. 115) were for such a purpose alone there could be no serious objection to it.
Your particular attention is drawn to sections 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14 as being objectionable, on account of the large and unnecessary powers asked for. These clauses apparently contemplate monopolization of powers on a very large scale. It is to be. noted also that there are no provisions in the Bill protecting the municipalities in regard to the use of streets or roads, nor anything requiring the company to acquire or pay for a right of way. Difficulty has already arisen in regard to this latter point in other cases, and it requires to be specifically provided for.
Under these circumstances it is recommended-
First, That sections 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14 be struck out, and that, in lieu thereof. there be substituted proper provisions giving authority for the construction of a transmission line, and for power to buy, transmit and sell power within Canada.
Second, That a clause be added declaring that the Act shall come into force only on proclamation of the Governor General in Council and upon such conditions as the Governor General in Council may by order provide, such conditions to be read as forming part of the Act.
The latter provisions will place upon the Governor in Council the responsibility of seeing that the Act is not made use of except for the purpose for which it is properly intended, and to protect the municipalities concerned.
Part of the objections raised by the chairman were removed by the Committee on Private Bills, but a great many of the objectionable features still remain. As the chairman of the Conservation Commission says, this Bill is merely a part of a much larger scheme promoted by a number of very wealthy American gentlemen, who desire to get control of the St. Lawrence power proposition on the St. Lawrence river. One significant fact was that the promoters would not say where they purposed getting their power. But the engineer and the chief promoters of this measure are applying for permission to dam the St. Lawrence, so that that is where they purpose getting their power. Another very great objection, is the fact that this is a private Bill, promoted for commercial purposes and private gain, and contains some very large expropriation powers. This is a vicious principle

to introduce into private legislation. What some member of the committee desired was that the promoters should specifically mention the clauses of the Railway Act they desire to apply to their company; but instead of doing this, they make the' general provisions of the Railway Act apply where it suits them. But, instead, of that, they made the general provisions of the Railway Act apply to the company where applicable. These powers are very broad and general. By reason of the privileges and rights conferred upon them, they accept some of the provisions of the Railway Act and reject others. They accept such clauses _ as they think applicable to their enterprise and reject those detrimental to their interest and disadvantageous to the company. A company applying to parliament for a private charter to carry on a private enterprise of this kind ought to be made to declare specifically the powers they desire to have, instead of making the general Railway Act applicable to the enterprise.
Another great defect in this Bill is that under it the company may enter and expropriate the lands of the municipality and construct transmission lines upon them without the consent of the municipality. This question was raised last year under the Bill of the Ontario Michigan Power Company. It was amended by inserting the clause 10, which says:
The company should not enter within the limits of any municipality with any transmission line or sell or distribute electrical or other power therein without the consent of such municipality expressed by by-law.
The promoters of the present Bill state that this provision is covered by section 247 of the Railway Act, but that clause merely provides that a company shall not sell or distribute electricity within a municipality except by the consent of a municipality. It does not prevent them from running transmission lines without the municipality's consent.

Do I understand the hon. gentleman (Mr. S. Sharpe) to say that, in his opinion, there should be a clause under which the company could not sell electricity within the municipalty without the consent of the municipality?
No, that is already provided by section 247 of the Railway Act.
If the company comes under that section?
Yes.
That is the expropriation section?

I refer to subsection 8 of section 247 of the Railway Act, which reads:
. Nothing contained in this section should ' be deemed to authorize the company to exer-' cise the powers therein mentioned for the purpose of selling or distributing light, heat, power or electricity in cities, towns or villages, without the company haying first obtained consent therefor by a by-law of the municipality.
This merely refers to the selling and distribution of electricity within a municipality, and has nothing to do with transmission lines. Under the Bill now under discussion the company can build their lines through any municipality by their powers of expropriation, without the consent of the municipality. Some of the municipalities which this company will traverse have already conferred rights on other companies to transmit electricity. If we grant the powers proposed in this Bill in its present shape, those powers will override the powers under that municipal by-law, and without the consent of the municipality this concern will be able to expropriate the works of the companies already doing business within the municipalities under by-law.
And doing business under provincial charter.

Yes. Another great objection to the Bill is in connection with the question of provincial rights, a question which has repeatedly come before this House in connection with such Bills. If the province has an asset which this company desires to expropriate, it can expropriate under the powers proposed to be conferred. Mr. Lynch Staunton, counsel for the Ontario government, appeared before the Private Bills Committee on this subject, and I may say that there were very few members present at that committee, mainly for the reason, I suppose, that there was a meeting of the Railway Committee at the same time. I think that the rules of the House should provide that no two such important committees as railways and private Bills should sit at the same time. At the time that this Bill was being discussed before the Private Bills Committee, the energies of many hon. members were being directed against the Bill proposed by the hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Conmee); that . is, we had the spectacle of two private companies making-
Raids at the same time

Yes, two raids at the same time, one in the Railway Committee and one in the Private Bills Committee; and both with respect to water-powers,
5321 MARCH 14, 1910 5322	
which they sought to obtain through legislation in this parliament. It is quite reasonable that this Bill should be discussed in the light of the policy of the HydroElectric Commission of the Ontario government. We have heard much discussion of this policy. It was alluded to this after-noofi by one hon. member, who, I am convinced, was not very familiar with the facts-who certainly did not speak by the book. He expressed a doubt that the policy of the Hydro-Electric Commission in Ontario had caused a reduction in the price of power. Everybody knows that the Hydro-Electric policy of the Ontario government has met with the absolute approval of both sides of the House in the local legislature. The present opposition in the legislature dare not challenge that policy-has never dared to challenge it. That policy has been submitted to manv municipalities and has been carried by ten to one. The people are unanimous in its favour, except certain interests that are affected by it. Everybody knows that this policy is carried out on the plan of the maximum of service at the minimum ol cost; and everybody knows that the private enterprises are carried on on exactly the opposite plan. Anything that will detract from the effectiveness of the Hydro-Electric Commission policy should not be encouraged by this parliament. The policy known as the Hydro-Electric has reference to every part of the province of Ontario. The commission, I understand, has laid out the province into several divisions, and has had its experts and engineers making reports on these divisions. I have here the fourth report, which is to be found on file in the library. It deals extensively, in a wise and comprehensive way, with this Ottawa and St. Lawrence district. Speaking of undeveloped locations-page 9-the report says: Along the St. Lawrence river, which has no laterals in this part of Ontario, except a email stream at Gananoque, a peculiar situation has been created by the construction of the various ship canals. These canals can be used to a limited extent as head races for power developments, but evidently extensive use is objectionable to the navigation interests, due to the creation of currents, and therefore no very extensive constructions of this type need be expected. The St. Lawrence has enormous potential water-powers, and the future outlook in this locality would seem to be in the nature of very extensive developments, possible only by placing dams in the main river, or else, as at Hoople Creek, near Cornwall, by means of an expensive head canal, circumventing and not interferring with the ehjp canals themselves. It proceeds: In general, it may be said that, with the exception of a small area, lying between the St.	Lawrence and Ottawa rivers and east of Smith's Falls, the whole district covered by this report is bountifully supplied with water-powers capable of being developed for reasonable costs per horse-power. Your commissioners, following the policy outlined in their earlier reports, have not thought it necessary to consider any but the more important undertakings, where electrical energy is being generated for power as well as lighting purposes, and transmitted some distance. A partial list of plants in the district coming under this head are Andrewsville, Mat-tawa, Pembroke, Perth, Renfrew and Morris-burg. The St. Lawrence Power Company and the Hawkesbury Electric Light and Power Company have not furnished the necessary information asked for by your commissioners. I will not delay by reading the full report, but it i3 exhaustive, and deals with water-powers and transmission lines in this particular district. I have a letter in my hand from a gentleman who is deeply interested in the success of the hydro-electric policy throughout Ontario. It is dated February 17, 1910, and reads a3 follows: My Dear Sir,-I note that Bill (No. 115), to incorporate the St. Lawrence Power Transmission Company, Limited, has been referred to the commission. When the Bill comes before the commission for consideration, 1 desire that the commission should know that as earlv as 1906, the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario had the second and tourtb reports on water-power prepared, copies ot which are inclosed. The territory covered by these reports lies between Toronto and Brock-ville. Eleven municipalities in the teritory have asked for estimates and negotiated with the commission for a supply of power, and others are about to apply. The object of the Hydro-Electric Power Commission is to supply power at cost to as many municipalities as possible, and the commission propose to provide a supply of power for all municipalities that can he advantageously served. If the Bill is passed, the company would have authority to transmit power into a large section of the territory to be supplied by the commission, and a dual system of transmission lines would be the result. The commission has always considered that where municipalities are prepared to co-operate and so increase the demand for power from one source that a dual system is a hindrance to municipalities in the working out of their plans, and such a system should not be encouraged. I shall be obliged if your commission will give the facts I have mentioned careful attention. Yours faithfully, Now the opposition that should be raised against this Bill is on the ground stated in that letter that it is a duplicate of those transmission lines. An hon. MEMBER. Who is the writer of the letter? [DOT] Mr. S. SHARPE. The letter was written in confidence to myself, but I will show it

to the hon. gentleman if he wishes to see it. As I was saying, the great objection the writer of this letter has to the Bill is the fact that it is duplicating these transmission lines. They have made a report which covers this very territory. If this transmission line is run along this territory it means that there will have to be dual rates in order to maintain two lines. The commission has made a report upon this very territory, and has provided a plan whereby municipalities can be served, and all it requires co-operation on the part of the municipalities in order to call into operation the wise policy of the Hydro-Electric Commission.
What municipalities have offered to take this power from the Hydro-Electric Commission?

I did not hear the discussion in the Private Bills Committee. Did any of the municipalities the hon. gentleman has just enumerated, Belleville, Cornwall, Brockville, Kingston, Renfrew, make any opposition to this Bill?
I think they were represented by the hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Broder) and the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid), and they offered strong opposition to the Bill.
As municipalities?

I do not suppose that the municipalities knew that this Bill was coming before the Private Bills Committee, although I suppose it would be advertised in the usual way. But this interview states that several of these municipalities have made application to the commission to develop and transmit electricity to the various municipalities, and they were in negotiation with other municipalities. The Hydro-Electric Commission served this very territory through which this transmission line is proposed to be run.
When and how?

That might be a very pertinent question for the hon. gentleman to direct to the promoters of this Bill. When they proposed to build a transmission line they had already proposed to get the power. The same sources of power for this transmission line are available for the HydroElectric Commission. The commission have pow'er to expropriate any power in Ontario situate within the province for the purpose of the municipalities, and if there is, no power available for the Hydro-Electric Commission, there is no power available for the promoters of this Bill.
I think it is well that this House should show their appreciation of the gravity of the situation as far as the natural resources of the country are concerned. The time of this House is occupied with fighting these power Bills. We are only coming to a proper sense of appreciation of the

value of these water-powers. An hon. gentleman this afternoon spoke about the fetish that we are worshipping with Tespect to these water-powers. It is only of late years that these powers have been utilized for the purpose of developing electricity, and we are only properly appreciating their value and that we should not alienate them without proper consideration. We have had companies incorporated year after year lately for the purpose of acquiring these water-powers. Great octopuses are reaching out and gathering in these powers before the people are coming to a proper sense of their value and utility. Private members are occupied more than half their time in framing objections and fighting the piratical propositions of these companies for the purpose of acquiring these water-powers. The discussion of a Bill that was proposed this afternoon is apropos to the discussion in reference to this Bill, inasmuch as the same point is involved, that the government should have some definite policy with reference to water-powers. They should have some definite policy in reference to the right to expropriate municipal lands or rights as well as provincial rights, and we should have some expression of opinion from the ministry in connection with these Bills. I think there should be some rule provided as to the propriety of the whip of either side of the House being sponsor for any private legislation, particularly when he enjoys the popularity that the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) enjoys on both sides of the House. We know that these private promoters have the faculty of ingratiating themselves in the good opinion first, of the whips, then of the other members, and we know with what facility the whips can always get the party in line. I think it would be wise that we should adopt some rule whereby the whip should not be the sponsor of any private Bill when it has for its purpose the taking away of provincial or municipal rights. In connection with this Bill this company seem to have unlimited finances behind them. It is stated in one of the Ottawa papers today that there are millions behind this proposition, and that this transmission line is merely a subsidiary undertaking in connection with the bigger scheme of damming the St. Lawrence river. They have practically taken advantage of every method to get both parties in line on this Bill. We had a prominent Reform lawyer before the Private Bills Committee advocating with great ability the many good features of this Bill, and, on the other hand, we had a Conservative lawyer advocating the splendid features of the Bill, in order to catch both sides of the House. Then we had the hon. member for West Lambton promoting this Bill and endeavouring to
get it through notwithstanding that there was great opposition in the Private Bills Committee.
As far as I am personally concerned, I am opposed to the whole principle of the Bill, but I think the promoters should consent to two amendments in the public interest. One of the amendments was suggested by the chairman of the Conservation Commission. They did not adopt that suggestion. It had reference to clause 10, and it was suggested by the chairman of the Conservation Commission:
That a clause be added declaring that the Act shall come into force only on proclamation of the Governor General in Council and upon such conditions as the Governor General in Council may by order provide, such conditions to be read as forming part of the Act.
The object of that amendment is to throw the responsibility upon the Governor General in Council of adopting the principle of the Bill. If the Bill is not a good one, the Governor General in Council will not bring it into force by his proclamation, and if he brings it into force, he can annex _ such conditions to it as he sees fit. But the promoters of the Bill did not adopt that suggestion in toto. They made a pretense of adopting it. The Bill as finally agreed to by the Private Bills Committee reads as follows:
10. The powers conferred upon the company by this Act shall not be exercisable until the company has first submitted to the Governor in Council plans of such works, and has received his assent thereto.
There is a vital difference between the amendment as suggested by the chairman of the Conservation Commission and that adopted by the Private Bills Committee. Under the clause that was suggested by Mr. Sifton in his letter to the Private Bills Committee, the responsibility of adopting the principle of the Bill is thrown upon the Governor in Council, whereas the amendment merely throws the responsibility upon him of assenting to certain plans. One is a question of principle, the other is merely a question of routine. As a matter of fact, when the company get their charter and their plans are submitted to the Governor General in Council, he merely consents to the plan. It is merely a matter of administration or routine, whereas the amendment suggested by the chairman of the Conservation Commission throws the responsibility of adopting the principle upon the Governor General in Council.	.

Do I understand the hon. member to advocate that this House should delegate to the Governor General in Council the policy to be adopted in regard to a matter of this kind? That would seem to

me to be a very peculiar policy to come from the opposition.
I would say in answer to the hon. member for Rainy River
It comes from the chairman of the Conservation Commission.

SHARPE-that this House is going to be asked to place in the estimates $50,000 to be placed at the disposal of this Conservation Commission. We are spending $50,000 to ascertain the best means of conserving our natural resources. A member of the Private Bills Committee has no means of ascertaining the true facts in connection with the Bill and cannot possibly pass an intelligent opinion upon it, but when the matter is left to the Governor General in Council, he can obtain the advice of the Conservation Commission and of their expert engineers. The Conservation Commission and the Governor General jn Council have money and engineers at their disposal, they can ascertain the true intent, meaning, purpose and objects of this company, and unless they are proper to be brought into operation, the provisions of the Bill need not be brought into operation, but the Governor General in Council has means at his command to ascertain these facts that a private member cannot possibly have.
The hon. member is willing to delegate all the powers of parliament, under such circumstances, to the Governor General in Council? I would like to have an answer to that point.

We are willing to incorporate the company, and if it is a proper company to be brought into operation upon the conditions being ascertained, the Governor General in Council should assume the responsibility of bringing it into existence.
I do not think the hon. member will get many to support that principle.

Another amendment which the promoters of this Bill should accept is in connection with the rights of municipalities:
The company shall not enter within the limits of any municipality with any transmission line, or sell or distribute electrical or other power therein without the consent of such municipality expressed by by-law.
That was inserted last year in my hon. friend's Bill, the Ontario and Michigan Power Company Bill.
That is already in the general law of Ontario, chapter 5 of the Statutes of 1909.
What has the Ontario legislature to do with this?	*
It has control over the municipalities and no company can distribute power in an Ontario municipality without its consent.
This is a transmission line.
That is how power is sold.
The hon. gentleman does not mean to say that the Ontario legislature can pass laws that will have superiority over the laws passed by this parliament?
No, I do not say that.

If this Bill is allowed to pass in its present shape it will override provincial legislation and will invade municipal and provincial rights without the consent of these municipalities. This Bill says too that the plans shall be approved by the Governor General in Council, but it makes no provision for their publication so that the municipalities will have notice that the plans are being submitted to the Governor in Council. In an important matter of this kind where a transmission line will affect municipal and provincial rights, as this does, the plans should be published in the local newspapers in the municipalities affected, and announcement should be made that the plans will be considered bv the Governor in Council and that the different interests will be heard before they are finally approved by the railway board.
Another amendment which I would propose is in connection with the question of provincial rights. This amendment was suggested in the Private Bills Committee and voted down by the friends of the promoters:
Nothing in this Act contained shall be construed to authorize the company to enter on, take or use any land or water, the property of any province, without having first obtained by order in council of the Lieutenant Governor the- consent of the province to such entry, taking or user.
That protects provincial rights and there should be a similar clause to protect municipal rights. Before the Private Bills Committee the representatives of Montreal protested vigorously
And we are here again for that clause.

Because this Bill in its present form gives the company power to enter Montreal and expropriate a right of way without the consent of the citv of Montreal. That is an extraordinary power

to be contained in such a Bill and the representatives of Montreal were quite right to appear before the Private Bills Committee and oppose it in its present form. There should be a clause to protect not only the provinces but the municipalities as well.
If the preamble carries and the Bill is discussed I purpose moving one or two amendments and discussing it further but at the same time I desire to register my general opposition to the whole Bill. My. main reason is that it is duplicating the very line the Hydro-Electric Commission purpose taking in connection with the wide and comprehensive policy the commission has adopted for transmitting power to the municipalities.

When the Bill was before the Private Bills Committee the promoters made it a special point that this transmission line was to be constructed to furnish power to Prescott and Brock-ville. When it was before the Private Bills Committee I suggested that a clause should be inserted providing that work was to be commenced within one year from the time the Bill was passed and to be completed within three years. The Private Bills Committee, however, inserted clause 15, providing:
This Act shall go into force on a day to be named by proclamation of the Governor in Council.
Suppose we pass . this Bill in its present shape, then they may not commence this transmission line for a number of years and this will prevent others from building a line and furnishing power to Prescott, Brockville and other municipalities.
Why?

The very fact of our passing this Bill will prevent others from building a transmission line. I would ask the committee to change clause 15 and to make it read that they must commence work within one year. This line can be built in two or three months and I submit that it is not fair to tie up the power that could be supplied to Prescott and Brockville by other_parties who have waterpower.
How does it tie up the power, what clause in the Bill?

In this way that this parliament grants another company power to build a transmission line. There is not sufficient power required at Prescott and Brockville to warrant two companies building transmission lines to supply that demand. If this company will agree to build a transmission line immediately and furnish power that is satisfactory to Prescott and Brockville; we want power 169
at these places. The St. Lawrence Company at Cornwall have plenty of power, they have admitted that at the Private Bills Committee.
Does the hon. gentleman say that if the Bill is amended so that they shall commence the work within one year the opposition to the Bill will be withdrawn?

So far as I am concerned, if they will agree to that my opposition is ended so far as that clause is concerned; but I also submit that the amendment suggested by JMr. S. Sharpe should be inserted, that is to protect provincial rights. The hon. member (Mr. Pardee) was quite willing in the Private Bills Committee to insert a clause that this company should not take property belonging to the municipality without the leave of the municipality.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: No.
That clause is in the Bill.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: That is provided for in the Railway Act.

If the hon. member (Mr. Pardee) is willing that this company shall not expropriate municipal property without the consent of the municipality why should he not insert a clause in the Bill that they shall not expropriate provincial property without the consent of the province?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Section 47, subsection 5, of the Railway Act absolutely protects the municipality.
It protects the municipality, but not the province.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: You do not agree with the member for Ontario (Mr. Sharpe), who said the municipalities were not protected.
If the amendment of the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) is parsed, and also an amendment that they shall commence within one year and complete within three years I shall be satisfied.

My hon. friend (Mr. Reid) objects to the Bill unless it provides that the construction shall be completed within a certain period, because otherwise, he says, other corporations, may be prevented from giving a service to the people; and my hon. friend from North Ontario taking an opposite view does not want the Bill passed because he says it will be an interference with the plans of the Hydro-Electric Commission. Let these two gentlemen reconcile their divergent views. As I do not belong to the province of Ontario, I



may be able to give ail imoartial opinion from the standpoint of an outsider. I cannot agree with the hon. member (Mr. Sharpe) as to the many benefits to be derived by the province of Ontario from the operations of the Hydro-Electric Commission. True, I have not made a careful study of the matter, but during the last ten years I have had considerable experience with water-powers, and I have yet to see a case wherein competition has made electricity dearer. I do not see what harm can come to the municipalities along the river St. Lawrence from having just as many transmission lines as possible, because I believe the result will be cheaper electricity to the people, and less profit to the company. In my province a man would be drummed out of public life who would do anything to prevent an electric company or a railway company from spending money, and1 placing thesi utilities- within reach of the people. If the amendment of the hon. member (Mr. Sharpe) should be adopted the promoter of this Bill might as well fold up his papers and withdraw it. There is no use disguising the fact that the opposition to this Bill is being put up by the Hydro-Electric Commission or their friends. It is the same old bogie we meet whenever water-powers have been mentioned in this House for the last five or six years. Every time you talk water-power you will find this Hydro-Electric Commission objecting, and why? It is in order to maintain for themselves an absolute monopoly of all electric energy in the province of Ontario, and from that policy I dissent. I do not believe in monopolies by private individuals, corporations, or provincial governments, and I do not believe it is in the best interests of the people of Ontario that the Hydro-Electric Commission should have the monopoly of all electric energy.

Is the hon. member aware that the Hydro-Electric Commission constructs these lines and charges the municipalities with the mere cost of construction, plus a small sum? What objection can there be to monopoly in such a case as that?
Yes, and I have been told that the Hydro-Electric Commission makes the municipality pay for peak loads which they may only use once in a year.
You are wrongly informed.

Not by any means, and they grant monopolies for thirty years in order to prevent any one-else getting into the cities, and they pretend to sell horsepower for $25 when as a matter of fact the cost amounts to $60 or $70.
That is not right.
Yes.
Just mention such a case

Wait a moment, my hon. friend from Westmorland had to call you down this afternoon. This commission pretends to sell electricity at a low rate, but that only means the charge for it at the substation outside the municipality, and then they have to pay their share of the cost of transmission lines, and the cost of transforming, and the cost of distribution, and the cost of different other things which sometimes amounts to $60, and $70 per horse-power.
Give an instance where the Hydro-Electric Commission stated they would furnish electricity for $25 per horse-power and charged $60 or" $70.
The town of Stratford is one, and the town of Ingersoll is another.
And the town of Galt.
What does Stratford pay?
As near as I can figure it out, it is $60 or $75 per horse-power.
It is $29.

Oh yes, but that is only at the outside station. The hon. gentleman wants to get acquainted with this business. They have to pay for different other things which adds to the cost. To come back to the Bill-my hon. friend (Mr. Reid) is mistaken as to the Railway Act with reference to municipalities. The Railway Act does not provide; that a municipality can by its mere ipse dixit refuse to allow an electric company to do business within its borders. Subsection 5 of section 24 provides that if the company cannot obtain the consent from a municipality, the company may apply to the board for leave to exercise the power, and upon such application it shall present a plan of the highway, square, or other public place, showing its powers in this territory, subject to whatever conditions they may consider fair. My hon. friend (Mr. Reid) vdll see that a municipality, under that Act, has not the absolute right to exclude an electric power company. But if the amendment of the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) should be adopted, it would give the province of Ontario the absolute right to exclude this company from any portion of the public domain of that province; and we may assume that the province, exercising the policy to which it is committed at present, would absolutely prevent this undertaking from going

on, and the whole thing would become a nullity.

Do I understand the hon. gentleman to argue that this Bill would give this transmission line power, under the Railway Act, to enter a municipality and do business there in so far as the furnishing of electric light is concerned?

No. Under the Railway .Act this company would have the right to go on the public streets or otner places in a municipality with its consent; but if it could not make a satisfactory arrangement with the municipality, it would have the right to apply to the railway board, and that board would grant its application subject to conditions. The company is obliged to go to the municipality first, but if the municipality will not be reasonable, it can apply to the railway board which has authority to act. If, however, the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) were adopted, the province of Ontario would have the right to absolutely forbid this company from crossing its property, and that would be the end of the whole transaction.

I understood in the Private Bills Committee that the intention was that whenever this company desired to enter or pass through a municipality the municipality alone would have the power to grant or refuse permission, and I understood that the promoters of the Bill were willing to have it amended in that sense.

The question arose as to what right should be given the company to enter a municipality. It was thought that if the Bill were passed as drawn, in which section 247 of the Railway Act was to apply only where applicable, that possibly there might be lack of definiteness; upon the request of one of the members of the committee, who was opposed to the Bill, section 247 was made to refer specifically to the matter of crossing or going through a municipality.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: This Bill is in the same form as that in which it came from the committee, where it was absolutely satisfactory to all the members, even my hon. friend.
No, it was not.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
I think the hon. member for Ontario contended that what the terms of this Bill should be and when it should go into operation should be settled by the Governor in Council. Of course, that was an absolutely novel and unique proposition. It simply meant leaving to the Governor in Council the right to legislate absolutely for the whole House, and was a proposition utterly untenable. Consequently we put in clause 15 to provide that the Act should come into force on the day fixed in the proclamation of the Governor in Council, and that clause is to be read

in conjunction with the one dealing with the plans and specifications. The clause relating to municipalities was struck out in committee, and it was agreed to by every member of the committee that section 247 of the Railway Act absolutely protected the municipalities. As regards municipal and provincial rights, which we hear so much of to-day, if you were to put a provision in the Bill such as hon. gentlemen opposite desire, you would put it into the hands of a province or a municipality to stop the construction of the work at any minute. Even if we were at our last link and putting up our last pole, the province or a municipality might prohibit our going a step further. Suppose this company had expended large sums of money arid suppose, at the completion of that work, it were necessary to put a pole or wire along the bed of a stream, and the province were to refuse to give us that power, we would be absolutely out of court and might just as well have thrown our money into the deep sea. It is all very well to talk of provincial rights, but surely there are some Dominion rights. Surely we have the right to give companies which we incorporate the power to carry on the works we have authorized them to do.
Would the hon. member give them the power to expropriate Dominion lands without the consent of the Dominion government?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: We aTe discussing provincial lands, just now.
That is a point I would like the hon. member to settle. They cannot, under this Bill, expropriate Dominion lands-

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: But put the converse question, and would it be fair the other way? Two wrongs do not make a right. _ It is the Dominion parliament that is doing this.
Then my suggestion would be, either take away this right that was given them over provincial land, or give them the power over Dominion lands.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
This parliament is asked to give rights within its jurisdiction. To say that before we give these rights that are within our jurisdiction we must go to the province and ask them if we may do so would be to render the granting of a charter here clearly ridiculous. So far as municipalities are concerned, they are absolutely protected under subsection 5 of section 247 which provides that if the company cannot obtain consent from the municipal council or other authority-which clearly show's that, in the first place they must go to the municipality to obtain that consent-then the Board of Railway Commissioners is empowered to step in and Mr. PARDEE.
say under what conditions they shall come in with their line. Surely, the municipality is protected under that. It is also provided under subsection 8 that nothing contained in this section shall be deemed to authorize a company to exercise the powers conferred upon it for the purpose of selling or distributing light, heat, power or electricity in cities, towns or villages unless the company has first obtained the consent of the municipality by bylaw to that effect.
Could not they sell to some one who would step in and sell?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: They cannot distribute without a by-law.
Yes, they can.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I think not.
I would remind the hon. member (Mr. Pardee) that in the London Bill the other day, we put in a special clause to cover that very point.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
I think it was entirely surplusage-it merely cumbered the Bill. My hon. friend from NSrth Ontario (Mr. S. Sharpe) talks about the gravity of the situation and about natural resources. Within the four corners of this Bill, water-powers are not mentioned. This is nothing more, and it is nothing less than a transmission line, pure and simple. You say, this is part of a larger scheme. But this committee must recollect that, if the company incorporated by this Bill cannot get the power to distribute-and, as I understand it, they have to come to this parliament for that-then the whole Bill is absolutely of no use to them. How, then, can the public be prejudiced, how can any one's rights be interferred with by the granting of a charter for a transmission line alone? So far as the Hydro-Electric Commission is concerned, it is very well to say that for six or seven years they have been contemplating coming in. I venture to say that, so far as the municipalities affected by this Bill are concerned, you will not find one man in fifty-not^ one man in a hundred-who, if there is a chance of having power transmitted by a bona fide company, will not hold up both hands for it. No municipality would think for a moment of getting in the road of competition in the distribution of electrical power, the same as competition in anything else. There is no reason why the Hydro-Electric Power Commission should be in a position to say to the people of this eastern portion of the province that they will come or stay awrny as they please, .but that, in the meantime, even though a bona fide company comes and proposes to distribute the power this parliament shall not grant the necessary authority. As to this argument of a dual system why it answers itself. Whether dual, treble or quadruple

-the more competition you have the better for the people. I submit that, so far as the argument against this Bill is concerned, my hon. friend from North Ontario (Mr. S. Sharpe) and my hon. friend from Grenville (Mr. J. D. Reid) in their endeavour to find objection, in their supersensitiveness to objections, have really bumped into each other. This Bill was objected to as vigorously as possible in committee.
My hon. friend from North Ontario told us, to use his own terms, that the Conservation Commission would protect the rights of the people. The Bill went to the Conservation Commission; we had no objection to that. It came back with a letter, which the hon. gentleman has read, from the chairman of that commission. And the hon. member (Mr. S. Sharpe) himself says that with one exception, the provisions of the Bill were cut out. It is true, nearly the whole Bill was cut out, But we felt that, if the Conservation Commission thought these clauses should come out-that there was danger, that there was somethin# lurking here not visible to the naked eye-we would take out these provisions. And we did take them out, down to the last suggestion in the letter of Mr. Sifton, the chairman of that commission. Surely, we have gone as far as it is possible to go. Every objection has been met, and every right safeguarded. The promoters of this Bill are asking nothing in the way of waterpower, they are not touching the natural resources of Ontario, they are here simply asking for a transmission line to run through certain counties and cities, And if they get the current to transmit, well and good, if not, so far as I can see, it is absolutely their own lookout.

I desire to say a word here, largely for the purpose of securing information. I have not followed the Bill; I was not a member of the committee before which it was heard and considered. But I had supposed that this Bill was a preliminary to some other Bill that might, within the very near future, be brought under the consideration of thi3 House. That is, I had supposed that this parliament would have under consideration at this session a Bill which would be a counterpart of a Bill passed by the legislature of the state of New York. Now, what I wish to know is this: Is it not within the knowledge of some hon. members of this committee that the authority to dam the St. Lawrence is at this moment held by a company, which company is associated with this power transmission company?
Same crowd.

As I understand it, some time in the nineties, a company was incorporated by the parliament of Canada with power to dam the St. Lawrence, and
that this company did exercise its powers in part. They have built a dam, and have generated power, and the Cornwall canal, and other establishments in that vicinity are to-day enjoying, I believe, the benefits accruing therefrom. We have heard, in times past, in this parliament a great deal of discussion with respect to that company, and concerning contracts entered into between them and the government of Canada. And, if I understand it, that company is a part and parcel of this company, and that the danger in connection with this Bill is because the parliament of Canada has already given the powers to generate electrical energy by damming the St. Lawrence, and that the original company has since changed hands. That company, I understand, did not have the powers necessary for the, transmission of the energy in many directions. Therefore it is they come here for these large powers which thev consider requisite and in connection with which they will exercise the powers already given by this parliament. The point to which I would invite your attention in this debate is this: I have in my hands a copy of the Bill passed by the New York state legislature, and when we know that in giving these powers to a company having the same purpose in view they insisted upon that company only exercising that- power for a consideration, I wonder why it is that the parliament of Canada is willing to grant this stupendous franchise for nothing. You say that is not involved in this Bill. I say that it is, because if there is any ground for suspicion that this privilege is to be exercised in conjunction with a company that we incorporated years ago in this parliament, it is time this parliament should halt and inquire how far the powers which we then gave to that original company are to be exercised. That great American company, in the exercise of their powers must pay into the state of New York a large sum of money annually. The very first tax upon them is $10,000. The purpose of the Bill is thus set forth:
An Act to incorporate the Long Sanlt Development Company, and to authorize said company to construct and maintain dams, canals, power-houses and locks at or near the Long Sault island for the purpose of improving the navigation of the St. Lawrence river and developing power from the waters thereof, and to construct and maintain a bridge, and carry on the manufacture of commodities.
Now that is the company which is incorporated by the state of New York. It can exercise all the powers and rights that they wish in connection with that portion of the River St. Lawrence which flows over American territory. They could not come oyer across the boundary iine into the Canadian waters of that river, and therefore it was necessary for them to secure the same powers in this parliament I apprehend

that they soon discovered that there was a company that had all the powers that were necessary and that were granted at a time when the full exercise of those powers was not realized. Now, as lion, members who live down in that section will know much better than I do,' there has been a dam constructed by that company on the Canadian side. If they will refer to the original Act they will find that company has powers which are still unexercised and which may be exercised in connection with other dams. For instance, they have a power-I am now speaking subject to correction, because I have not studied the Bill-they have power to construct a dam in connection with this company which has been incorporated by the state of New York. A company incorporated a few years ago by this parliament has the power to build in conjunction with the American company a dam for its purposes on the St. Lawrence river.
They have no such power.

I am informed they have. I am informed that those powers have been granted by this parliament. If that is a fact, I cannot vote for this Bill, because I see lurking in it a menace to Canadian interests. If, however, it can be shown to me that this is merely a transmission line for power that may be generated under the authority which they are yet to secure from this parliament or some other legislative body then I would not have any great objection to this Bill.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: They only have the right to import, not to export, even suppose they had those powers he speaks of.
I see no advantage in it.

Mv hon. friend misapprehends my point. Not with respect to expropriation, because that is regulated; even though they had the power, I understand that could be regulated. If the parliament of Canada can realize that they had granted powers which they did not contemplate would be exercised in the way that it is now proposed to exercise them, then it is time for us to consider how far we should supplement the powers which we have already given to a company which controls the rights which were granted by the parliament of Canada twenty years ago.
How does this Bill affect that?

If that company got certain powers by that original Act to dam the St. Lawrence, but has no power of Mr. EMMERSON.
transmission in Canada and cannot exercise that power without our supplementing it, and giving through the medium of this Act advantages and franchises which are of value, then we can well understand why they are coming here now and seeking these privileges. Therefore I say that this parliament should hesitate, they should at least enact this legislation with their eyes open. If it were true, and could be demonstrated to parliament that, without realizing the full extent of the po-wers which they gave in the Bill of 1901-I think that was the year.
The hon. member for West Lambton would be able to tell us what the date was.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: About 1894.
It must be ten years ago. There must be some limitation to it.
They have exercised their rights and they have built a dam.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: There is no dam there.

The hon. gentleman may be confusing that with the contract that was given to M. P. Davis and Company, for all the surplus power of the Cornwall canal for 84 years, and which was entered into about 1896. There was a renewal when the present government came into power. It was for 21 years', and it was renewed for four times, and although he had control of that power he could not distribute it without the power to construct a distribution line. It may be in connection with that, although there is another power company in addition to that.

There is another power company in addition to that, a dam was built, the company is in existence to-day, and I am informed that it is controlled by this great American syndicate that have acquired permission from the legislature of New York state, and are now seeking powers from this parliament to enable them to complete their great scheme of controlling the powers of the St. Lawrence river in connection with the Long Sault dams. If these facts are true, surely we, as a parliament, should have respect enough for ourselves to hold our powers in as high esteem as the legislature of the state of New York place upon the powers that they have to grant. When the scheme is consummated, and when they construct these dams and create these powers what will be the result? The state of New York will be receiving annually a very large sum of money from the company. The province of Ontario and the Dominion of Canada will not get one cent -no, they will not even get 'thank you '

for it. This company of American capitalists will simply laugh at the parliament of Canada for being so guileless as to grant these powers without a thought as to the full effect and force of the powers that they have thus granted. That is the point I raise and it seems to me we should hesitate in a matter of this kind and at least learn as to whether there is a basis for these statements which are openly made. I had heard of opposition to this measure. I had read in the Toronto papers and the papers of Canada generally of the opposition to this transmission power Bill. I could not understand why there should be such serious objection to the incorporation of a company of this character for the purpose of transmitting power. If they had no power to transmit they would have to purchase it from somebody else. But that did not involve interference with the waters of the St. Lawrence. It in no way affected anybody's rights to transmit this power. They had to acquire it, they had to purchase it from somebody and distribute it. I therefore assumed that the objection to the Bill arose from the fact that there was in contemplation an application to the parliament of Canada along the lines of the successful application that was made to the state legislature of New York for a consideration, and that the applicants would be here seeking the powers which were given to their sister corporation in the state of New York.
In what year was the power given, by the legislature of New York state?
Several years ago. Reference can be had to it in the statutes, but I have a typewritten memorandum in regard to it
Are these the people that propose to construct a dam at the Long Sault?

At the Long Sault, 1 did not think that this transmission Bill was a dangerous Bill until information *came to me from a reliable source. I was not interested, I am not now in any way interested in the matter only as a member *of this committee, and therefore I have no connection with it. But information came to me to the effect that this transmission power company had rights in connection with the St. Lawrence under powers that were granted to a former company, a company which they now control, and which will be incorporated as part of their scheme in connection with this transmission power company, should they secui'e legislation from the parliament of Canada. If there is any truth in it, if there is any basis of foundation for these statements, then I say that it would be the duty of every
Canadian to say: No, we will not grant to you gentlemen these powers that you want; we, it is true, granted to you certain powers in connection with the building of dams on the St. Lawrence, but we did not contemplate that anything of this kind would take place; we did not contemplate, when we gave you these powers, that it would result in interference with the navigation of the St. Lawrence, which will be effected as a national scheme; we did not take that into consideration; you have all these powers given to you for this purpose that are no good to you unless you get this supplementary legislation that you are coming here and asking for; it is true that we might impose upon you terms such as the New York state legislature imposed upon you, but we are going to hesitate to grant you any of these powers until at least a full and complete understanding is had with respect to the objects that you have in view, what your purposes are, how far you propose to interfere with that international stream, and how far you propose to affect Canada in relation to her position as a co-user of the waters of the St. Lawrence. These are matters of supreme moment, these are matters which the government of Canada certainly should take into consideration before this Bill takes many steps forward in this parliament. If there is nothing in what I am stating, if these statements that are made by men of responsibility, are not true, then, of course, it is only a question of the incorporation of a transmission power company which is stated to have been properly safeguarded by the committee. But I think it goes further, and I think that lurking about it is a something that shows, when there is so much interest in' it, and when there are so many great American capitalists interested in it, that this Bill is worthy of inquiry on the part of parliament, that this parliament should hesitate before taking a leap in the dark, before committing itself to the disposal of powers that will be used to the advantage of a foreign country and to the detriment of our own.

I wish to make a few remarks in reference to this Bill. There has been a good deal said about the HydroElectric Commission of Ontario. The hon. member for Carleton, New Brunswick (Mr. Carvell) seems to know just what they are charging here, there and everywhere. He must have got his inspiration from the hon. member for Rainy River. That hon. gentleman has locked horns with that commission in Port Arthur, and I think he came out of the struggle with the horns off. The people there, had a chance to pronounce on his scheme in connection with the Ontario and Michigan Power Company and the Hydro-Electric Commission. Port
Then you force every one to come under the Hydro-Electric Commission and make it a monopoly?

You are making it much deaTer. I think the province should have a right to say whether these people shall be permitted to put up poles or: towers on property of the province. Subsection 4 of section II provides:
Wherever in the Railway Act the word 'land ' occurs, it shall include any privilege or easement required by the company for constructing or operating the works authorized by this Act, under, over or along any land, without the necessity of acquiring a title in fee simple.
Is that a fair thing, to say that these people shall run their lines over head over any man's premises without being obliged to buy the right of way?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Read subsection 6 of that clause.
That does not overrride this.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Yes it does.

Then we might strike out clause 4. There have been lawsuits in Montreal with the Power, Heat and Light Company to determine this matter. There should be no doubt as to the rights of individuals over whose lands they pass. The ordinary man in the country cannot go to law with a great corporation with millions behind it. For that reason, it seems to me it should be made so plain that there would be no doubt as to the rights of the

company so far as these matters are concerned. If a motion is not moved by some one else, I shall propose one later that will amend clause 12. It seems to me that the right of the provinces in respect to property under their control should be protected.
