I merely wish to enter my earnest protest against the Bill passing in its present form. It certainly interferes with provincial and municipal rights, and the Hydro-Electric Commission are opposed to it. The chairman of the Conservation Commission has been utterly opposed to it, and very few of the clauses which the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) gave us to understand were struck out in compliance with that request seem to have been struck out. In the HydroElectric Power Commission's report No. 4, on page 21, will be found a table of estimated annual charges, on fully developed generating plants in the very same towns through which these lines are liable to pass.
Transmission of Power.
In connection with the hydraulic developments in the Ottawa Vallay and that portion of the province bordering on the St. Lawrence river, four transmission schemes have been considered, viz., one, 20,000 volts, three phase, from Iroquois through Prescott to Brock-ville; one, 30,000 volts, three phase (scheme A), from High Palls through Perth and Smiths Falls to Brockville, Prescott and Carleton Place; one, 20,000 volts, three phase (scheme B), from High Falls through Perth and Smiths Falls, terminating at Carleton Place; one, 20,000 volts, three phase, from Fountain Falls through the Cobalt mining district, terminating at Haileybury.
In the following estimates, the use of high class wooden poles with concrete bases is assumed, the telephone line being mounted on the same poles.
It gives a thorough estimate of the cost of the line. The commission has at present under consideration a proposition similar to that contained in the Bill which it is sought to force through the House. The member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) in his wisdom, told the people of Ontario what they should do about this matter, and he said the town of Galt would have to pay $5 per horsepower. If you will turn to the first report of the Hydro-Electric Commission you will find that the cost of twenty-four horsepower in the town of Galt for the full load would only be $17.35 , for three-quarters load $17.79, and for half load $19.90. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) also said that the town of Stratford would have to pay $75 per horse-power, and no doubt he was prompted to say these things by some of his friends on the other side, because you will not find many men in Ontario who will get up to condemn the action of the HydroElectric Commission, and their splendid administration of their affairs. Now, in
Stratford the cost of twenty-four horsepower for a full load is $20.48, for a three-quarters load $21.41, and for half a load $24.04. The above cost of power is based on the estimated rate of $12 per twenty-four horse-power per annum for high tension power at Niagara Falls. I call the attention of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) to these facts just to show that his statement is absurd.
Is the Hydro-Electric Commission selling a single horse-power at Stratford at the prices quoted by the hon. gentleman?

The hon. gentleman knows they are not in a position to sell power up to the present time, but that is a carefully prepared estimate by expert engineers of the cost at which these different municipalities will be supplied, and on which they have accepted the building of a transmission line. The hon. member fot Westmorland stated that he had in his possession a Bill which was passed by the New York legislature showing that they had absolute control of water-powers in that state, and along the boundary line. Why should the people in the province of Ontario be interfered with in this regard and why should they not expect that a reasonable . amount of money should be collected from these transmission lines. I quote from ' Hansard ' the speech of the hon. member for Westmorland:
I have received, on an application which I made some weeks ago, a copy of a Bill passed by the legislature of the state of New York, being ' an Act to incorporate the Long Sault Development Company, and to authorize said company to construct and maintain dams, canals, power-houses and locks at or near Long Sault island, for the purpose of improving the navigation of the St. Lawrence river and developing power from the waters thereof, and to construct and maintain a bridge and carry on the manufacture of commodities.' Having a copy of that Bill m my hand, I will call the attention of the committee to this fact, that in the very inception the company is required ' to pay into the treasury of the state the fixed sum of $10,000, and m addition to the payment just mentioned, the company shall pay into the treasury of the state for the year 1910 the fixed sum of $15,000, and for the year 1911 the fixed sum of $20,000. For each year after 1911 the said corporation shall pay at the following rates upon the average amount of electrical horse-power generated during such year under the authority of this Act, that is to say: upon all amounts up to 25,000 electrical liorse-power, at the rate of 75 cents per horse-power ; upon all amounts in excess of 25,000 electrical horsepower and up to 100,000 horse-power, at the rate of 50 cents per liorse-power; _ upon all amounts in excess of 100,000 electrical horsepower, at the rate of 25 cents per horsepower. In case said corporation shall generate or develop water-power as mechanical power without transmuting the same into electrical power, then for so much of said

water-power as may be developed payments shall be made at the above mentioned rates per mechanical horse-power/
Well, that is a practical common sense business arrangement, and the province of Ontario is perfectly justified in claiming, so far as the transmission of power to that section of the country is concerned, that they should have something to say in regard to what they would like to collect from that company, and, how they would like to control the transmission of power in that district. I shall certainly vote against the Bill as it is at present framed.

That gives them all the power they want. I understand the St. Lawrence Power Company have disposed of their rights and interests to the promoters of this Bill. When we read section 9 of the Act of 1901 we can learn why the present promoters are not applying for an extension of the rights under this Act of 1901, and it is for the simple reason that the Act of 1901 provides that they shall not exercise rights in any municipality without first obtaining the consent of the municipality. Section 9 reads:
9. The company, for the purpose of constructing and maintaining its works may, with the consent of the municipal council or other authority having jurisdiction over the same, enter on any highway, square or other public place, and as often as the company thinks proper, may, with the like consent, break up and open any highway or public place.
Under the Act of 1901 they must get the consent of the municipality but under the Bill now before the House they will have expropriation powers without the consent of the municipality. So we can readily understand why they are not asking for ail extension of powers under the original Act of 1901. They are simply a subsidiary company getting distribution powers under the Railway Act and with full powers to expropriate, which they could not obtain if they were to ask an extension of these powers. They could in that case only exercise these powers and privileges with the consent of the municipalities. In view of the many objections raised, not only by my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) but by many others, I think that this Bill should be referred back to the private Bills committee for further consideration. I move therefore that the committee rise and report progress and ask leave to sit again.

I desire more particularly to refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Westmorland because he is labouring under an entire delusion as to what has occurred. He is under the impression that this company had obtained the power to build dams and had actually constructed them. There is no foundation for that statement. It never acquired any power to build a dam, it, has no power to dam any part of the St. Lawrence river, and has not built any dam. The dams to which my hon. friend refers are the famous Sheiks island dams which are a part of the Cornwall canal, and were constructed by the Dominion government. The construction of those dams and the building of the Cornwall canal developed incidentally a certain amount of waterpower. That water-power belongs to the Dominion, as a part of the Cornwall canal, and was leased by the Dominion government to the St. Lawrence Power Company.
Is not that owned by this company?
No, it- is owned by tlie Dominion of Canada and is held under lease. The water-power generated by those dams in the Cornwall canal is under lease to this company. '
And the company is owned by these parties.

They have no right to generate any other power except what is developed by the construction of these works by the Dominion government. My hon. friend might just as well refer to all the other powers leased along the Cornwall and Welland canals. At the towh of Cornwall, the various mills have obtained by lease from the Dominion government water-powers which are developed by drawing water from the canal. The St. Lawrence Power Company do the same thing. They draw water from the canal at a point further up and discharge into the river.
What do they pay?

$1,000 a year That was a bargain entered into by hon. gentlemen opposite when in power. The dams were constructed during the regime of the Conservative party, and were leased to Mr. Davis prior to the change.
And renewed by the present administration some years ago.

Yes. The hon. gentleman has referred to the Bill obtained from the New York State legislature authorizing a certain American company to dam the St. Lawrence, and he assumes that, that confers upon that company the power to dam a portion of the St. Lawrence, That is not the case at all. It requires the assent of the federal government of this country coupled with the authority of the State of New York, to authorize the damming of the St. Lawrence, because the St. Lawrence is a navigable stream.
Does the hon. gentleman not know that there is a Bill at present before the House of representatives confirming the law of the State of New York and the damming of the St. Lawrence-Bill No. 14531.

I do not see how that affects the argument. The federal government at Washington and the New York State government combined could not dam the St. Lawrence without the consent of Canada. Canada must be consulted.
TAYLOR, Canada has been consulted and has given her consent.

No, she has not. The only application made to Canada is the application which is before the International Waterways Commission. This company has applied to the joint commission for a recommendation, so far as that commission can give it. The International
Waterways Commission has been investigating that application for some .two years. The proposition was first referred to a certain board of engineers to investigate and report. That board reported that the plan was feasible, but the International Waterways Commission is still considering the question. It is to hold shortly ajiother sitting and take further evidence and proposes to have further investigation by engineers. The result is that there is no danger whatever, such as the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) contemplates, of any power being given for the damming of the St. Lawrence without first obtaining the consent of this parliament.

This International Waterways Commission is supposed to pronounce either for or against. Their decision will only affect our legislation because the Americans are acting independently of it. Have they not already got the consent of their own branch of the commission?

I understand that the American branch of the commission have reported to their authorities in favour of the scheme and that may affect the American federal legislation. But the Canadian branch has not, and the Canadian branch is conducting this investigation. What the final report may be, nobody knows; but no matter what may bo the report of the commission, that has no effect as law. Nothing can have effect without the consent of this parliament, so that there is absolutely no danger of this damming scheme becoming the law of this country or of any one obtaining the privilege of damming the St. Lawrence until a Bill to that effect passes this House. The present Bill is solely for a transmission line. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that the company expect to get power to transmit over this line through this particular scheme. No doubt if they succeed in obtaining the consent of parliament to dam the St. Lawrence, they will. But they can get the power elsewhere. Power can be developed from the Long Sault rapids without this scheme going through in its entirety, and for that reason the transmission line may be a necessity and may be useful, quite independent of the scheme of damming the St. Lawrence. A very large amount of power has already been developed at this point. There is the power scheme first started by English capitalists in American territory. The Americans did not object at all to English capital going in and developing their own power. The Englishmen were unfortunate enough to lose all their money, and the works they had constructed went over to a new company. That work has been completed and a very large development is taking place from the Long Sault rapids. A considerable development is taking

place on the Canadian side by means of the works of the Canadian government, and further development is possible without the actual damming of the river, but the large scheme would be carried out by the damming of the St. Lawrence. For that reason I do not see why hon. gentlemen should be so much alarmed about the effects of this Bill. The Bill itself can confer no other Tights than are contained in it, and those are simply and solely for the construction of a transmission line from Montreal to Kingston. I do not see why the Ontario government should be consulted. As will be seen at once, the Ontario government, and the branch of that government known as the Hydro-Electric Commission, take the stand that any opposition to their schemes or their possible schemes should not be allowed by this parliament. And if they can stop any other scheme, no doubt, with the views they entertain, they will stop it. It was admitted bv Mr. Staunton, when arguing in the Private Bills Committee on behalf of the Ontario government, that that government claimed the right of property in the bed of all streams. They claim that they own the soil under the bed of the St. Lawrence river. That is confirmed, I believe by the Privy Council. There are several streams that would have to be crossed by this line, and the pro-, vincial government could, under the amendment suggested, step in and say: You must not plant a pole in the bed of that stream; you must not lay the foundation of a tower. And, entertaining the views they do, that every possible scheme in opposition to the Hydro-Electric Commission must be squelched and killed, it follows, as a matter of course, that, under the amendment proposed, this scheme could be nipped at many points between the boundary of Quebec and Kingston.
Will the hon. member name a stream that would require a pole in the middle of its bed?
Yes, at the city of Kingston, crossing the mouth of the Rideau river.
The Rideau does not flow there.
What is the stream there?

There is Cataraqui creek; you could jump across it.
Mr. ROBERT SMITH There is the one over which a bridge about a quarter of a mile long is carried, the bridge that the troops have to cross in going from the city of Kingston to the camp ground.
It is not a hundred feet wide.
It is not fifty.
There is a very long bridge there.
There is no line across there.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes) perhaps, does not understand that is not the only right the government might have. If the Ontario government own the bed of a stream, they have a right to prevent a line crossing that stream in the air. You cannot run a line, as a matter of law, across a man's land without buying that right, even though it does not touch his land. The same principle would apply to the property of the Ontario government in the stream.
Why should the Ontario government's rights be interfered with?

For the same reason that the Ontario government's rights are not considered when any other great national undertaking is going on. For instance if we wished to build a railroad from Montreal to Kingston, we would not consider the Ontario government. And the transmission of power to-day is growing as important to the people as the building of a railway. And, when we have a transmission line that is of national or interprovincial importance, the parliament of Canada has the power to provide for that line, and they ought to exercise that power in their discretion.

This appears to be a larger question than we understood that it was when the discussion began. I happen to be a member of the Private Bills Committee and I attended rather regularly when the Bill was under discussion, and I want to confess that we did not get anything like all the information that was necessary, for I have heard a great deal to-night and have received a great deal of information on this subject, much that we did not get in the Private Bills Committee when the Bill was cut down very materially from the shape in which it was introduced. The only point I want to make is with regard to the statements made by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Em-merson). The hon. member himself does not say absolutely that those statements are correct, because he does not know of his own knowledge. But he says that he has what he considers reliable information, and it is to the effect that this original company was started in 1901, was given certain powers in connection with the damming of the St. Lawrence river, powers that might not be given to-day, in the light

what we know now of the value of water-powers and of the facility with which power may be sent for long distances. Though this Bill does not deal with water-powers but simply proposes a transmission line-yet if, by passing this Bill, we enable that company, that big American company, which now owns the charter granted in 1901, to do something we would not grant power to do to-day, and if in the meantime they having carried out the provisions of their charter, then I say the hon. member for Westmorland is -right and that we should hesitate about passing this Bill until we find out exactly the position in which this House stands. Far be it from me to seek to prevent any company or body of men from coming and developing the natural resources of this country. But here is an American concern that has privileges got from this parliament, privileges that, when accorded by the legislature of the State of New York for that side of the river will be upon the condition of the company paying $20,000 or $25,000 a year. If half the power got by damming the St. Lawrence belongs to Canada, I say we should hesitate before giving our half for nothing when the American side is being paid for at the rate of perhaps $25,000 a year. What I suggest is that we do not go on with the Bill at present, but either refer it to a special committee or send it again to the Committee on Private Bills for the purpose of ascertaining exactly the position of the matter and for the purpose of ascertaining whether the statements made by the hon. member for Westmorland are correct or not. I think that the promoter of the Bill will make greater progress if we are given an opportunity to understand exactly the position we are in with relation to this Bill.

I understand that the New York State Legislature has already passed an Act to authorize the construction of that dam, and that there is now a Bill before the United States House of Representatives, Bill (No. 14531) to confirm the Act of the New York State legislature- whether that Bill will pass or not is a matter of concern to many. Under the terms of this Act, how is the St. Lawrence river to be controlled? The great navigable portion of it is controlled by one lock, and the bed of it is to be handed over to the state of New York for ever, so that the growing navigation of the St. Lawrence river is to be practically handed over to the control of a monopolistic company for the generation of electrical power from which the state of New York will get a few thousand dollars a year, the Ontario nothing, and this government, I suppose, nothing but a little rake-off for politics. There is the situation as I am told it is. I would like the hon. member for Westmorland to look at this aspect of the case and tell us whether it is
or is not true that by coupling up this company with the existing company and taking advantage of the New York and Washington legislation they can have the power to dam the St. Lawrence river. These gentlemen are worth watering. There is no great hurry in passing this Bill. It will stand over certainly for another session, and even this session long enough for this matter to be looked into. If this company can, under this Act, take possession by expropriation of the bed of the St. Lawrence river as far as the Ontario government owns it, and if they can control the waterway by expropriation, as they can under this Act, to the centre of that river, then the navigation of that river is closed in perpetuity. Every year that St. Lawrence river is a highway, traffic is increasing in volume, the navigation of these rapids is absolutely safe at the present time. Such a thing as a vessel of any size being wrecked is unheard of. More and more navigation requires that this river should be kept open and free. Now I maintain that in the interest of the province of Ontario, in the interest of the Dominion of Canada, in the interest of the St. Lawrence river, and in the interest of good fellowship with the United States, there should be no legislation passed here that will permit the damming of that river. We want to live in amity with our friends across the river, we want to stand 'shoulder to shoulder with them in promoting the interests of humanity the world over. But if these interests are permitted to get into the hands of private companies, it will bring discord, it will tend to breed dissension. That reason alone should be sufficient to prevent any such measure going through this House. It is a matter well worth looking into. The gentlemen who are behind this scheme have placed $2,000,000 for promotion. Now what promotion means I do not know, perhaps some one can tell us. But I am informed that $2,000,000 in capital has been set aside for promotion, and perhaps that explains the energy with which this Bill is being pushed through. How much did they receive for selling it?

I am not going to inquire into that, it is not germane to the question. Now, not only did they have the power under this Act in 1901 to secure, acquire, use, maintain and operate canals, water courses, race ways and water-powers, in or adjacent to the St. Lawrence river, on the north side thereof, but they have also the power to construct dams, wing dams and sluices, and buildings, in connection therewith. Certain powers are granted the company by the legislature of the State of New York. We have granted certain powers. There can be a holding company that can assemble all these powers, control the whole of the waters there and all the water-powers, and I apprehend that would not be a Canadian holding company but would be a company originating in the United States and composed of gentlemen of great capital in the United States. It is true that under our law there can be no exercise of these powers on the St. Lawrence even by a company incorporated by this parliament unless the plans were filed and met the approval of the Department of Public Works. I apprehend that has been done with respect to the works which that company, that is the St. Lawrence Power Company, have already constructed. I apprehend' that when they come to exercise the powers which they seek and require to exercise they can take this Act and under its authority can prepare additional plans and go to the Department of Public Works, and if their plans are approved of, they can have a complete system controlling the water-powers of the St. Lawrence, with everybody at their mercy m that vicinity and for a long distance removed from there. It seems to me that this legislation is such, taking into consideration all that it involves, all that it seems to involve, all that it may involve of which we do not at this moment know, that it is right and just and proper for this committee to now hesitate, to say we shall require further information, we shall require to know more as to the purposes of the company to see whether it is proposed to have an amalgamation. It is true the legislature of the State of New York did not have the full powers to enable that company to exercise all the rights that they require. They have to go to the Congress of the United States, the federal authority, but they do it there by legislation. We have done it already, we have legislated in this regard. We, in all such cases under the general powers given to the Public Works Department, authorize that 170

department to have a control, to give their approval to grant a license practically for the exercise of any powers which we may have enacted in behalf of any company. I say that for these reasons, if there were no others, I would oppose this Bill. I would not wish to have any question arise in a matter of this kind as between the province of Ontario and the Dominion of Canada. There is no necessity for anything of that kind. It is something that is beyond even the question of provincial and federal rights, it is something that affects the citizenship of Canadians, that might injure or might protect the business interests, the industrial interests on our side of the line, and if there is a possibility in that regard, if there are any dangers, if there are any hopes, surely we should guard against the dangers and we should preserve the hopes of the people of Canada.
Has the State of New York power to sell the water-powers along the St. Lawrence river tributary to the State of New York?

The New York legislature exercised rights which under the constitution belongs to them; they have the ownership in the soil under the waters of the St. Lawrence south of the international boundary, and by virtue of that ownership they assumed to exercise legislative authority in connection with the powers granted to this company. The congress of the United States controls the navigation and the international aspects of the river, and congress would not permit the exercise of these powers without granting legislation supplementing the legislation of the state of New York, and approving of it.

Does the hon. gentleman contend that the authority of the state of New York, plus the authority of the United States government, would enable that company to dam the St. Lawrence south of the international boundary line without the consent of Canada?

That question does not arise in connection with this legislation, but I admit most unquestionably that in the case of navigable waters and international streams the consent of the government of Canada must be first had. But what I say is: these people can do us no injury by reason of the legislation they have already secured from the United States or by legislation which they may secure. That can only become a menace and a peril to our conditions by reason of whatever unwise legislation we may pass here, and by reason of the action of the Dominion government. But we must not place the whole responsibility on the government, we have the responsibility as legislators ourselves. It seems to me that

whereas we in the past may have given powers which we did not contemplate would g,o so far, that now when we are called upon to supplement these powers we should hold the reins in our own hands and say that they cannot have these additional powers unless there is a full and complete understanding with respect to the exercise of them.
Does not the United States federal legislation make the erection of a dam conditional on similar legislation being obtained from Canada?
That is to be found in the Bill I have read.

When this mil was first introduced it was evidently thought to be an innocent measure, but now the hon. member for Assiniboia admits that many new phases of the Bill have presented themselves even to-night and which were not considered by the Private Bills Committee. The Bill we are now considering is a second reprint, which is conclusive proof that the Private Bills Committee tound it necessary to eliminate some of the powers sought by this company in the original Bill, and consequently it demands careful consideration at the hands of the House. Hon. gentlemen opposite would lead us to believe that the Ontario hydro electric commission only proposes to furnish power to western Ontario, but I commend to them the fourth report of the commission, in which they will find that in the St. Lawrence district (eastern Ontario) the commission proposes to supply power to six municipalities, in the central Ottawa valley district to 13 municipalities and in the upper Ottawa valley district to 7 municipalities. While, up to the present time the hydro electric commission and the Ontario government have concentrated on the development of the Niagara power it must be remembered that they intend to extend their operations in the interest of the people to every part of the province. The hon. gentleman from New Brunswick (Mr. Carvell) suggested that the hydro electric commission and the Ontario government were making an effort to compel municipalities to come under the commission, but I would mention to my hon. friend that the option has to be submitted to the voters of the municipalities before they can have the right, to receive power from the hydro commission, and, therefore, the whole thing rests with the municipalities themselves. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) spoke about monopolists^ but I would remind my ihon. friend that there are two kinds of monopolists. There are private individuals who are constantly 'coming to this House endeavouring to get control of public utilities in their Mr. EMMERSON.
own interests, and there are the other monopolists like the province of Ontario who seek to develop and utilize our natural water-powers in the interest of the whole people of the province, and without any idea of making gain for themselves. Let me tell hon. gentlemen opposite that this is the foremost plank in the platform of the Ontario government. There are 107 members in the legislature, and although the government have a large majority, there is yet an active and enterprising minority led by an able man, and not one of that minority has ventured to say a word against the continuance of the hydraulic electric power commission and its efforts in the interest of the people of Ontario. There was some little criticism in the legislature as to details, but there was no opposition to the principle. Let me remind these gentlemen opposite also that a general election has taken place in the province since the Ontario government had the courage to adopt that as a plank in their platform, and that the government of the province has been sustained by the people by an overwhelming majority. I, therefore, contend that the provincial government should be consulted in matters of this kind, and that applies not only to the government of Ontario but to the governments of all the provinces who are anxious that the rights of their provinces should be protected. The Liberal party in former days claimed to be the great champions of provincial rights, but we have not heard su much about that claim since they became all powerful at Ottawa.
However I do not wish to introduce that phase of the question for discussion. What I want to point out is that it is high time the Dominion and the various provincial governments should come to some agreement in order that the rights of the people, both provincial and Dominion, should be protected, and protected not in the interests of men who come here from time to time seeking charters in order that they may sell them again. All these matters should be carefully considered, not alone by this government, but by this government in negotiation with the provincial governments, and not have the time of this House and its committees wasted upon these constant discussions regarding federal and provincial rights. This is a matter which should be settled between the provincial and Dominion governments. A clause should be put in all these Bills to provide that no charter granted by this parliament should be sold [DOT]without the sanction of the Governor in Council. That would put a stop to some of the bartering and sale of charters. But if we allow Bills of this kind to pass, we are encouraging this kind of business and it will continue. I want to enter my protest as strong as passible against the granting of these important

'privileges without taking every precaution to protect the public.

The hon. member (Mr. Car-veil) has overlooked the reports of the Hydro-Electric that are in circulation.

That is not the first report sent out in the way of a prospectus that has not fulfilled what is propnesied. Let me tell my hon. friend from East Lamb-ton (Mr. Armstrong) that this talk about hoping to sell power in Galt and Stratford at $20 or $21 means distribution at a central station. Let me give two illustrations. Down home, or rather just across the border, in the state of Maine, in the town of Halton, they are buying electricity at two and a half cents a kilowatt hour, but it costs the people ten cents per kilowatt hour for their electricity. The difference goes in the cost of distribution. In the towns of Perth and Andover, in the constituency of Victoria, N.B., the electricity costs four cents at the station, and costs ten cents when it is distributed. When you talk of the price of delivering at the station, that is not a criterion of what it will cost to distribute it to the people.
Does not the hon. member know that in the face of such things as he is stating, the people have voted strongly in favour of the Hydro-Electric power?
They were deceived.
The people of Fort William were not deceived.

I am ready to leave these two hon. gentlemen to fight that out, while I get back to the Bill. The object, as I have said, is to distribute electricity, and to give the people the benefit of this utility. I contend that the measure ought not to go back to the committee, and it ought not to be subject to what the province of Ontario might decide. For, as as pointed out by the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Robert Smith) the moment
a proposition of that kind is put in the Bill the Ontario government would find means, to destroy the enterprise.

Does the hon. member think that the state of New York is justified in demanding, and receiving from the Long Sault power the large sums of money they are receiving from year to year, and that the province of Ontario ghould not receive any remuneration?

Under this Bill, the price at which this commodity should be distributed, and sold, is in the hands of the Canadian Railway Commission. If you place a big royalty upon it, the people will have to pay that much more for it; if you do not place that much royalty the people will get it for less.

I would like to call the attention of the committee to the statements made by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson), and the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell). With regard to the Bill of the state of New York, to which he has referred, I understood him to approve of that Bill. I would like to know whether that is the case-is it a Bill that he would approve of it either in Ontario, or the Dominion parliament passed it? Would the hon. member oblige me with an answer?

I do not know that it is involved at all in my argument, a3 to whether I do approve, or do not approve. One thing I do approve of, and that is, if we grant these powers to a private company, I approve of the action of the state of New York in imposing obligations upon them. They are not doins? it for their health, they are not going to the legislatures for these powers for any other interest except their own. They propose to make money out of it, and I think it is right that the province, and the Dominion, in granting these franchises should impose obligations.

My hon. friend has brought in a Bill, and has placed it on ' Hansard,' and has given it a certain amount of approval. Now I do not think that my hon. friend nor any other member can approve of that Bill. I say that between that Bill and the legislation which we are passing from day to day, and the legislation in the very Bill under consideration, there is no comparison in the public interest. Under that Bill the state of New York gets about $30,000, and then they get a small percentage per horse power per annum. There is not a word in the Bill that protects the people of the state of New York either as to prices, or hours of service, or conditions of service. There the water-power is alienated from the people of the state for a paltry sum, and put into the hands of a private company. When you put in the

Bill before us a condition that the Board of Railway Commissioners, the high court which the government has established for the protection of private interests as against railway or other companies, shall control the rates to be charged, then you put in conditions that conserve to the people the benefit of these great facilities. Thera is no comparison as regards the public interest between the legislation in the state of New York and the legislation which we are considering here.

Does my hon. friend say that the company has the right to fix their own charges in the general Bill of the state of New York? The private company to which my hon. friend refers has no right to fix the charges, they are fixed under a general law of the state of New York. My hon. friend understands that very well.

No, I do not understand it that way, if that is the case it is of recent date, but the reverse. I know that by a report made a couple of years ago by the president of the United States, wherein he pointed out that that was the weak point in the legislation of the various states of the union, that it should be guarded by the federal power, and upon that very ground he vetoed the Ontario and Minnesota Power Company's Bill, which was a federal Bill. Let me point out to the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) wherein I think he and other hon. gentlemen are not consistent. We had a Bill to-dav that was severely criticised because it had a provision to allow the sale of a surplus of electricity in the case of a railway. Tha*t was criticised for several hours, and no sooner had it passed than the hon. gentleman passed another Bill which had on it the name of a prominent gentleman who is leader of the opposition in the Senate (Mr. Lougheed) a canal Bill, in which were all the powers my hon. friends are objecting to in this Bill. I have in my hand an Act, chap. 128, to incorporate the St. Clair and Erie Ship canal. Hon. gentlemen spent the whole afternoon criticising a Bill having 'the same powers, they voted for in that Bill, which gives power 'to sell in the province of Ontario power generated from the St. Clair river and the St. Clair lake, and to exercise all the powers to which they are objecting now.
Does it give them all the rapids on the St. Clair river?
I cannot answer that question. It gives them power to generate electricity front the St. Clair river and lake, to sell it and to distribute it.
How could they get power in a canal where there are only two locks, one at the commencement and one at the other end, where there is no fall at all?

My hon. friend knows very little about power, or he would not ask that question. Where you have a lake such as Lake St. Clair to supply the power, [DOT]and where you have the privilege of making a conduit, there is no limit to the power you can generate except the capacity of the lake to supply it. Now if it is the policy of the hon. gentleman opposite that when one of their friends has a Bill it goes through, no matter what powers it carries, but when some one else has a Bill it must wait for the Hydro-Electric Commission, I do not think that is a sound policy, either in the interest of the Dominion or of the province of Ontario.

The hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) said that members on this side of the House who are opposing this Bill are guilty of some crime, because they say that it is in the interest of this country that the line should' be built by private companies. I want to tell him that if he goes into a municipality and submits that question, and endeavours to satisfy the ratepayers that they are better off in the hands of a private company than in the hands of the HydroElectric Commission, he will find himself badly left. I know that in the city of Hamilton, where we have the largest power producers in the province, the question has been submitted three or four times to the "ratepayers, and has been carried in favour of the Hydro Commission nearly three to one every time. The hon. gentleman also said that the horse-power was going to cost $75 per horse-power from the Hydro Commission. He has not proof for that statement, it is mere imagination on his 'own part; his figures is about three times as high as they ought to be. In the city of Hamilton our contract provides for $17.92 per horse-power. Power is $9.42 at the Falls, and $8.52 goes to make up the cost of the trunk line, the loss in transmission, building the plant in the city, and in other ways bringing the power right to the motor ready for use.
What do the people of Hamilton pay for electric light, and until what hour?
They pay many different prices.
What is the average price?
There are as many as three dozen different prices charged in the city of Hamilton.
I ask the hon. gentleman a fair question. What do the people pay?

I cannot tell you how they make their charges but I paid somewhere in the neighbourhood of $30 per

year for light for my house, which I consider very high. I pay $35 per horsepower in Hamilton to-day and I only use the power for eight hours. If I were getting my power from the Hydro-Electric Commission I would be paying $17.92 and 'only paying for the power for eight hours while under the present arrangement I pay $35 for eight hours. We were paying $85 per lamp for our street lighting for ten years in the city of Hamilton which claims to be the electrical city of the Dominion. Since the Hydro-Electric Commission has been inaugurated we are getting it for $47.50 per lamp.
I can tell the hon. gentleman that in my town, which is a company town, we are only paying $35 per year per lamp.

I do not know anything about your service, but I know that the Hydro-Electric Commission is entitled to the credit for the cost of lights being reduced from $85 to $47.50. We have been paying anywhere from $35 to $40 per horsepower. The Cataract Power Company offered to give us power for $16 per horsepower and ten per cent less than the commission's price, no matter what it may be. Still, in the face of that the rate-payers' would not take their offer but turned it down three to one. Surely, you do not mean to tell me that you would advise the people of this country to place themselves in the hands of a private company and pay their price for power when they could get their power from the Ontario government at cost price. Not only that but the Ontario government can borrow money at a less rate than any company can get it for, and surely the Ontario government is in a position to furnish power cheaper than any private company could furnish it for. I will venture to say that if you put a clause in to provide that this company should furnish power at cost price to the consumers you would not get anybody to home and ask us for a Bill of this kind. I said that we paid $17.92 per horse-power. Toronto pays $18.10 and Toronto gets 10,000 horse-power while we only take 1,000. If we were to take 10,000 horse-power the same as they do in Toronto our power price would be cut down about $4. Neither you nor anybody else can tell us what Stratford's power price would be unless you know how many horse-power they will take. If they took 500 horse-power the price would be in the neighbourhood of $30 perhaps $29, but it would not exceed $30 or $31. You cannot say that it would be possible to get any better prices than those which I have stated here because the Ontario government has employed the best engineers that could be got in this country to make these assessments and valuations, and the cost of trunk line, copper wire and all those things has only been a trfle over half what the estimate was. As it is we are getting power at $17.92.
Do I understand that the prices that the hon. gentleman is quoting are prices that the consumer has to pay for power in these different cities?
The price I am quoting is the price that we pav for power. If the municipality sees fit to charge its customers a profit it can do so.
My question was if that was the price after they nave distributed it or is that the price in bulk?
It will cost $17.92 delivered from the motor to any customer in the city of Hamilton.
That is at the power station?
Yes.
Does my hon. ...friend know what it will cost to distribute fhat to the consumer?

Along the trunk line through the heart of the city it will not cost any more than that, but where there are lines at a distance leading to factories it will cost more. Will it not cost more by your company too? You cannot carry it along fences and sidewalks; no matter what power it is, you require a line to carry it.

Before the question is put I would like to say that if this Bill involves the damming of the St. Lawrence, interference with navigation or a possible alteration in that great inland waterway, it is a very large proposition. I believe that the question is at the present moment before \the Waterwavs Commission. It appears, however, according to the argument of the hon. member for Westmorland, that it is involved in the very Bill that we have before the House. The hon. member for Carleton, New Brunswick (Mr. Carvell) referred to section 8 of the Act of 1901. The hon.< member for Westmorland and other hon. members have asserted that that charter is now controlled by the gentlemen who are promoting this Bill. The hon. member for Carleton referred to section 8 but he did not refer to the important part of section 8. The important part of section 8 is .this-I will eliminate the immaterial words.
The company may construct canals and water-powers in or adjacent to the St. Lawrence river, on the north side thereof, at any point eastward from Hoople's creek, in the county of Stormont, to the eastern end of the Soulanges canal, and may construct dams,

wing-dams, sluices, conduits and buildings in connection therewith.
There is power to construct a canal and water-power and to construct and maintain dams in connection with them.
Dams upon the St. Lawrence?

I will read it again:
The company may construct canals in or adjacent to the St. Lawrence river, on the north side thereof, at any point eastward from Hoople's creek, in the county of Stormont in the province of Ontario, to the easi-ern end of the Soulanges canal, and may construct dams, wing-dams, sluices, conduits and buildings in connection therewith.
I understand that legal opinions have been given by gentlemen of very high rank in the profession to the effect that under that power, coupled with the power contained in the Bill which has been passed by the legislature of New York, a dam may be constructed and maintained across the St. Lawrence from the Canadian side to the United States side. I do not know whether these powers are sufficient for that purpose. It would require one to investigate the locality and to apply the words of the statute to the physical conditions before he could come to a very definite or sure conclusion as to that. But, at all events the argument is a plausible one, the argument has been made, and legal opinions have been cited in support of it. Well then, if that be the case, the proposal before the House at the present time, embodied in this Bill, is to confer certain powers on the company now proposed to be incorporated which already controls these powers contained in the Act of 1901, and which, therefore, upon the passage of this Bill, would be in a position to control all necessary legislation on the Canadian side, the legislation on the other side having been secured or the company having made application therefor. It would seem to me that these considerations might very well give the government some concern, and I would not think it advisable that the committee should pass this Bill until the government are in a position to announce their policy in regard to it, and say whether or not, particularly in view of the applications before the Waterways Commission, they should give their sanction to legislation which would have that result.
Something has been said as to the rights of the province of Ontario, and hon. gentlemen have been inclined to make rather light of the position of Ontario. The people of Ontario, through their government, have decided that they will embark upon the project of Mr R. L. BORDEN.
undertaking the development of water-powers in that province and supplying power to the people of that province at cost. By what warrant should the parliament of Canada undertake to give any corporation power to interfere with that project? Is there any good reason in the public interest which can be adduced in favour of such a proposal? The people of Ontario having decided through their legislators, and government that it is in the public interest of that province that water-powers in the province of Ontario should be developed not by private corporations for gain, but by the people of the province in order that every person requiring power in that province should receive it at cost, is it within the fair purview of the parliament of Canada to pass any legislation which will interfere with that project? If any other province in Canada should enter upon and establish the same policy is there any good reason why the parliament of Canada should empower a corporation created for gain to interfere with a public utility of that kind proposed to be carried on by the province itself in the interest of the people of the province? And not only does this Bill propose to do that, but according to hon. gentlemen who have viewed this proposal with favour, the province of Ontario is to have its own lands expropriated, lands which it may require for the purposes of this project, and is to have its own scheme of development interfered with in order that a private corporation may be enabled to make money out of the expropriation of those lands, and out of the scheme carried on by that expropriation. Assuming that the parliament of Canada possesses such a power, it should not be exercised. The people of any province in Canada having determined to enter upon a project of this kind, a project of development of their own natural resources in the interests of the people of the province, should hot have that project interfered with in any way by legislation passed by the parliament of Canada in favour of those who seek to develop the same water-powers for the purpose of gain. Such legislation would seem to me to be most undesirable for this parliament to embark upon, and yet if the argument of hon. gentlemen is correct as to the powers of this parliament, that certain result would follow.
The hon. member for Carleton, New Brunswick, (Mr. Carvell) referred to the desirability of granting these powers, because ho said it might result in the creation of power on the United States side which would thus be imported into Canada, so giving to the people of this country greater opportunities of obtaining power than would otherwise be the case. So far as the development of power on the Canadian side or the United States side of the

St. Lawrence river is concerned, it seems to me that would depend a great deal on where the dam is constructed. You. might construct a dam on the St. Lawrence at one place and find the power nearly altogether on the American side; you might construct it at another place some distance away, and find that the power would be developed on the Canadian side. So I would not agree in the view that it is eminently desirable to pass this legislation, because under it the power to be created will be created on the United States side, and not on the Canadian.

My hon. friend misunderstood my statement. I made no such statement. The hon. member foT Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) stated that from his knowledge of the location the power would be developed on the American side. I said: So much the more necessity for this, if you cannot get the power on the Canadian side.

I apologize if I misunderstood my hon. friend; that is the way I understood his reference to the statement of the hon. member for Westmorland. It seems to me this consideration is another reason why we should not be too hasty about this legislation. If the St. Lawrence is to be dammed to create power -and as to the expediency of that, as at present advised, I would have a great deal of doubt,-I think it might be important to come to a conclusion as to the best place in the interests of the country for building such a dam and creatig power, for the very reason to which I have just alluded.

If I understand my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) aright, his principal objection to this Bill is that in some way it would be interfering with the project of the Hydro-Electric Commission of the province of Ontario.
I did not say that was the principal one.
If that were so quite a strong argument could be presented, but has any one suggested that the Ontario government or the Hydro-Electric Commission propose to develop this water-power?
Certainly.

No one has suggested that; it does not appear in the report that they propose to develop this power and the complete answer to the suggestion is that the Ontario government has no power on earth to develop this water-power. It is a power contained in a navigable river which, under the British North America Act, is obsolutely under the control of this parliament. Another insuperable objection is that it is an international river, and no
power can be created there by the building of a dam unless that dam extends all the way across the river into American territory and I do not think any province has power to engage in the construction of a work which of necessity extends outside of the limits of the province. Therefore, for two reasons, neither the Ontario government nor the Hydro-Electric Commission created by it would have power to engage in this work, first because it is a navigable water, jurisdiction over which rests absolutely with this parliament, and secondly, because it is an international river, and for that reason the legislature of the province of Ontario would have no authority over it.
Then how did they get it at Niagara?
They do not, they rent from a company incorporated entirely outside the Hydro-Electric Commission.
A provincial charter?

They got a provincial charter, but if I mistake not they came to this parliament and also got it confirmed. But the reason, and the only reason, why they were enabled to go ahead there, was that they leased the ground from the Park Commission. Then there is no dam at Niagara Falls.
It being an international stream the minister would say that power could not be developed by the province and I ask how it was done there?

Because the works there are wholly on the Ontario side. Here it is proposed to erect a dam and the same must extend across the river in order to develop power. The Ontario legislature could not, in my judgment, authorize the construction of a dam to connect with a dam on the American side, because it would be all one work and beyond the jurisdiction of the province of Ontario. Neither could it authorize an obstruction in a navigable river. I do not deny that the Ontario government has constructed works for the development of water-powers in navigable waters. In that respect, I think-and it is worth the attention of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) who dwells so strongly on provincial rights-in that respect, I think they have encroached upon the jurisdiction of this parliament and have sought to do what this parliament and this parliament alone can do. It does seem to me that I ought to call the attention of the Committee to the fact that this Bill does not profess to give any authority to develop water-power upon the St. Lawrence or anywhere else. It merely incorporates a company for the purpose of distributing electrical energy.

Don't you think the Bill should say where they intend to get tho electric current from?
5.379
I do not think so. Before they commence operations the plans must be approved by the Governor General in Council, and the Bill will only come into operation by proclamation.
Does the minister state there is no proposition here to develop power along the St. Lawrence?
Not in this Bill.
Read subsection 5 of section 11.
These expropriation powers would be the power to string wires and place poles, but not the right to develop water-powers.
Has not the power to be obtained from the St. Lawrence river?
There is not a word in this Bill which gives authority to develop water-power along the St. Lawrence.
Does not the minister think they will develop their power on the St. Lawrence?
This Bill simply enables them to rent from another company which may develop power.
Where does the minister think they will get their power?

My own idea is that they will get their power from a company which may develop it along the St. Lawrence. I do not know that to be the case but I suspect it. This Bill simply incorporates a transmission company which would have to make an arrangement with another company for its power. The development of power upon the St. Lawrence must be provided for by another statute, but this Bill does not give the slightest authority to dam the St.Lawrence or construct any works in the St. Lawrence or anywhere else except such works as are essential for a transmission line. As head of the department which has been investigating this subject, the matter has come before me and lion, gentlemen are doubtless aware that the plans of the company were submitted to the government for the development of water-powers on the St. Lawrence. It was directed that these plans should be referred to the chief engineer of the Department of Railways, the chief engineer of Public Works, and the chief engineer of Marine and Fisheries.
Under what statute did the company profess to be acting when it submitted these plans?
They did not state, but I understood it to be under the St. Lawrence Power Company charter granted by this parliament some years ago. I also
understood from them that they expected to have to come back to parliament to get authority to dam the St. Lawrence.
They have it under the other statute.

So my hon. friend (Mr. Emmerson) thinks, but they did not lead us to understand that they had. The three engineers to whom the plans were referred reported adversely to the plans as originally proposed, and they suggested certain modifications which were accepted. The engineers reported that the project was feasible, that the dam could be erected without interference with navigation, and the matter is now before the International Waterways Commission. I can assure the committee-
I understand that the Waterways Commission have stated that while they are ready to hear any one, they are not ready to deal with the question.

The International Waterways Commissioners are hearing parties, pro and con, in order to get all the information possible, as the government desire they should do. They heard the statement of the transportation interest and representatives from the city of Montreal and others.
That is some time ago.
Some few weeks ago.
What power has the International Waterways Commission to deal with this matter?

They simply advise. It must be borne in mind that there is no doubt that the American section of the International Waterways Commission seems to be very strongly of the opinion that it is to the public advantage to develop the water-powers in the St. Lawrence at the Long Sault, and that not only will navigation not be interfered with, but that it will be improved. It is, of course, desirable that the Canadian section should examine into the subject from every possible standpoint and be quite sure that the decision will be in accordance with the public interest.
The minister was about to give some assurance to the committee when he was interrupted.

I was going to assure the committee that no plans would be approved of, no arrangement would be approved of, no agreement would be ratified by the government which does not amply protect Canadian interests.* So far as the Department of Public Works is concerned, I can assure the committee that the plans will not be approved of unless upon the express stipulation, which will be thorough-

ly safeguarded, that one-half of the waterpower which will be developed will be reserved absolutely for the use of the people on the Canadian side of the line.
Are these the dam plans?
Yes.
The thing is under consideration then?
That is the view my department has arrived at, and that will be made a sina qua non of any action the department will take.
Has your department power to do that without the consent of parliament?

I think not. Parliament will have to consent to the matter in the end, and my recollection is that some time ago, in answer to a question put by the hon. member (Mr. Hughes) the Prime Minister stated that before the plans were approved of, the whole matter would be submitted to parliament for consideration, and before definite action would be taken, parliament must be satisfied that the work will be in the interest of Canada.

Were these plans which were submitted by the St. Lawrence Power Company to your department for approval, plans for the construction of a work to connect with another work that would come out from the American shore?

Yes, the plans were for damming the river across from the Canadian side to the American side, and also for the building of a lock for the purpose of improving navigation, the idea being to give an additional lock to the one that is already there, and which was constructed, and- is owned by the Canadian government.
Does the plan provide for a lock on the American side?
Yes, and that is strongly objected to by the engineers of the department. They urge that the lock should be built on the Canadian side.
Were those plans not submitted to the Waterways Commission?
I understand they were.
But the people who appeared before that commission had not access to them.

When these gentlemen came before the government they were told to go before the commission, and submit their plans with the view of all parties being notified so that they should have an opportunity of seeing the plans. Then, after the commission had decided the matter, it would be further taken up, and considered by the government.
Is the hon. minister' aware that the Waterways Commission absolutely refused to consider the details of the matter at all?

Such information has not come to me and I am not aware of it having come to any other member of the government, or any other department. With regard to the compensation to be paid, I, as Minister of Public Works, have been called on to consider the matter with the view of determining what would be fair to Canada in case we should finally approve of these works; and I am prepared to say that, so far as my department is concerned-and it will have a good deal to do with the fixing of rates-it will recommend to council that no agreement be entered into and no approval be given the works of the company unless there goes into the treasury of "Canada as much revenue from this power as will go into the treasury of the state of New York. I shall insist that Canada shall be treated on an equal footing with the United States; and although our information is that at the point where it is proposed to build this dam, about ninety per cent of the water is on the American side, yet I shall insist, if we take any action in the matter at all-and 1 do not say that we shall-that at least one-half of the power shall be absolutely reserved for use on the Canadian side, and the revenue we shall receive shall be reasonable, and not be less than that received by the state of New York under the Bill to which my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) has referred.
Are the works under the Act of 1901?

I do not think so. The plans are submitted for approval by the company which was incorporated under the statute of 1901. But I understand that before the company will be allowed to proceed any further, it will require to have the consent of this House, and must come to parliament for further legislation. That was the assurance which the right hon. the Prime Minister gave the House in answer to my hon. friend from Victoria and Hafiburton (Mr. Hughes).
Why should the hon. minister expect that the money derived from this source should go to the Dominion treasury, and not to the local government? In New York it goes to the state government.

There is a great difference between the jurisdiction of the state of New York over rivers, and that of a Dominion province. The state of New York has jurisdiction over, not only the soil, but the waters, and rivers within its territory, whereas a province of Canada has no jurisdiction over navigable waters.
What jurisdiction has New York over its waters?
Congress has no jurisdiction.
But I understand that application was made to Congress by the state of New York for legislation in that connection.

I believe there has been legislation by Congress to remove any doubts, but at all events the state of New York has power to grant a charter while, in my judgment, a provincial legislature has not. For that reason I would say that the treasury of Canada is entitled to receive the revenue from this water-power, the sole jurisdiction to deal with which is vested in the Dominion parliament.
Will my hon. friend say that the soil of a river is vested in the Crown in the right of Canada.

That is a point on which I do not care to express an opinion, nor [DOT] do I think would my hon. friend. I do not think the question is settled as to where the ownership of the soil in navigable water rests. It may belong to the riparian owner, and in this case the riparian owners, I understand, are the St. Lawrence Power Company, for that company has acquired the land where these works are to be situated. That would be the law in my province. There the property in the soil, above the ebb and flow of the tide rests in the riparian owners.

I have not examined the question at all, and would not care to pronounce an opinion, but I understood the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Robert Smith) to say it had been settled by a decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
Mr. Stanton on behalf of the Ontario government so argued.
I am not aware of any such decision. If the land had not been granted, undoubtedly it would rest in the provincial government. That was the case at Niagara Falls.
Does my hon. friend mean the land bordering the river or covered with water?

The land covered with water. In the case of the company which developed the power at Niagara Falls, my hon. friend will remember that the Niagara Park Commission are the riparian owners, and as such they gave a lease to a company which developed the water-power. That company leased the power to the HydroElectric Commission. But that is not the case at Long Sault. The land there has Mr. PUGSLEY.
all been granted by the Ontario government, and I understand that a large portion, if not the whole of it, has been acquired by the St. Lawrence Power Company.
A great deal would depend on the terms of the grant. It might be made so as to convey the land as far as the middle line of the stream, or it might be made otherwise.
I am speaking of a grant in the ordinary terms.

Has the minister considered what would be the effect which a dam across the St. Lawrence would have on the Ashburton treaty, or whether the two governments combined have authority to close the navigation of that river?
The contention is that the navigation is not to be closed, but improved.
There can be no question that Great Britain would have to be a consenting party to any legislation providing for the building of a dam.

It might be that Great Britain should be a consenting party. At nil events, there is no question that it could be done; it is a matter of detail. So far as the project itself is concerned, apart from the Bill before the House, I do not hesitate to say, speaking my own individual opinion, that, in view of the fact that an enormous water-pawer is there undeveloped, which, with development, could produce some 600,000 horse-power, the question is not one to be turned lightly aside. If that water-power can be developed at reasonable cost so that the people of Ontario can be furnished with cheap power for industrial and lighting purposes, and if navigation will not be injuriously affected, I think that the question is one that is well worthy the consideration of every one who has to do with legislation. Therefore, I am disposed to give the matter my most earnest consideration. I am disposed to look into the plans with great care. And, at the same time, as I have said, so far as I am concerned, I shall consent to no approval of the plans, to no agreement being made, to no development going on, unless there is absolutely and irrevocably secured to Canada half the developed water-power and also equal remuneration, so far as the rates are concerned, for the treasury of Canada as for the treasury of New York.

I would like to ask the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugs-ley). Why the necessity of this legislation until these questions are determined? This company have come before this-government already, as I understand it, and have been referred to the Waterways Commission for suggestions. It is quite apparent that the

only way that they hope to acquire power to be distributed is by means of the proposed damming of the St. Lawrence and the carrying out of this scheme. Until this is determined by both governments, why the haste to grant this legislation? Why this leap in the dark?

I will answer as best I can. I do not know what is in the minds of the promoters of the Bill, but it does not occur to me that the Bill provides for great haste, because it is only to come into force on a day to be fixed by proclamation of the Governor in Council, and the Governor in Council will not issue that proclamation until the agreements are entered into, plans are fully considered, and it is understood that the works can be constructed in the public interest and without injury to navigation,-and, I would assume,-they would not issue the proclamation until these agreements were submitted and ratified by parliament.

The minister has frankly admitted that this Bill is really part of a larger scheme. There cannot be any doubt of that after the frank statement of the minister. It seems to me it might have been fairer to parliament and to the people, if some of these details could have been set before us

If the hon. member will pardon me: I saw it stated somewhere, that the chairman of the Conservation Commission had written a letter to the committee m which he pointed out this very fact, that they were undoubtedly connected together, referring to the fact of the incorporators being the same,-and at his suggestion all the objectionable features were struck out.
Not all.

I think so. I think the Bill is as harmless as any legislation you can have. And, in any case, it is not to become law until it is approved by the Governor in Council.
Mr.^ R. L. BORDEN. The Bill is harmless if the larger project of which it is part is harmless. I would ask the minister, if he has any objection to bringing down the plans which are under consideration. As the minister has referred to them in debate, we have the right to ask for them. But I do not put it so much on that ground as on the ground of public interest, that these plans, which have evidently been under consideration for a long time, should be disclosed to parliament in order that we may know exactly what the promoters of this scheme have in contemplation, and what the government is now considering Would there be any objection?

I think not. Of course, they are not completed. They are not in
the possession of the government at present, because they were referred to the Waterways Commission. I see no objection to producing them; I think it quite reasonable and fair and would be glad they should be produced. At the same time, I do not withdraw the statement I made, that they are not essential to the consideration of this Bill.

That depends on whether this Bill is really a part of a larger scheme. The minister stated his opinion-and he knows more about the matter than any other hon. member-that the promoters of this Bill expect, under the provisions of this measure, to get their power from a certain source. The Bill will be useless until the larger project is carried out. So there cannot be any great haste about this Bill, as my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) has observed. Speaking of the necessity of providing power for eastern Ontario, I have not heard of any great outcry from the people of that section for a further supply of power. I have been informed by hon. members from the very locality in question that there is a considerable amount of power that cannot find a market.

Will the hon. member (Mr. R. L. Borden) permit me to interrupt. I have been told by an authority which I cannot ignore and which I fully believe, that more than one important industry has moved from eastern Ontario to western Ontario just in order to get close to electrical power. The people in the vicinity of Brockville are very much in earnest over this. They feel that that section of the country is suffering by reason of the western development from the benefits of which they are excluded.

There is a power developed at Iroquois, on which 500 horse-power is already available, with 2,000 more to be developed. The representative of that concern has been running around Prescott and Brockville for three months and offering them power at very reasonable rates
What is 500 horse-power?
He is able to offer 2,500.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: How are they going to get it to Brockville?

How is this company
going to get from Cornwall to Brockville?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Over the transmission line.

They can do it in the same way. It is 35 miles nearer. And, when we come down to that, the power right here in the vicinity of Ottawa is as near Brockville as the Cornwall power. There is no such terrible sweat over this matter. The Minister of Public Works

(Mr. Pugsley) saw fit to make the question of power paramount in this matter. I have always thought that the great navigation system of the St. Lawrence was paramount to the water-power. There is another fact that ought to stare every Canadian in the face: not a solitary American interest will suffer; every interest that runs the risk of injury is a Canadian interest, they have everything- to gain and we have everything to lose. Nobody knows what effect a dam at the Long Sault- will have upon the river above that point. The outlet of Lake Superior, for instance, is 600 feet higher than the level, say, at Quebec, and you are proposing to dam that river about half way down. The people living along the vicinity of that river have a right to be apprehensive as to the effect of that dam. Engineers have been known to make great mistakes before, in the Quebec bridge for instance, and the mistake they made even at Massena in putting in that enormous power. We are supposed to he governed by these scientific engineers, while the man of common sense is left out of the question altogether. These are questions that should not be dealt with in this flippant way by hon. gentlemen from New Brunswick and other places, who do not care a straw whether we are drowned out in Ontario or not. So far as I am concerned, local interests demand my attention, and as a representative of that section of that country 1 shall not neglect my duty.
Has the Minister of Public Works submitted to the Justice Department the question as to whether this government has any control over navigable waters except for purposes of-navigation?

I do not think it needs one lawyer to submit to another lawyer the question whether this government has not sole jurisdiction to prevent any obstruction in a navigable river, whether by a dam or any other method. That rests entirely with this parliament, under the British North America Act.
Has the hon. gentleman considered the effect of the treaty governing the navigation on this river?

Yes, I have considered that. We recognize that this parliament could not pass any legislation which would authorize a dam to be constructed in a river without putting in a condition that it shall be subject to the approval of the executive government of the United States.

I want to emphasize the position taken by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain), and to show the hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) that he is mistaken in what he says with regard to the law of the state of New York.

There is in the state of New York a commission which governs the rates and all charters on transmission lines. _Let him look at the Consolidated Laws of New York for 1909, volume 4, and he will find on page 3395 these words:

That law was only passed last year. It does not affect this Bill.
