Question, question.

Now that promotion stuff had not better show7 itself too soon tonight. The Minister of Public Works has

stated that there are 500,000 or 600,000 horse-power to be developed at the Sault dam. He has given the whole case away. It seems this matter has been under the consideration of the department for a long time, the scheme has been held up his coat sleeve, it has been engineered by gentlemen interested in it, and these little acces-t series to the St. Lawrence dam are going to be slipped through, and later on we will be asked to confirm the construction of the dam on the pretense of this 600,000 horsepower that are going to be developed. Why, Sir, within 30 miles of the city of Ottawa there is not 600,000 horse-power lying undeveloped, but 3,000,000 horse-power available and undeveloped, and this is accessible to all those towns like Brockville and Prescott, over which the Minister of Public Works has been moaning, just as accessible to them as is the water-power from the town of Cornwall. Moreover, in the construction of the Georgian Bay canal there will be another 3,000,000 horse-power developed within short range of these very places on the St. Lawrence river. The minister, being so well informed, is possibly aware of the fact that gentlemen connected with this water-power have already been canvassing cities and towns in the state of New York and disposing of hundreds of thousands of horse-power to be derived from the construction of the dam which they have assured the people in the United States is already arranged for with the government of Canada. Might I ask the minister if he has given any guarantee to these people that the Bill will be passed?
There has been no guarantee of any kind given, the matter is simply under consideration. No decision has been arrived at, and no assurance of any kind has been given.

They have had the minister's word at one time, for he has assured them that they must give at least one-half the power to Canada.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. If anything is done.

There is another important point. The shore on the north side of the St. Lawrence river is low ; the shore on the south side is comparatively high. Under past conditions spring freshets have again and again done a great deal of damage to the immediate shores on the north side of the St. Lawrence river. If this enormous dam is constructed, raising the water to a very great height, when the spring freshets and the ice jam come along, still further damming the waters up, they may possibly overflow the whole shore of the St. Lawrence. The height of land between the St. Lawrence and the Ottawa is just a few miles from the St. Lawrence. Therefore, it is easily within the bounds of possibility that if this dam were constructed the whole eastern part of the province would be flooded by the jamming of the ice at the dam. But to my mind there is a. more important element than the mere mercenary aspect of the case. The old historic river St. Lawrence is there, and we want the free navigation of that river. We do not want to go through any lock on the American side. We prefer to have it the same as it is at Sault Ste. Marie, and also the same as it is between Lakes Erie and Ontario. We want to go through canals on our own side and control them, we want free canals and the free navigation of the river, so that the products of our country may reach the ocean untrammelled by any dam. I would certainly recommend that this Bill be held over until the whole matter could be carefully looked info. I am satisfied that the minister will make as much progress with it as if he were to try to rush it through at the present time. I very much regret to see the anxiety displayed by a number of gentlemen who have no interest in the question, have never seen the river St. Lawrence or the rapids, and probably never will, to push this Bill through, though it concerns a work in which they can have no possible interest excepting an acquired interest.

I think we can fairly state that this Bill came before this committee, if indeed it did not come before the House on its introduction, under false, nretenses. It occurs to me that every fear I have expressed in regard to this Bill has been confirmed. I venture to say that the St. Lawrence Power Company's Bill of 1901 passed through parliament without ever a thought being given to the possibility that it contained powers that would enable the company to dam the St. Lawrence river in connection with any other company that might be incorporated under an American charter. I will go farther and say that the very promoters of that Bill in 1901 had no thought of the greater scheme which they evidently now have, or which somebody for them has, in contemplation. Apparently these gentlemen have come to-the Department of Public Works and have asked for the approval of a plan. They surely would not go to the expense of procuring the necessary data to enable them to prepare the plans in the first place- even only to prepare them-without they thought that they had the power and authority from parliament to erect the works which are set forth in these plans. It must be apparent to every member of this committee that these applicants were and are under the impression that they were authorized by their own legislation to construct their dam on the St. Lawrence to the American boundary. Else why would

they prepare plans? They must, on laying their plans before the Minister of Public Works, have placed before him the authority under which they came. No man goes to the Minister of Railways and Canals seeking the approval of a route map unless he takes with him the act of this parliament authorizing the construction of the railway to be built on that route. I venture to assert that there would be no one so foolish as to go to the Minister of Public Works and ask him to approve of a plan unless he showed the minister the authority under which he wished to construct the works in accordance with those plans. Evidently they thought they had the power or the authority from this parliament. How many people in Canada thought they had it? We have read the discussions in the public newspapers in reference to this matter, we have read of the hearings that were had before the Waterways Commission; how many readers of these newspapers but were under the impression that this was preliminary to the applicants coming to parliament to seek legislation and to seek powers? No one ever dreamed that these people had these powers or thought they had the powers. It has been mentioned even by members of parliament that such a Bill would be before parliament. Evidently the applicants have no such idea, evidently they think that they have the whole matter arranged and that all they now need is the approval of plans. What is the use of submitting it to the Waterways Commission when the suggestion is made that these gentlemen have that power as far as this parliament is concerned? It has been repeatedly stated that this Bill does not authorize them to build dams. Certainly it does not. They do not seek to get such powers. Any objection which I have taken to this Bill has not been on any such ground, but it is for this reason I have stated that they had hoped to build this dam under the authority of the Act of 1901, when it was never contemplated by parliament that any such works should be so constructed, and when it is necessary that these people, who wish to work out this scheme, shall get supplementary powers, we should withhold such supplementary powers until we regulate in some way the legislation of 1901 with respect to the powers which they claim we gave them, -and which perhaps we did, to enable them to construct a dam on the St. Lawrence in conjunction with American legislation. That is the objection I have to the enactment of this legislation. The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) has asked, and very properly asked: Is there anv objection to having the plans laid before this committee before this legislation proceeds? I think that is a fair request and Mr. EMMERSON.
I think that the Minister of Public Works should accede to it because it is a fair proposition. What does this legislation mean? How many of us know? I do not. How many hon. members know what it does contemplate? It evidently means the transmission of power in connection with some scheme that is to be carried out under legislation already had from this parliament, and that legislation warranted the promoters in preparing plans for the carrying out of this scheme. What are those plans? It would give us and the country an insight into the objects and proposals of these applicants and would be only fair that every member of this committee should have the plans before him to see just what thev have in mind, what they propose and desire to carry out and what they wish us to give this legislation for now in order to enable them to carry it out to its full completion, because the generation of power without the ability to distribute and utilize it would be of no advantage to them. I would suggest that the committee should rise and before we further consider the matter the plans should be before us. It is an important matter. No Bill of a private nature more far reaching in its consequence has been brought to the notice of a committee of parliament for many vears. It affects not only our internal affairs, our provincial affairs, but it affects our international relations under a treaty of the empire. I submit that we should not be called on at this time to decide yea or nay with respect to this Bill, .we should first have an opportunity of viewing the plans.
I would suggest to the Minister of Finance that the committee ought to rise at this stage.

I would yield at once to the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Emmerson) if it were not for the fact that this Bill gives no authority whatever to construct any works on the St. Lawrence river, and for the further reason that the Prime Minister has made the statement to this House that before any authority is given to construct any dam in the St. Lawrence, the matter shall first be submitted to and approved of by this parliament. Nothing could be fairer than that. No matter what the company thinks its powers are, there is a reserve power vested in the Governor in Council, and that will not be exercised and this company allowed to go ahead until the whole matter is submitted to parliament.

The very fact that the minister has mentioned ought to give us pause. It would seem that it is too big a question to leave in the hands of the

Governor in Council for submission to parliament.
I said it had to be submitted to parliament.

I cannot conceive that the Minister of Public Works and the government would send the engineers of three different departments to investigate and report on it unless they were inclined to concur in the view of the St. Lawrence Power Company that authority exists at the present time. It seem a remarkable state of affairs to exist if the minister's statement is to be accepted without qualification. Here is a company which on the premises laid down by the minister has no power to build a dam on the St. Lawrence, and yet we find this government on the application of this company which has no statutory powers sending engineers of three, departments to investigate. Does any one imagine that this would have been done unless there was something more in the supposed authority and power than the minister has disclosed to usp Why should the minister, at the instance of people who, according to his statement, have absolutely no power to do anything of the kind, have caused to be sent the engineers of three departments to investigate and report on these plans?
Why is it left to the Waterways Commission?

Yes. There seems to be a great deal more at the back of this than any one suspected. I am astonished to learn that this project has gone so far without anything being known to parliament. It is not of such trivial importance as the minister suggests. At the present time a vessel can go from the ocean into the great lakes, and never leave Canadian waters. 'Under the proposals of the government nothing of the kind can take place because, as I said, the Minister-
The same lock will exist on the Canadian side, all vessels going up through the river pass through that lock.
I understood from the scheme as disclosed to me by the minister that the lock would be on the American side.
There will be two locks, one on the American side.

If I am not correct in my appreciation of what the minister said, I withdraw any argument on that point, but apart from that it is a very big proposal and one which concerns the commerce of this country from end to end, concerns every part of Canada, concerns the future interests of this country in several very important respects. Inasmuch as this Bill is not to go into force until pro-171
claimed by order in council, inasmuch as the minister himself has said that, according to his understanding, this company is to get its power from this source, why is there such tremendous haste to press this Bill? There seems to be no occasion for haste in any of the circumstances disclosed. I concur in the suggestion of my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Emmer-son) that the plans should be laid on the table of the House before this Bill which is only part of a greater project should be submitted to this committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In answer to the suggestion of the leader of the opposition, I am not aware that the government have made any proposals at all. This is a private Bill, and I have no desire to have it treated differently from any other private Bill. I have not followed the matter as closely as some hon. gentlemen. I am very much impressed by the fact that this Bill was examined by the Committee on Private Bills, that objection was taken, it was referred to the Conservation Commission, amendments were proposed and the committee, as I understand, unanimously reported the Bill.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was so (stated in the House. At all events, the committee reported the Bill. There are occasions when members of the House who have given close personal attention to a matter feel free to go outside of the report of the committee, but the general trend of the House is that where a Bill is investigated and examined by a committee and reported, the judgment of the committee should be sustained. Speaking for myself, I see no objection to it going through. It is a private Bill, we have adopted it, and whatever the sense of the House may be, we may as well take it.

The Minister of Public Works has announced that when this Bill is passed the government will have all the powers that are needed to enable this company to dam the St. Lawrence, and that all this company will have to do would be to submit the plans to the Department of Public Works and have them approved. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) told us there was no connection between the promoters of this Bill and the parties incorporated in the Bill in 1901 and he further said that the Act of 1901 was void. He told us also that the company incorporated in 1901 never developed power, and in that statement he was corrected by the hon. member for Stormont. But the Minister of Public Works let the feline out of the sack when he told us that this company far from being defunct had actually prepared plans and laid them before his department for approval, under, I presume, the navigable waters Act.
Not at all.

At any rate the plans were before the minister and the minister has been considering them, and apparently they are awaiting the approval of the^ government and the passage of this Bill. The Minister of Public Works has also stated that he would give authority to this company rather than to the province, because he says the province has no power to construct a dam to the boundary of the United States. But surely this parliament can invest the province with exactly the same powers that it may invest a private corporation with, and in view of the fact that the province is developing power at cost to supply the people cheaply, surely, if the minister were actuated by the proper spirit he would empower the province rather than a private corporation whose object is to make a profit. The Minister of Public Works also said that he would take the revenues to the Dominion rather than to the province, because as he understands it the ownership of the bed of the stream is in the Dominion.
I did not say so; I said it was because the jurisdiction over these water-powers rests entirely with the Dominion parliament.
I understood the minister to say that the ownership of the foreshore, down to the water at least, did not rest with the province.
If the land was granted I did not think it did.

If I remember right in Caldwell vs. Hurdman it was held that the province had the right to grant these water lots on the bed and foreshore of the Ottawa river which was a navigable stream. If in that case the title rested with the province it would seem to raise some question as to whether or not the title to the bed and foreshore of the St. Lawrence is not in the province of Ontario. It seems to me that this House instead of guessing at what .its rights are should defer discussion on the Bill until they are ascertained. Surely the Minister of Public Works is willing to give to the province a power which it is exercising in the public interest, surely he would prefer to give that power to the province rather than to a private corporation, surely the House would hesitate before it dams up and- annihilates a portion of an international waterway established such by solemn treaty between two nations; surely the government will not attempt to rush through this legislation without considering all these questions. If that be the case, the Canadian locks will no longer serve the purposes of t-ransnortation and we will be driven to using these locks built on the American side, the title to which is to be vested in the State of New York Mr. COWAN.
When the discussion began, I saw no particular reason why I should oppose the Bill, but I think abundant reasons have been developed in the course of the discussion, and no interest will suffer if the matter is allowed to remain until opportunity be given to examine the plans and to ascertain the status and rights of all par-ties.

I understood from the Minister of Public Works a few minutes ago that, when he was negotiating with the promoters of this scheme-the original company chartered in 1901-he declared that in case any arrangement should be agreed to, the Dominion treasury would receive as much as the state of New York. What I want to ask him is what provision lie has made to protect the citizens of this country. Would this company come under the Board of Railway Commissioners which would regulate the prices the Canadian public would have to pay?

The company waited upon me through its representative, was the company called the St. Lawrence Power Company, incorporated by the state of New York. They were desirous of getting the requisite authority from the Canadian government and parliament to carry out their scheme. I stated to them-and they seemed disposed to acquiesce in the view-that, so far as my department was concerned, we should insist that the power should be equally divided or rather that at least one-half should be absolutely reserved for use on the Canadian side, and also that we should receive the same revenue as that derived by the stale of New York, and in addition that the rates should be under the control of the Board of the Railway Commission, so that both the public interest would be protected, and we would get our share of the revenue.

That is information which the hon. gentleman did not give us before. A moment ago when a question was put to him about the navigation of the river, he said that the locks were there, and the boats could go up as they do now. But in case this dam is built, and1 built at the head of the locks, and the water raised fifteen or twenty feet, how are the boats going to get up the Canadian side?
My hon. friend is misinformed. The plan submitted by the engineers show no such state of affairs. They refused to approve any plans which would interfere with the Canadian locks.
I know the canal and the locks, and all aDout it. If you build a dam to raise the water

Whatever parliament will be asked to do-if the matter ever goes that far-the plans will all be submitted

for the information of the House. I would have no objection to submitting them at any time; but before parliament will be asked to take steps, the plans will be laid on the table.

We are asked to make a very important step now, and we ought to see the plans. It is now half past one in the morning, and in view of the fact that this Bill was before the Private Bills Committee and that committee made a report by no means unanimous, several amendments having been submitted, and only voted down by a majority of two or three

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Was there a minority report?

No, but the minority did not approve of the committee's action, and the majority was a very slight one. As the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) says., we have had a great deal of new light since the Private Bills Committee made its report. No one knew in that committee that this company was part of the parent company of 1901, which was given the power of damming the river. That was never mentioned then.
I am told it was mentioned and mentioned several times, in addition to having a letter from the chairman to that effect.
It was not admitted by the Minister of Public Works as he has admitted it to-night. Nobody knew that he had sent his engineers to look the ground over.
There would have been a bigger majority if that had been known.

My hon. friend knows better. The hon. member for Westmorland has expressed a different opinion. He admits that he has been enlightened by the information we have had from the Minister of Public Works, and so has every other hon. member. I certainly think that the Bill should stand over, and the opinion of the Minister of Justice be taken on the matter. Before we pass this legislation, which will enable the company to proceed under the Act passed in 1901, giving it full powers to go on, and build dams and wings and locks and anything it likes, we should hesitate, and take time for reflection.

A little while ago the Minister of Public Works referred to a promise made by the Prime Minister. I have been endeavouring to find out what that promise is, but have not succeeded, and in view of the fact that this is rather an important Bill, I think the government should not press it through committee tonight. Since the Act of 1901 gives the corn-171*
pany power to build that dam, has not the Prime Minister's promise been violated, that the company could do nothing farther without coming to parliament?

My hon. friend surely is not serious in putting that question? What the right hon. the Prime Minister said was that the matter would be laid before parliament, and parliament be asked to give its opinion upon it, but that referred to future action.
But the company already has the authority, and does not need to go to parliament. It is independent of the Prime Minister.
No, because it cannot anything until it gets its plans approved, and my right hon. colleague said that it could not get permission to go ahead until its application had been submitted to parliament.

The hon. the Minister of Finance referred to the fact that this Bill had received the sanction of the Committee on Private Bills. Is he aware that developments have taken place here to-night which he did not hear of before?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was not before the Committee on Private Bills, and so did not hear anything.
Will the Minister of Public Works say that facts have not been developed to-night that were never heard before the Private Bills Committee?
I am not able to admit that because, from the statements made, I would conclude that the Private Bills Committee was informed of everything material.
Will my hon. friend not admit that he himself has made statements to-night which for the first time have been made to the country?

I do not think so, because this matter has been in the press for months. A good many months ago it was reported that the engineers had considered the matter and had made a report; that that report had been referred back to them and they had made a new report which had gone to the Waterway Commission.
The minister has kept tab on the press.
I always read the papers.
Was there any system by which all this was done and yet the House and the country kept in the dark? Will the minister tell me what is to be the height of this dam?

Believing, as I did, that that had nothing to do with the Bill before

the House, I have not the information with me.

The minister remembers so clearly what is in the newspapers, I should think he could remember a little item like that. Has he any report of the effect the raising of this water by the dam is likely to have on the Canadian shore and upon the Canadian locks?
Question.
Hon. members opposite can earn their money easier than this.
My view is that the hon. member (Mr. Hughes) is not acting in a manner worthy of himself and his standing in this House in making the vile insinuation with regard to gentlemen on this side-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member should not use the expression 'vile insinuation.'

I will not argue, Mr. Chairman, but at once withdraw the expression. But I think, on reflection, my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes), even though the hour is late and he is perhaps unconscious of what he says, when he realizes the extraordinary nature of the insinuation he has made, will withdraw it.

If the minister will pay attention to the gentlemen behind Iiim, many of them from other provinces and who never saw the St. Lawrence rapids, and will try to keep them in order, I shall be glad. But I deny his right to lecture me in this House. I was asking, when I was interrupted by the unseemly conduct of gentlemen behind the minister

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman should not use that expression.
I will retract that, if you s&5
No conditions.

I will withdraw it unconditionally. The conduct struck me as unseemly, but I will not use the expression. New, will the minister tell me the effect of tins dam on the Canadian shore between Cornwall and the Galops rapids?
I regret that I cannot give the information. These matters will be very carefully considered before the government takes action.

I am surprised the minister wants to leave this question to be decided by his engineers. If we consider how the engineers, not only in his, but in other departments, have given decisions for some little time, I think it will be safer to leave the matter in the hands of hon. members of this House. In his own department, we have seen an engineer put an upset price of 20 cents a yard on dredging and that dredging afterwards said to be done at a reasonable price at 90 cents a yard. And we have investigations going on in the Public Accounts Committee in regard to the decisions of engineers on the Transcontinental, and the people have_ no great confidence so far as their workings are concerned. Now, here is a great work which the government is going to grant power to undertake-for, I take it ^ from what the minister has stated, that it is the intention of the government to grant this franchise to dam the St. Lawrence river.
I have not given any intimation of that kind. The government has not decided the matter.

They could not get through first a Bill giving power _ to dam the St. Lawrence. That Bill will come after. The hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) tells us that this company had practically deceived us in bringing the matter before the committee. Let me tell the minister what the company did do. The promoters of this Bill went into every town, beginning at Prescott, and told the people they could not give them power unless the dam was put across the St. Lawrence. They took people down to Cornwall, paying all their expenses and entertained them. They have men employed in every town from Cornwall to Brockville to promote this scheme. They have newspapers subsidized throughout the Dominion to influence the public in favour of this work. I have heard on good authority that they have placed $2,000,000 simply to pay out for this great scheme. And let me tell the minister that the company behind this scheme is greater than all the railways and the Standard Oil Company put together. Here is an article in a magazine that explains what this trust is. I will read a little of it-
Read it all.

Well, perhaps I will. I think it will be interesting to gentlemen on the other side. For I have confidence in hon. members opposite that, if they knew what this scheme was, they would not go into it so lightly. I believe they want to know the facts and to do what is fair. There are many members opposite who do not know anything about this matter. But we who live along the St. Lawrence river know the conditions, and vre want the com-

mittee to treat us justly. Let me read part of a magazine article that will be interesting. It is headed: 'A gigantic new trust in sight ':	.
It is found in the great water-powers of the country. And those are to-day well on the way to control by a trust bigger than any that has ever been dreamed of; a trust that, if it shall be able to carry out the systematic plan now in. hand will be as wealthy as if it owned all the railroads of the nation, with standard oil and United States steel on top. Then a few score of the minor trusts tossed in for good measure.
This is the water-power trust. Its existence was first suspected by government officials five years ago. Since then it has been gathering in the best power sights in every part of the country. It has subsidiaries that operate in Canada. It has grown to such proportions, and its purpose to monopolize the water-power of a continent that has become so plainly apparent, that President Roosevelt thus referred to it not long ago in his veto of the James River Dam Bill:
The people of the country are threatened by a monopoly far more powerful because in far closer touch with their domestic and industrial life, than anything known to our experience. A single generation will see the exhaustion of our natural resources of oil and gas and such a rise in the price of coal as will make the prices of electrically transmitted water-power a controlling factor in transportation, in manufacturing, and in household lighting and heating.
President Roosevelt told congress that thirteen corporations or interests, centering in the General Electric and the Westinghouse Electric, now controlled one-third of the developed water-power of the country, and added:
This astonishing consolidation has taken place practically within the last five years. The movement is still in its infancy, and unless it is controlled the history of the oil industry will be repeated in the hydro-electrio power industry, with results far more oppressive and disastrous to the people. It is true that the great bulk of our potential waterpower is as yet undeveloped, but the sites which are now controlled by combinations are those which offer the greatest advantages and therefore hold a strategic position.
That message said President Roosevelt, a few days after it had been delivered, was one of the most important in my whole administration. This proposal, now far under way to accomplishment, of monopolizing the nations water-power, has a significance which ought to be made clear to the people.
Up at the top of this scheme stand the General Electric Company, with $65,000,000 capital and $15,000,000 funded debt, and the Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Company with $28,000,000 stock and $29,000,000 funded debt. The General Electric owns all the shares of the Edison and Thompson-TTous-ton Company and the British Thompsor-Hous-ton; the Sprague Electric Company, the Stanley Electric Manufacturing Company, and the Electric Bond and Share Company are controlled; and the company is identified in various ways with many other corporations.
Relations between the General Electric and Westinghouse are indicated by the fact that since 1896 their patents have been pooled. The Westinghouse Company controls the stock of British, Canadian and French Westinghouse Companies, both General Electric and Westinghouse interests appear in the officiary or directorates of the numerous corporations that are broadly denominated as related to the water-power trust. The investigations by the government have caused the following companies to he classified as of general electric affiliation:	,
United Electric Securities, _ Electrical Securities Corporation, Electric Bond and Share Company, Schenectady Power Company, Caroline Power and Light Company, Rockingham (North Carolina) Power Company, Animas Power and Water Company (Colorado), Central Colorado Power Company, Montgomery (Alabama) Light and Water Power Company, Summit County Power Company (Colorado), Butte Electric and Power Company (Montana), Montana Power Transmission Company, Madison River Power Company (Montana), Billings and Eastern Montana Power Company, Washington Water Power Company (Washington and Idaho), Great Western Power Company (California); besides a number of others whose connection with general electric is indicated. _
The Westinghouse group, as classified by the government investigators, includes the Security Investment Company (New York), The Electric Properties Company (New York), the ' Smith interests/ the Atlantic Water and Electric Power Company, Ontario Power Company (Canadian), Niagara, Book port and Ontario Power Company (New York), Electric Power Securities Company (New York).
There are a great many more that I will not read. Also the power at Massena on the American side is owned by this same combination. The Minister of Public Works, if he will tell what he knows, will stand up here and tell us that the St. Lawrence Power Company is in this same power trust.
I do not know anything of the kind.

Well, he can find out if he inquires. Let us go into the history of this St. Lawrence Power Company. Four or five years ago this company could have been taken over by the government for about $300,000. In a report in the Department of Railways and Canals, he will find that the question came up as to the lighting of the Cornwall canal. And by the way, that has been referred to as a contract given by the Conservative party and which his government has to carry out. Let me tell the minister about that contract. That contract was given in .Tune, 1896, just before the Conservative party went out of power.
What do you suppose it was given them for?

I have no idea what it was given for. The minister hints that

perhaps it was given for some wrong purpose. The minute the Liberal party came into power they cancelled several contracts on the canal that were given in June. There were contracts let a few days before the government went out of power for the building of canals which this government promptly cancelled. They did not cancel this contract but about four weeks before the next election an order in council was asked for by the then Minister of Railways and Canals providing that permission be given him to bring into force a contract to pay the St. Lawrence Power Company $50,000 yearly for lighting the Cornwall canal. After they had given the minister power to pay $50,000 a year, two or three weeks before the election, the contract was changed from 21 years to 84 years. Will the Minister of Public Works tell me whv that was done prior to the election of 10"U?
I reallv cannot,

Not exactly. He would have a better idea than I why these things were done because he has been a minister not only here, but in the New Brunswick government and similar things have taken place under his own administration.
I think my hon. friend is a past master.

No. I have not had the experience that the minister has. This combination on the other side want to- dam the St. Lawrence river. They knew that if they came to this parliament to get permission to do it they could not obtain it with the St. Lawrence poweT company in existence. M. P. Davis had his waterpower there. He would immediately raise the question that this was going to interfere with his rights, and the result as that this combination had to give M. P. Davis, some say $750,000 and others say $1,000,000, simply for this power that he had in order to get his franchise and thus prevent any opposition from that source. When the Railway Commission come to deal with this matter the owners of the St. Lawrence Power will say that they have been obliged to pay $1,000,000 for it, that they have their money invested in it, that they have to get a certain revenue and, therefore, the commission should fix a price on what it cost them to purchase the power from M. P. Davis. The result would be that the people of eastern Ontario would be subject to this great monopoly. As far as the transmission line is concerned, why did they not tell the people in Prescott and Brockville what they told the committee? They went to Prescott and Brockville and told the people that they had not any power to sell at Cornwall, that power must be developed Mr. J. D. REID.
and that it was absolutely necessary to dam the St. Lawrence. In the committee the other day they said that they had plenty of power now developed at Cornwall under the present franchise. Ever since that power has been developed at Cornwall we have wanted them to run a transmission line to Prescott and Bro-ck-ville, but they never would do so. M. P. Davis and others said there was not sufficient power required to pay for running the transmission line up there. They never thought it necessary to run a transmission line up there until this scheme of damming the St. Lawrence was brought to the front and they thought that such an agitation would take place amongst the people of the St. Lawrence counties that the members of this House would grant them the right to dam the river. On the other side of the river at Massena they have an immense water-power that they are using at the present time. The minister knows that locality well. There is what is called the South Sault on the American side. It could be dammed and not 'hurt navigation at all and then it would probably develop 200,000 or 300,000 horse-power. I think the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. R. Smith) knows where I mean.

I would not endorse the hon. gentleman's statement that you could develop 200,000 or 300,000 horsepower. It is estimated, I believe, that you could develop 65,000 horse-oower and that would be conditional upon the building of a wing dam.
Well it may be that you could only develop 65,000 horse-power at the South Sault.
That is if the big dam is continued across. It will be about 30,000 with a dam only at the South Sault.

Well, I do not know, but it would not hurt navigation at all. If this company are willing to take the power and bring it along the river front they have, according to their statement-in the Private Bills 'Committee, sufficient power at Cornwall at present to- supply all the river front and they have the power at Massena as well. But this whole thing is part of -a great scheme. According to the papers right here in Ottawa there is a company being formed. I have only read it in the newspapers, but I know from the gentlemen who are connected with it that it is true. Senator Edwards and a number of other gentlemen are organizing a company that will develop 500,000 horse-power along the Ottawa river. From Ottawa to Prescott it is 52 miles. From Prescott to Cornwall it is 60 miles.

Where are they to get
500,000	horse-power near Ottawa?

I saw a fair estimate and the statement gave the falls and so on. I asked Senator Edwards the other day if he intended doing it, and he said certainly, and that he expected in about a year to have this power supply ready.
I	suggested in the Private Bills Committee that the St. Lawrence Power Company are the ones who are going to furnish this power. They admitted in the Private Bills Committee that they were going to do it through the company at Cornwall, and I asked them why not bring in a Bill to amend clause li in their charter. Clause
II	gives them power to run a transmission line about 12 miles west and down to Soulanges. Why not bring in a Bill to have that amended so that they could extend their transmission line to Brockville and Kingston? But that would not answer their purpose. I wonder if the minister saw the first Bill. This Bill is not like the first one.
This Bill is perfectly harmless.

About as harmless as the minister. They would not do that, and that showed that there is a scheme behind it. The minister has let the cat out of the bag. I cannot understand why the minister wants to force this Bill through without giving the members an opportunity of seeing the plans.
The minister is not forcing the Bill through, he has nothing to do "with it except as a member of the committee.
The minister knows that if he asked to have the committee rise it would rise at once.
It is not for me to say if the committee shall rise or not.
I think the Minister of Finance should give us an opportunity of looking into this scheme, and should not try to press us too hard to-night.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not pressing the Bill one way or the other, but I would like to see some progress. There has been a very fair discussion, and my own judgment is that the House should divide. The Bill need not go to a third reading to-night, it could stand until another day, and there would be ample opportunity to discuss the matter further.
We should have an opportunity of looking at the plans and seeing the general position.
Has the hon. gentleman never seen the plans?
I never saw them.
They have been published in many newspapers in the last two years, and the promoters have explained them in the hon. gentleman's own town before the International Waterways Commission.

I have not seen the plans, and the promoters knew I was opposed to the scheme and I suppose would not show them to me. As- to the newspaper plans, no newspaper would publish the large plans that would come before the government.

If the plans were published in the newspapers it would ue under the authority of the Minister of Public Works. I am surprised they should be so published beiore being submitted to the House. In wnat newspapers were they published.
My hon. friend would like to find out also whether they were published in Conservative newspapers as well.
My hon. friend is very suspicious on a point on which he is very guilty.
I did not know they were published and I have not seen them in the newspapers. In connection with this Bill we have nothing to do with them as this is merely a transmission line.

Has the minister considered that the tourist passenger traffic going down the St. Lawrence will be interfered with, and also the large rafts of timber? Does he remember that the International Waterways Commission feared an ice jam if a dam were erected in Niagara river near Fort Erie, and would there not be a similar danger of damage to property on the St. Lawrence river if this dam were erected?	.
I did not introduce the Bill.
The minister is largely responsible for its introduction.

Not at all. If the question of approving of works in the St. Lawrence should come before me as minister I shall feel it my duty to give all these matters my most careful consideration. The Bill gives no power to dam the St. Lawrence, or to place any kind of obstruction in that river.

I suggested some time ago that the plans setting out this scheme should be laid before us before we are compelled to reach a decision on this Bill!. The Minister of Finance who is leading the House said he had no objection personally to that suggestion.
1 Mr. FIELDING. No.

It is a fair request and if the Bill is allowed to stand for the present no harm can be done. The Senate adjourns on Wednesday next until the 6th of April, and consequently there will he no delay in the final passage of the measure. It seems to me that too much of a party tinge has been given to this question. I did not consider it a party matter at all and before I knew the opinion of other members I formed my own judgment. I am honest and sincere in desiring to see these plans before the Bill is passed. 1 would go home, but I do not want to run away from my convictions. If the committee should now rise it would add to our good health and good humour.
We are all good humoured.
We are trying to be, hut we are not any more than we can help.

The procedure to-night is a repetition of the procedure before the Private Bills Committee. We considered it for a whole month there and there was a certain group of members who were bound to block the Bill, one member going so far as to say that he was there specially for that purpose. I have listened attentively to every speech delivered to-night and there has not been one single argument or idea advanced that was not advanced before the committee and fully considered. I can tell these hon. gentlemen that those of us who are in favour of the Bill will stay here until Saturday night if necessary.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Black) was elected to preside over the Private Bills Committee in the absence of the regular chairman and before the preamble had been fully discussed he insisted on taking the vote of the committee.
The preamble was not discussed until all the other clauses were discussed.

When the hon. gentleman could not get a vote on the preamble he said they would dispense with the passing of the preamble and discuss the clauses one by one. I do not know what the hon. gentleman's interest in the Bill is, but he displayed the same anxiety about it in the Private Bills Committee that he does here. There must be some overwhelming, compelling interest in this Bill; there seems to be some personal canvass and some personal interest in it, because we have here this morning five cabinet ministers and more members than there have been in the House for a long time.
What about your side?

We are protecting the public interest. No private Bill in my experience has received such favourable at-Mr. FIELDING.
tention at the hands of the government since the Canada Life Bill which was an attack on the rights of certain policy-holders. I would like to ask the Minister of Public Works when these plans were first submitted to him and how long he has had ' them ' under his consideration?
The first plans were submitted, I should think, nearly two years ago. Then there were amended plans which must have been submitted six months ago.
When were the engineers sent?
I should think eight or ten months ago.

That should excite the suspicion of the House more than ever. The fact that the Minister of Public Works has had the plans under consideration two years, that the engineers have reported some eight months ago, and that this House has not received any information concerning these plans or reports, is certainly very extraordinary. Surely it is important that we should have all that information which has been so long before the minister. Why not allow this matter to stand over until the House has been given possession of it? We have had the whole day taken up with this private Bill, when there are public Bills in the names of private members which are kept back on that account. The plans, which the minister has had so long, were never submitted to the Private Bills Committee. Surely that committee should have been put in possession of them before making its report. You cannot sever the two companies. The promoters are the same in each, and the names are almost identical. One of the great objections I have to the Bill is the large power of expropriation which it gives and then the Railway Act is made applicable to the company where-ever possible. In section 151 of that Act there are 17 subsections. Subsection C allows the company to expropriate any property whatever for its purposes. Subsection L allows it to divert or alter the course of any river, stream, or watercourse, or highway, for certain purposes. All these powers are given to this company under the terms of this Bill. Judging by the interest taken in it by the cabinet ministers, this measure has the endorsation of the government, and the government is determined to press it through at all hazards. But surely, in the public interest, it ought to be allowed to stand over and hon. members given an opportunity to inspect the plans.

I have no disposition to prevent discussion, and so long as any member has anything advantageous to

place before the House we should remain. I think, so far as I can understand the situation, this is a Bill for a transmission line only and although I am not familiar with the particular section of the country it covers, judging by our experience in the vicinity of the Niagara peninsula, the more transmission lines we have in operation the better for the community. Take the cities of Hamilton and Dundas, perhaps the only two towns in Canada where we have electric competition, they are the two that have the cheapest electric energy. And I am glad to say that they are the two chief localities sought after by manufacturing and other interests, as a location for their establishments. What is good for our locality ought to be good for others. We are all pleased with the introduction of hydro-electric power into our vicinity. It has created competition, and we have the benefit of that competition. The only objection that can be urged against the HydroElectric Commission is their method of obtaining right of way and the unfair prices they pay the farmers. I can see no reason why the company under discussion should not have a transmission line in the vicinity of the St. Lawrence river and the Hydro-Electric Commission as well. The two lines should give better results than one; and while the Hydro-Electric Commission do not propose to make any profit, but deliver the energy to the consumer at actual cost, there is a good deal of difference of opinion as to whether that is the cheapest method. In Hamilton, for instance, the Cataract Power Company offer freely to give power to the consumer at 10 per cent less than the lowest hydro-electric cost. A week ago Saturday I passed some construction work of the hydro-electric and I am satisfied that the footings they were putting in cost three times more than private corporations would pay or than it would have cost the hydroelectric had they done the work as they did some other work last year. All this extra expenditure on construction is added to the cost, and that no doubt accounts for private corporations being able to deliver power 10 per cent cheaper and still have a profit. But be that as it may, I think that competition is a splendid thing. Let us have the hydro-electric, and this transmission line, and a hundred others if possible As to the amount of revenue the government should get out of the St. Lawrence powers, if one half goes to Canada, that is perhaps all we are entitled to. But I do not think the government should pride themselves about getting a very large toll. I think that the amount of revenue would be better applied to the cheapening of power to the consumer through the Dominion Railway Commission. For these reasons, if this company is entirely on its own
account, as the Bill before the House shows*, and is a transmission line, it certainly cannot do any harm to give it opportunity to construct a transmission line and let the trials of strength be between their transmission lines rather than between the two sides of this House. If the HydroElectric Commission should have to come to this House for authority to build a line along side it, and in competition with it, I would be delighted to give them that privilege, and see the two companies and as many more as can be had, to build transmission lines and give competition and increased accommodation and energy, which would be for the advantage of this country and stimulate our industrial development.
I would urge upon the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), if the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) will permit him, to adjourn the House.
So early?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will the hon. member (Mr. Hughes) see if he can get the minister's (Mr. Pugsley) consent?
I know that the smile of the Minister of Finance is very influential, but when the Minister of Public Works frowns and curls his brow, even the Minister of Finance must sit up.
If the hon. member (Mr. Hughes) would do a little more work and a little less talk, he would get through.

But I have data here that, ' I am sure, will be of interest to the members of the House. Now, the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman), one of the quiet, modest, unassuming ministers, is possibly doing more to benefit this country than is the Minister of Public Works' (Mr. Pugsley). The Minister of Public Works we find connected with sawdust wharfs, electrical development, the damming of the St. Lawrence-everything where you find the promoter and the man behind the machine. But the Minister of Inland Revenue is quietly developing the peat industry. Water-power is not our only source of energy. It is true that, with'the power that can Be developed by the construction of the Georgian Bay canal, we shall have 6,000,000 horse-power capable of development.
Mr. PUGSLEY". Half an hour ago, it was 3,000,000.

I said 3,000,000 within thirty miles of the city. I really must repeat my statements, if the minister pays so little attention to them as he has evidently done to this one. I said 3,000,000 horse-power already available; 3,000,000 more through the construction of the Georgian Bay canal-and three and three are

six. I was about to point out that there are also thousands oi acres of peat in the eastern part of Ontario and in the adjoining province of Quebec. The Minister of Inland Revenue, with commendable honesty and energy, is assisting in the development of the peat industry. There is every hope that the time is near at hand when, with the producer gas from peat,, we shall be able to produce energy at one-half the cost of producing it by water-power. Why, then, this mad haste to dam the St. Lawrence? It must mot be forgotten also that other sources of energy are opening to us. Radium, which is now being produced on a commercial scale, opens wonderful. possibilities for the future. Scientific journals of this week tell us that a pinch of radium, such as will lie on the thumbnail, will drive a 15,000-ton ship at fifteen knots an hour for 6,000 miles continuously. But science is still advancing, and another material, .called, I believe, polonium, has been discovered which is one thousand times more powerful than is radium. WTith all these opportunities opening before us, why destroy the navigation of the St. Lawrence for the sake of a power scheme? Why court international complications with the United States in this project of damming the St. Lawrence?
Reference has been made to this Bill when it was before the Committee on Private Bills. I have distinct recollection, when in the Railway Committee, of seeing gentlemen rush into that committee and hustle the fellows out to the Private Bills Committee, and there, without having the slightest knowledge of what they were voting on, they would put through a Bill or vote down a motion for amendment. That was what at first excited the suspicion of members of this House-the fact that these gentlemen, led by some of the ministers, who threw their whole soul into iU-the Minister of Public Works or, if not he, the horny-handed son of toil, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) who would be looking after it, voted in this way. I say this first excited the suspicion of honest men. It appears from this discussion tonight that the Minister of Public Works has had this matter of damming the St. Lawrence at his finger ends for two years, yet has never taken the House of Commons into his confidence. This justifies the conduct of members of the opposition in fighting this Bill. And I can give the hon. minister (Mr. Pugsley) my word that he will find that, from one end of this country to the other, more than the Liberal-Conservatives are a little surprised as to developments that have taken place in this matter.
Now I asked the minister if he could give me some elevations, and he could not, I will be pleased to give him some knowledge. The elevation of the River St. Lawrence Mr. HUGHES.
at Cornwall is 155 feet at the site where the dam is. The elevation of the Grand Trunk station at Cornwall is 191 feet; the elevation at Mille Roches is 225 feet, at Morrisburg 268 feet, at Iroquois 242 feet, at Prescott 247 feet. The great rise in the stream occurs in the -first eight or ten miles above Cornwall. Now I am satisfied that, from the elevation of the country, from the lowness of the banks on the Canadian side, if this dam is erected and if an ice jam occurs, there is no telling how many miles the whole country between the St. Lawrence and the Ottawa rivers may be flooded.

I rise to a point of order. The Bill under discussion has nothing to do with elevations or with building dams. The hon. member is discussing matters wholly foreign to the Bill before the House, and I ask your ruling.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The discussion has certainly taken a very wide range. The item that has been called is section 1, and there is also a motion that the committee rise and report progress. It appears to me that arguments have been brought to bear on this particular question referring to improvements on the St. Lawrence, that were not very relevant, and yet they appeared sufficiently relevant to be allowed. While I regret the width and range of the debate, yet I do not feel at liberty to rule it out of order.

I had nearly completed the elevation idea in the absence of a profile. But there is another aspect. War might possibly occur between Canada and the United States, and it might be necessary, in the interest of Canada, that the free navigation of that river should be maintained. It would be a standing menace to peace between these two countries if that river was dammed. In case of war Canada should have free control of the St. Lawrence. It is impossible to-day for any enemy to cross the river for a number of miles above Cornwall. We have an impassable barrier, in the Long Sault rapids. Our frontier is much more easily defended by having the St. Lawrence unimpeded by dams than it would be if a dam were constructed there and a lake created which could be easily crossed in boats instead of the rapids which now exist. The shipment of the produce of our country is carried on to a greater extent in boats than it formerly was, and the waterways will become the great highways of commerce in the future. Therefore, we must preserve the River St. Lawrence unimpeded in the interest of transportation. To-day freighters laden with grain go through the Long Sault rapids in the time th'at they would be getting through the first lock of the canal if they had to go down through the canal system.
Did the hon. gentleman ever hear of a boat laden with grain going through these rapids?
I have been on freighters when they went" through the rapids, Freighters go through these rapids every week in the summer time.
Grain freighters do not.
The hon. gentleman will not deny that freighters go through these rapids in summer time?
If they only drew six or seven feet of water they might go through.
Nine feet.
No, not nine feet.

There are only two points in the rapids where there is any possibility of hitting at less than nine feet. A few charges of dynamite will clear the channel, and permit vessels drawing, from twelve to fifteen feet to pass down. Does the hon. gentleman not know that the Long Sault Rapids have fifty feet of water throughout the greater part of them? Therefore, I maintain that in the interest of honest government we should stop this charter hunting, this charter-mongering, this handing over, without any plausible excuse, of the rights and interests of this country to men who have never contributed one dollar to its upbuilding. The Minister of Public Works, if he were true to the interests of Canada, instead of sitting here to-night engineering this scheme through, would stand up and fight these people, and compel them to come here and show what they are going to do. If he had the interests of the country at heart would he be here to-night engineering this scheme to dam this river to the detriment of the Dominion government and in the interests of a foreign corporation? No, he would stand shoulder to shoulder with the opposition in fighting this company and insisting that these men should not be granted the corporate powers, which they are now seeking. That is where the Minister of Public Works should be if he were a true patriot, instead of the true friend of charter hunters.

I asked the Minister of Public Works what newspapers these plans were published in in Ontario, and he was good enough to make the answer that he knew nothing about the publication of the plans in any newspapers. I would like to ask the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Robert Smith) in what newspapers these plans were published. I would like my hon. friend to state in what newspapers these plans were published so that we could send to the library and have them here because it is almost impossible to arrive at any sound conclusion in the absence of the plans.

The particular publication that I saw myself was in the Cornwall ' Standard ' but I was informed by others that they had seen them in certain Toronto papers. When the promoters applied to the International Waterways Commission, first at Buffalo, and then at Toronto, these plans were produced, and the newspapers as a matter of news, and of enterprise copied them.
What date?
Hon. gentlemen will remember the sitting of the International Waterways Commission some weeks ago. There is to be another sitting to take further evidence in Montreal in a few days.

Surely the hon. gentleman who suggested that there was unreasonable opposition on this side of the House was not serious? The strongest language and the most vigorous opposition to this Bill have come from the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) a member of the Private Bills Committee who said that, the new points which have come up for discussion to-night are a great surprise to him and the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) who stated that the Bill was introduced under false pretenses. I appeal again to the Minister of Finance to grant the request not onlv of this side of the House, but of the ex-Minister of Railways.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If this were the final stage I could understand the obiections, but the Bill was discussed at length before the Private Bills Committee and has been discussed the greater part of to-day. No one can say there has been any lack of the fullest opportunity for discussion and I cannot see what the plans have to do with this Bill. I think we ought to divide, that we ought to dispose of the matter at this stage. The Bill need not then go to the third reading at once and there would be amiple opportunity for hon. gentlemen to place themselves on record on the third reading. "
Does the minister think we are going to pass all the clauses of this Bill to-night?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know why we should not.
Not on your life.
I would call the minister's attention to the objections of his political friends which I cited.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know of any sides in this matter. This is not a party

541S
matter. If these hon. members had not heard of these important points earlier they have had no lack of information on them during the last two hours.
The Minister of Public Works has admitted that there is a scheme to dam the St. Lawrence, and that this Bill is part of the scheme.
No.
When we have these plans they will show whether it is part of the scheme or not. There must be some object in trying to shove this Bill through without the members understanding it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No private Bill of the present session has received so much discussion.
Or needed it so much.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That may be so, but at all events it certainly is time now to endeavour to get on with the public business.

It is all very well to talk .about reserving half of the power for Canada, but Canada does not need half of this 30,000 horse-power now, and it will be exported to the United States, and vested rights would intervene and we will never be able to get that power back. The hon. member for Hants (Mr. Black) said he was prepared to sit here until Saturday night. Well, we on this side are prepared to do the same. I know that the govern^ ment are anxious to get on with some government business, but this will not help them. It is now a quarter past three in the morning and we have to meet at three p.m. If the suggestion I have made be accepted, this Bill will go through in much less time on Monday than it possibly can now. Let the committee rise and the plans be brought down and laid on the table, and let the Minister of Public Works consult with the Department of Justice before proceeding further with the measure; and on Monday next the Bill will go through in less time than it has the slightest chance of doing now.

I am always glad to meet an offer of compromise, but you can never compromise if one side insists on having everything its own way. Our hon. friend wants something unreasonable. He wants us to bring down plans which might relate to some other Bill. There are none in connection with this Bill.
The hon. gentleman has admitted himself that this Bill and the other one were practically the same Bill.

My hon. friend onght to be ingenuous enough to suggest some other way out of the difficulty. I have always said that before any work will be Mr. FIELDING.
commenced on the St. Lawrence, the company will have to come here and get legislative authority.

But the minister's word is not statute law.
Mr: TURRIFF. Early in the discussion I said that in my opinion it would be advisable for the Bill to stand over in order that we might ascertain if the statements made by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) were well founded. I am still of the opinion, and am prepared to vote that way. At the same time I am not prepared to sit here all night and day simply for the purpose of obstructing. I want to vote for what I really think is right. This is a private Bill, and I do not consider that in voting against the majority on this side, I am voting in any way against the government or Liberal party. But I might say to the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) that if a member on this side happens to vote with him on any subject, it does not help that member to pat him on the back. It only makes it a little more difficult for the man who wants to take an independent position. If hon. members opposite do not wish to take a vote, I would suggest as a compromise that we pass the preamble of the Bill, and that the committee should then rise.

There are one or two clauses that require to be amended. Sup-pose we should allow the preamble to pass and put the Bill through the other stages later on, I would want it understood that the proposed amendments may be moved.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Undoubtedly my hon. friend would have to give notice. The Bill would then be referred -back and he would be at liberty to do that at any stage. I would undertake to say the third reading would not be pressed until the hon. gentleman gave his notice. Let me suggest, that if there be any particular clause specially objectionable, let the clause be held over and let the committee make progress with the rest of the Bill.
We would then be debarred from discussing the general features of the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman wmuld be debarred from discussing the clauses already passed, but not the clauses he wishes to hold over.
As I understand, by reference to some of the papers, in the month of February when the commission met in Toronto, they made a report. Did the Minister of Public Works have that report sent to them?
The commissioners did not make any report.

' Would it not be wise to investigate some of the statements made by the commissioners. In taking up the Cornwall 'Standard' of Friday, February 25, I find that, during the discussion, chairman Gibbons explained the Act introduced in the United States congress to authorize the construction of this work said it was subject to a special provision by which the powers of the company could be taken away at any time if they interfered with national interests. There is certainly no such provision in this Bill:
And that the commencement of this work was subject to the consent of the Canadian government, he thought, and if the commission came to the conclusion that the scheme was practicable and feasible, and would not interfere with the interests of. navigation, that we might assume that the Canadian government would be as astute as the United States government in protecting the interests of our oountry.
The Minister of Public Works knows that when the commission met in Toronto, the strongest objection was raised along different lines. As far as the commission are concerned, I think they should be made aware of these different statements. I have just picked up a few and judging from what I have read, the Montreal Harbour Commission is strongly opposed to this Bill going through.
He does not mean this Bill.

Am I to understand that several members from Montreal tonight were quite willing to get up and do their utmost to stop the passage of this measure? One of them made that statement on a front bench. If that is the position we are in, that several Quebec members are strongly opposed to this measure, and have not the liberty to speak on it, and the Montreal Harbour Commission, and the Light, Heat and Power Company are opposed to it-
Quite naturally.

We have heard nothing about these objections. Has the commission had placed before it the fact that this scheme will lower the water in the St. Lawrence? Of course that may not seem, to some hon. gentlemen, of great importance. It is of great importance, and, in addition, some of the navigation companies have been sending in the strongest kind of condemnation of this Bill. So, it is not an unreasonable request that this Bill should be -allowed to remain over, and 1 hope the Minister of Public Works will see the justice of that request and accede to it.

I think tnat hon. gentlemen ought to consider that this matter
has been before the House for a couple of months. It has been fully discussed before the Private Bills- Committee. This is not a question of the navigation of the St. Lawrence or the building of a dam. The discussion to-night has been entirely wide of the Bill. It is the suspicion that this Bill may involve questions of navigation and the constructing of a dam across the river that causes this discussion.
Did not the commission take all these matters into consideration?
What the commission had before them was the building of a dam and not this Bill.
Are they not so connected as to be inseparable??

I do not think so. No doubt, as the minister has said, there may be in view the obtaining of power from its development at the Long Sault rapids. But even so, we have the word of the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) that before anything is done, everything will be brought before this parliament. The company will have to get a Bill under these circumstances.
Under the Act of 1901 have not they got the authority to dam the St. Lawrence?
The American Bill provides that the consent of the Canadian parliament must be had.
They have already got our consent.
No, they have no ratification of plans; they cannot build a dam.

I cannot understand why there is such persistent opposition to allowing this Bill to go over. It cannot be because the company want to make use of this lifeless transmission line, because they cannot make use of it until tne plans are approved by the Minister of Public Works and the government. But I believe the reason the government are pushing this Bill so strongly is apparent. If the company had the power under the Act of 1901, the 'power thev are now asking, they would not be here. That law does not give them the power to build transmission lines within a municipality, except by that municipality's consent. This Bill proposes t-o give them that power subject to the usual expropriation powers of the Railway Act. It is only by expropriation powers that they can force their transmission lines through the municipalities. They have the horse in the shape of the St. Lawrence power; they want us to give them the harness to put on that horse. And then they will have

everything they require as completely as though they had had it given them under a special Bill. But if they were to come now asking for these combined powers, in our present knowledge of what is involved and with our present judgment, would we give them these powers? I say we would not. We have no right to give them these powers, then, under the plea of a mere supplementary Bill. What is the position of the two parties? It is said this is not a party question. I cannot understand then why members of the cabinet will remain here until a quarter to four in the morning to do-what? To give private individuals the power to make money out of a public asset of this country as against the HydroElectric Commission, which proposes to utilize these powers for the benefit of the public. No municipality has asked the government to nass this Bill. The 'Globe1 newspaper, the representative of the Liberal party, has protested in the most strenuous terpis against the passing of the Bill. Can any member of this House on the other side say that his position is in the interests of the public, standing as he does against the Hydro-Electric Commission, a body which was incorporated for the very purpose of conserving these water-powers and giving power to the public at cost, without the intervention of the middleman? It is idle for my hon. friends opposite to say that we are here for the purpose of obstruction only. We are trying to further the policy inaugurated by the Whitney government which has been supported, not only by a vote of 65 to 17 in the legislature, but by a popular majority of 100,000 in the province.
That is honest.

Quite as honest as the hon. member (Mr. Carvell) being here in the interest of the middlemen. I would like to ask the Minister of Public Works when he conceived the idea that this company was going to pay as much for power as the state of New York is Charging the company on the other side of the line? I assume that policy was conceived after the statements made by the member for Westmorland whereby it was proved that the state of New York were charging the companies over there not only a lump sum but paying a horse-power rate therefor. On the other side of the line they charge a large annual sum for the use of natural resources: on this side we get the benefit of the utilization of those powers, and the people get an annual sum in the shape of cheaper electricity as it is administered by the Hydro-Electric Commission.

A little time ago the
Minister of Public Works made the statement that this was not a government mea-Mr. MIDDLEBRO.
sure but a private Bill. I would like the Minister of Public Works or the Minister of Finance to point out in the history of the parliament of Canada where five ministers of the Crown sat up all night fighting in the interests of a private Bill. I tell the Minister of Public Works that this is a government measure. He has confessed that for two years he has been carrying on secret negotiations with gentlemen who are behind the power scheme to dam the St. Lawrence, and he has never once given the people of Canada that knowledge which we squeezed out of him to-night. In the title attributed to the Sovereign of England are to be found the words 'Defender of the Faith'. The Minister of Public Works, I am afraid, will go down to history with the label plastered over his crest:	'Defender of
United States trusts'. He will go down to history as the man who sat up all night in order to betray, by his actions, the rights of the people of Canada in the waterway of the St. Lawrence river. He will go down as the man who engineered the closing of the St, Lawrence to the people of Canada in the interests of United States corporations and trusts and not as the man who stood up to defend the rights of the people of this country. He will go down as the man who increased the freight rates on the produce of the farmers, increased the passenger rates on the farmers, and closed up that magnificent river which has been the delight of tourists in all periods of the nation's history. He will go down as the man who increased the cost of electric power by handing it over to a gigantic monopoly. He will be known as the man who stood cheek by jowl with the corporate interests and trusts of the United States. He will go down in history, not as a traitor in war, not as a man who would serve his country in time of war, but as the man who in time of peace, gave to the United States the enormous advantage which would accrue to them if war should ever occur between the two nations. We wondered why the Liberal members were so active on that committee. We thought it was an ordinary transmission Bill, until we saw the canvassing and the drumming up of members to come down and vote, then our suspicions were aroused, and our curiosity was excited in this matter. Five ministers of the Crown were found sitting here at four o'clock in the morning fighting for what they term a private Bill, and' yet we are told that it has all been talked over by the government for two years, and although they are quite familiar with all the details, they refuse to bring them down for our information. I want to know why it is that thev are giving over to a gigan'ic corporation the control of the River St.

Lawrence, to the detriment- of the people of this country? Why are these people favoured by a Minister of the Crown, and why has he promised to jam through this Bill? This Bill is necessary to make the other Bill effective and the two Bills taken together are necessary to make the whole conspiracy complete and take from the Dominion the control of its waterways.
