I do not blame the promoters. Grafters come around at all times and on all sides, but I blame the men who are here -as trustees of the company for neglecting the interests of the people. Before I proceed further I would ask the Minister of Finance-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is doing well, and I do not complain.
I am ready; I am in good trim. But I really would insist that the minister should get home to bed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not see why my hon. friend should be so unkind.

It is the reverse. I have a warm feeling for the minister. In the vicinity of Ottawa we can develop 6,000,000 horse-power from water, and in the eastern part of Ontario, we can develop, under the plans that are being carried out by the Minister of Inland Revenue another 6,000,000, and possibly 10,000,000 more. Therefore, we can produce in this locality by water and peat alone nearly one-third of the power consumed on the continent of North America. With the data before us why in the name of all that is decent should these sworn ministers of the Crown be parties to engineering through this House any such Bill as this. It behooves us as trustees of the people to see that the water-powers of the St. Lawrence are not handed over one hour before it is necessary to hand them over, and then we must harness them with such safeguards in the interest of the people as will prevent any great monopoly from controlling them. President Roosevelt in the United States sought to save the people's water-powers. The Minister of Public Works, the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Finance, and a couple of other ministers with the whole party behind them are working to take away the people's wrater-powers. The interests in the gigantic power trust are said to be greater than the- combined railway, Standard Oil, and Steel Corporation interests, of the United States of America. In the minister's meetings with these gentlemen promoting this project, has he obtained any idea whether or not they are in this gigantic water-power trust.
I regret I am unable to give my hon. friend the information.
The minister is aware that they are in a very good trust of their own.
I am not aware of that.

After listening to the splendid address just delivered by my hon. friend from Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) I am sure that the government must feel that this measure is -worthy of much more consideration than it has received in the past. In following out the line of argument taken by my hon. friend I wish to read for the benefit of the Minister of Finance an article from the Daily ' Star ' of February 28. (The hon. member reads the article). In the face of that very strong article, which appears on the editorial page of the Montreal ' Star,' I cannot but feel that the Minister of Finance would be acting in accordance with the interests of the country if he . would allow this Bill to stand over until we have an opnortunity to investigate it thoroughly. I have another article here from the Montreal * Star ' of February 25, headed, ' Must keep control of waterways.' It gives a strong resolution passed by the Montreal executive of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association opposing this measure. Thus we have not only the Conservation Commission, speaking by its chairman

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: The chairman is not against it. Read his leter.

He practically condemned it, there is no question about that. We have not only the Conservation Commission, but also the Hydro-Electric Commission of Ontario, which is developing water-powers and furnishing electrical energy at the lowest possible cost, having contracts with the Niagara Power Company

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Does the hon. member expect that the Hydro-Electric Commission is going to transmit Niagara power to Eastern Ontario?

They will not undertake such a proposition. " But here the hon. member (Mr. Pardee) proposes to give away one of the most valuable water-powers in the country for private interests and for nothing. And here we have a strong resolution of the Manufacturers' Association in Montreal in condemnation of the proposition. I am sure that if we had time to look up others, we could find many of them. And we may be sure that, when private capital controls these privileges, they will charge high rates and then they will pump enough water into the proposition to make those rates seem necessary.
Their rates are subject to the Railway Commission.

Does the hon. member suppose that the towns to be supplied

will be in the same position as if the HydroElectric Commission had the control of affairs?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Much better.
The hon. member (Mr. Pardee) knows full well that he dare not go into_western Ontario and take that-position.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Yes, he dare.

No man from On

tario dare go to the western part of the province and take the position that the Hydro-Electric Commission are not giving the people of Ontario power at the minimum cost.
He dare not say it here.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Yes, he dare say it here or anywhere. I say that the Hydro-Electric Commission are not furnishing power at many points in Ontario at the prices they promise.
That is a very mild way of putting it. It is open to two meanings. ' Not furnish power at the prices they promised.' They may have furnished it at lower prices.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I mean higher.
Will the hon. member name a few places of which that is true?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I will not interrupt the discussion. Let the hon. member go on.

The hon. member's argument against the Hydro-Electric Commission is a very weak one. Now, this resolution of the Manufacturers' Association was passed unanimously. It is another evidence of the feeling against this Bill. I sincerely hope the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) will see the justice of our case and not keep us here any longer. It is a quarter to five in the morning.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member (Mr. Armstrong) is keeping himself. I would not keep him for a moment.

But I should not be serving the interest of the people I represent, and of the province from which I come if I did not resist the attempt to force down our throats this most unjust measure. Now, I have another article here from the Montreal ' Star,' February 21st, under the heading, ' Long Sault Dam':

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It may be well for me to say once in every two hours, so that there may be a record of it, that there is no foundation for the talk of hon. gentlemen opposite about this Bill being forced through to-night. Several hours ago I said that if hon. gentlemen would indicate the particular clauses they -would like to hold over we would let them stand over and not Mr. ARMSTRONG
take the Bill out of the committee stage. Therefore, any statement that we are trying t-o force this Bill through to-night is not according to the record.
The Minister of Finance is undertaking to give us a lecture.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thought I should mention that point just once every two hours.

The responsibility for what has occurred to-night rests on the ministers. It is not often in a British parliament that you see the majority holding up the public business for the sake of a private Bill. It leads us to think that there must be something behind this. I notice a significant absence of t*.e Ontario members here to-night, and I know that not one of the Ontario members except our friend from Rainy River, who has something coming afterwards that he wants put through, would have the hardy hardihood to stand up here and say anything against the power policy of the Ontario government. We have the member for Carleton, N.B., (Mr. Carvell) taking an active part in favour of this measure, and we always look with a little suspicion on a measure that he advocates. We also view with suspicion the Minister of Finance taking an active part in a private Bill, or in fact any public Bill that he is mixed up with. I am not here to block the public business, but I am here to see the rights of the people of the province of Ontario safeguarded. The Hydro-Electric Commission has done noble work in Ontario, and the people of the province endorsed the government by an immense majority last election, and the Liberals in the Ontario house are taking a manly stand in favour of the policy of the government in this regard. For some reason which I do not understand, but which I may refer to later on, we have the ministers and the members from Quebec and Manitoba and New Brunswick, especially New brunswick, endeavouring to foist on the people of Ontario something they detest. We are to-night fighting for the interests of the people of Ontario, and gentlemen on the other side can make up their minds that we will stay here till Sunday morning if need be.

Everything to-night indicates that the government are behind this private Bill, and I would ask them to listen to what the Toronto * Globe ' of February the 9th says about it. If this Bill goes through, the government will have power to grant the privilege of damming the St. Lawrence without coming to this House at all. I have that information from a gentleman in this concern.

It has already been pointed out that the premier stated that the

scheme would first be brought before parliament and submitted to our consideration; and the Minister of Public Works on two other occasions this evening made the same statement, that the matter would not be dealt with until it was ratified by this House.

The hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton put a question earlier in the session to the Prime Minister as to whether the government would consent to the damming of the St. Lawrence river at the Long Sault without the matter first coming to parliament, and the Prime Minister stated in the most equivocal language that it would not. The government has power to approve the plans or otherwise, and he stated distinctly that the government would take no action until the matter had first been approved by parliament.
The Minister of Public Works also states that if this dam is granted the government will see that we get the same rates for power that they do on the American side.
Provided it is granted by parliament. The government is not going to grant it, parliament will have to deal with it first.
Let me ask the minister : * What does the government charge per horse-nower along the canals or anywhere else?
The charge varies according to the location and value of the power.

They already charged a nominal rate of $2 per horse-power, and a few years ago they raised the rate to $4 per power. They state that they will develop, I think, 800,000 horse-power, of which we will get 400,000. Now, if we take it at the lowest rate, the people of this country will receive $800,OCO per annum.

If they build this dam they will have to construct not only the dam but the conduits, the head gates, the pen stocks, and all that sort of thing. That is all done in the case of canals; therefore we cannot expect to get the same revenue out of these that we could from a lock.

If the hon. gentleman would take a trip along the St. Lawrence canal he would recognize that his statements are not borne out by the facts. Take Iroquois. The gentleman who has the power there is trying to sell it in these towns. He had to dig a place away from the canal, then he had to build his dams, and realize before he put in his power at all.

Will the hon. gentleman say that that gentleman who is developing power on the Iroquois canal is not 172
using much of the canal built by the government for the purpose of getting water from the head of the rapids? Is he taking water out of the government canal into the river?	.
If these people build the dam across the St. Lawrence they will be emptying the water, and I cannot see what difference that makes at all. *
At Lachine and Cornwall, and places on the Welland and other places where power is being used, the power is already created, so far as hydraulic pressure is concerned, by the works of the government.

But I am satisfied that the development of power under this proposed power scheme Bill will not cost so much per horse-power as the development of power from the Cornwall canal. Yet the government charges $4 per horse power in that case. If the government were to make the same charge in this case, the revenue to the public would be $1,600,000 per annum. I suppose not more than five or ten per cent of the possible power can be used in Canada at the present time. We could not expect them to spend the money for development and not use the power developed. So, they would have to export the power.
I would not allow them.
Would not allow them to export?
No.
It has been allowed in other cases.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: There is a provision against it in this Bill.
But did not the hon. member (Mr. Pardee) propose that it should be allowed?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Almost as soon as we took the matter up in the committee, the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. J. D. Reid) said that the great objection was to the export of power, and it was agreed that the right to export power should be cut out.
But when it was suggested that an audit should be made under which the power should not be sold to any company that had the right to export it, the hon. member (Mr. Pardee) refused that.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: That is right.
So, this power would go to build up industries in the United States.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: No, under the hon. gentleman's own scheme, which he has been talking about all night, there would be as much power sent to the other side of the line as under ours. This is to build up industries here.
Why, they intend to take it from Massena and for a hundred miles A the other side and there are large cities there calling for a great deal of power.
We would not let them take it. We could insist on half of it being kept in Canada.

But another company may be formed with the right to export power, and that is the way of getting round it. And vested rights will be formed, and once they are formed the United States would not allow us to interfere with those vested rights on their side. The minister knows that 95 per cent of the water is on the American side.
That would not be the case after the dam was built. The object of the dam would be to equalize and control the flow. It will cost a little money, but it can be done.

Not in that locality, on account of the way the river runs and the way the islands are situated. And the Americans will claim more than half the power, and the government is not going to war about it.
But the Minister of Public Works told us that this scheme was coupled up with the other scheme.

In answer to a question of mine the Minister of Public Works stated that the power would come from a dam
on the .St. Lawrence

I said I had no knowledge whatever .about the matter, but I surmised that if the power were developed on the St. Lawrence they would use it. There is nothing in the Bill to prevent them getting power anywhere else.

That was quite sufficient to give the members of the committee to understand that this transmission company would get their power generated by the other company. I ask the Minister of Finance what objection he has to this amendment to the Bill which was moved in the committee and voted down by his supporters:-
Nothing in this act contained shall be construed to authorize the company to enter on, take or use any land or water, the property of any province without having first obtained by order in council of the lieutenant governor of the consent of the province to such entry taking or user.
Surely that is a fair proposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There must have been some good reasons advanced in support of voting down that resolution. I take it for granted that my hon. friend thinks that this company will in some way or other be brought into conflict with the Ontario Hydro-Electric Commission. I have no quarrel with the Ontario government on that, but I have always understood that what they desired was not a monopoly but competition. If that be so they cannot object to some other corporation entering the field. If this corporation cannot supply power cheaper than the Ontario HydroElectric Commission then they will get no customers. However, I have not studied the question sufficiently to deliver a judgment off-hand on the resolution read by my hon. friend.

The minister has fairly stated that the policy of the Ontario government is to create competition so as to cheapen power. But when the Ontario government has expended a large amount of money in pursuance of that policy, this government is not justified in taking away their rights.
What money did the Ontario government expend?
The credit of'the province for some millions.
The Ontario government finances that, but the municipalities pay the whole burden.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: And it does not apply to anything east of Toronto.

The province of Ontario have not been able to cover the whole province as yet, but it is their intention to supply power to the very municipalities that this Bill proposes to supply power to. What objection has the Minister of Public Works to the resolution I read?

When we get down to business and come to a section in connection with which that resolution might be moved, I can assure the hon. gentleman that the committee will give it fair consideration. Let us get down to business and not act like children.

It seems to me it is the Minister of Public Works and his supporters who are acting like children. This is a very serious Bill, there is an important principle involved in it and we are perfectly justified in lighting it.
What is the principle? [DOT]

It is the principle of provincial rights. Why did not the minister accept a fair sugegstion and postpone this Bill until the plans, were here, so that we

might consider the matter from a business point of view.
Is the hon. gentleman aware that the plans have nothing to do with this Bill and that they are plans which are before the Waterways Commission in connection with another matter.
I know all about that; I know it is not only this Bill we are considering but the whole scheme connected with it. Personally I am opposed to obstruction and in favour of expediting business.
Then expedite business.
We will not be bluffed by the other side of the House. We have as much good stuff on our side as you have on yours.
The plans were not asked for until twelve o'clock last night and they could not be brought here. Ordinarily my hon. friend (Mr. Price) is a sensible business man.
Thank you.

And the hon. gentleman is ashamed of the way the business has been conducted here to-night. Hon. gentlemen opposite must recognize that the majority must rule. If the preamble of this Bill and some non-contentious clauses are passed I will send to the chairman of the International Waterways Commission and have the plans sent here if possible. I am prepared to do anything to prevent the unseemly spectacle we have had here all night.

I know that the majority must rule, but at the same time the minority have rights which it is their duty to fight for. I am not a lawyer but a business man, and I want to see the business of the House expedited.
Why not pass the preamble then.
I do not think the proposition is reasonable.
What do you see in the present Bill that you object to.
I do not know much about the Bill.
Hear, hear.
I know enough to know that it affects the rights of the city of Montreal and that the rights of that city should be respected.
The Bill does no touch the city of Montreal.

I believe it does.
172 h
Yes, I beg your pardon it does include the city, of Montreal.

I honestly stated that I know very little about the Bill but notwithstanding that the hon. gentleman has been with the Bill throughout the committee stage I seem to know more about it than he does. I think the hon. gentleman should not be so ready to correct without reason a novice such as I am.

The Minister of Public Works said a moment ago that we are acting childishly. I would like to know from him who are the parties that are acting childishly. He says the majority must rule. Who are the majority in this case? It is not a government Bill, it is a private Bill, and one man has just as much right in this House as another on a private Bill. If it were a government Bill, I would yield immediately.
What I meant was this, that instead of wasting the time by unnecessary talk at this late hour in the morning, let us take a vote and then we will know' where the majority is.

I have been in this House for 28 years, and this is the first time that I ever saw the time of the House wasted in this manner on a private Bill. Now, if that dam is erected, I want to ask how boats can go up and down the -river and through that canal.
Under the pro-poed plan the Cornwall canal will not be interfered with in any way, and there will be no more to prevent boats going up and down than there is to-day.
Is the water not to be raised by the dam?
The water is not to be raised at the head of the Cornwall canal. They are not going to raise the water so high as to be above the head of the canal.
The dam will be practically at the head of the canal.

The dam is not to be at the head of the canal. It will not be sufficiently high to raise the water as high as the head of the Cornwall canal. The pronosed dam is some five miles below the head of the Cornwall canal; there is a large descent in the river at that distance, and it is not proposed to raise the water as high as the head of the Cornwall canal.
Question.
It is now a quarter to seven o'clock. The Minister of Public Works said we were childish, because the majority must rule.

I did not say the hon. gentlemen were chi'dish. I said we should

get to work instead of staying here and wasting the time of the committee and wasting the money of the public by useless discussion.

The government is responsible in fathering a private Bill in which they have no interest unless they are backing up a monopoly, and it is the duty of the opposition to prevent the country being looted, and if necessary to do that we will remain here until Satutrday night.
Let us take a vote, and we will see where the majority is.
The vote is not going to be taken. When the minister says that he is not speaking for the government, when he says that the government make this Bill their Bill.

I said nothing of the kind. I did not intend any such reference to be drawn from my remarks. There would be no truth whatever in such a remark. I said let us take a vote and then we will see where the majority is. The majority may be on one side or the other

The Cornwall canal leaves the river at the east end of the town of Cornwall; it runs along the shore of the river, passing through a number of locks. On the Canadian side the distance from the head of the canal down to the dam is probably eight miles. There are islands intervening between the two. channels. On Sheik's island, on the Canadian side, there is a drop of about thirty feet and the proposed dam is considerably further down.

As I understand the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Robert Smith) the dam across the river will raise the water probably thirty feet, but it will have no effect upon the lock. Consequently the Cornwall canal will not be affected. Of course, the hon. gentleman, I understand, is thoroughly convinced that the dam will cross at this place.
I speak of what the plans propose.
But I asked for information, and now the hon. member seems to be in doubt about it.
I say that that is the proposition the company is making to the government.

Then the plans have been submitted to the Department of Public Works. I would like to ask the hon. minister (Mr. Pugsley) if he quite agrees with the hon. member for Stormont. He has seen the plans and knows about them.

I did not think then, and do not think now, that the plans of the contemplated works in the St. Law-Mr. PUGSLEY.
rence had anything to do with this Bill, and I am not prepared to give the information he is asking for. But the plans were submitted to the government and are now before the International Waterways Commission. As I recollect them, they show the dam a considerable distance below the locks of the Cornwall canal, and I believe the engineer stated that these construction works would not affect the Cornwall canal. But all this will be considered when the matter comes up for determination.

Now, we have taken up a great deal of time, and I would draw the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) to the situation. I think this is about the first time I have had the honour of addressing him. I feel a little diffident about it. At the same time, no one more thoroughly appreciates his bonhomie and good humor than I do. Now it seems to me we have been wasting a good deal of time.
Hear, hear.

But whose fault is it? It is now a little after seven o'clock. I can say to the minister that if he wishes to go on, we can go on in this way until Saturday evening. But there is no sense in this sort of thing. We should act like business men and like representatives of the Canadian people.
Then, why not do so?

Quite right. That is what we want to do. We have strong objections to this Bill-not so much to the Bill, perhaps, as to what goes with it. It seems to me it would be better in the interest of both sides, if you put this off until the next day for private Bills, and, in the meantime, let the information be laid before the House. We are prepared to take a proper view of the subject, and if we are to be defeated, as we believe we are, why, we shall be defeated. But would it not be better to make some arrangement and facilitate business? Of course, if the minister does not want to do that, we are ready to fight.
There has been some discussion of the position of the locks. Would the hon. member for Stormont tell us where these dams are to be placed?

The first proposed dam on the American side is from the foot of Long Sault island to the American side, and there they propose to put in a lock. The next is from the foot of Long Sault island to Barnhardt's island, and the last dam goes from the foot of Barnhardt's to the bank of the Cornwall canal, about eight miles below the head of the canal and four miles out from the foot.

I object to this secondary evidence concerning documents that are in existence and that could be produced in short order. In no court of justice would that kind of evidence be listened to for a moment. One member says the dam is at one place and another member says the dam is another place and we cannot tell where the dam is. The Minister of Public Works, says that the dam may be below Montreal or above Montreal but he says that no matter -where the dam is. it will not affect the Cornwall canal. If the plans were here we would know where the dam is and we would know whether it would affect the canal or not, and so we have spent the whole night here because the Minister of Public Works has forgotten where the dam is. The Minister of Public Works has told us that the majority must rule, yes, but the majority must rule according to justice, and if there is nothing to hide bring forth your plans and then, if everything is satisfactory, we will pass your government measure.

It is unnecessary for me to state again that this is not a government measure and that the government is not behind it. Any member of the government or any supporter ot the government can vote on it just as he pleases.

Let the minister not pretend that he has not made this a party measure; he knows it is a party measure and that every man on that side of the House is at his back. I tell the minister and the party behind him that the moment they attempt to divert the public resources of Canada from the use of the people into the coffers of a private corporation, the party on this side of the House will oppose that. Does the member for West Lambton pretend to say that this company will not get its power from the St. Lawrence Power Company.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I do not know, and the Bill does riot say anything about it.

Then if the hon. member does not know, in all justice postpone the consideration of the Bill until he ascertains the fact that this company will get its power from the St. Lawrence Power Company which in conjunction with an American company intends to dam) the St. Lawrence. Let any member on the other side of the House stand ud and tell me that this company will not get its power from the St. Lawrence Power Company; let them stand up individually because I want to get them on record. I cannot understand how men become so tied up to private corporations as to become blind to the public interest.
Does the hon. membeij say we are tied up to private corporations.
As far as I can judge the hon. member for Wolfe and Richmond and all of his ilk to-night are tied up body and soul to the passage of this Bill.

I rise to a point of order. The hon. member (Mr. Cowan) has made the statement that the member for Richmond and Wolfe and all his ilk are tied up to private corporations. I ask Mr. Chairman, that you compel him to withdraw that statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I did not understand the member for Vancouver (Mr. Cowan) to use exactly the words the hon. gentleman has indicated. I will let the hon. member state himself the exact words he used.
I say that I understand that the hon. member for Richmond and Wolfe and gentlemen on his side of the House are tied up body and soul, using it figuratively, to the passage or this Biil.
I rise to a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Richmond and Wolfe rose to a point of order and quoted words which he understood to be used by the member for Vancouver. I do not think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Tobin) quoted them exactly; I think the statement made by the member for Vancouver represents the words he used and while the language is very strong I know of no rule that he has actually violated.

I have no desire to charge gentlemen on the other side with the intention to make this Bill law. If any gentleman on the other side is against this Bill I shall be glad to let him say so. I notice the peculiar reiteration with which the Minister of Public Works has said that it would be better to let us have a vote and get this thing through. You will notice the peculiar lack of principle in that suggestion; not a lack of cunning, not a lack of art in the railroading of a Bill through the House, but a peculiar lack of principle. Am I to understand that the minister is opposed to any further powers being given under the Act of 1901?
I stated that no decision had been come to by the government in the matter.

But the plan Has been laid before the government, these plans are for the minister's^ eye and not for the members of this committee, and yet the whole case is based upon these plans, which are hidden from us, which are concealed from us, which are withheld from us, which are pigeon-holed in the minister's department and which he dare not lay on the table.
I stated already that they were before the International Waterways Comssimion.

I am ready to take my seat if any man will be good enough to suggest the remotest semblance of a ghost of a reason for withholding the plans from this House. I get no reply. Am I to assume that their ingenuity is exhausted? Am I to assume that silence is their only recourse? Am I to assume that this Minister of Public Works and his party behind him are so absolutely run to earth that they have not one word to say why they are withholding these plans from this House? It has been suggested that they are asleep, Mr. Chairman. I have visual proof that they are not asleep, and I believe if they were asleep that nature, who has that happy faculty of revealing the truth at unexpected times, would reveal to this House the location of those plans and their nature. No, Mr. Chairman, it is not a sufficient answer to say that the minister and his followers are asleep, because I know that if that were the case the truth would out. Is the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) in favour of diverting this water-power belonging to the public into the possession of a private corporation of the United States?
That is not the question before the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is growing up a habit of hon. members addressing each other across the floor, while still keeping their seats. The hon. member who is addressing the House should be allowed to do so.

Listening to the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) I am particularly anxious to get the measure of his ideas. Before I leave for breakfast I would like to ascertain where the hon. member thinks this company will get the power it is to transmit. The hon. gentleman does not Teply, and my curiosity is unsatisfied. Mr. Speaker, I desire to treat this thing seriously, but it is hard to do so an view of the absurdity of basing the -whole case upon plans seen with eyes of one colour by the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Robert Smith) and seen as through a glass darkly by the Minister of Public Works. And these gentlemen who have seen these plans come and tell us their forgettings -about them, and, in the end, we know nothing either about the plans or about the dam.

The hon. member for Vancouver has told us that he intends to go home and get breakfast. I have known people to talk strangely because of something in their stomachs, but I have never heard one talk so strangely as the hon. gentleman because of nothing in his stomach. I am sorry that he has seen fit to Mr. COWAN.
mar this pleasant evening. For, -while this has been obstruction pure and simple, it has, on the whole, been carried on in a very pleasant manner. The speech of the hon. member for Victoria and Hali-burton (Mr. Hughes) was a jewel. He did not say anything unpleasant; in fact, he did not say anything at all. He said nothing but what others said for him, so he was not called upon to draw on his mental resources or even greatly on his physical resources. The hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) obstructed in a thoroughly gentlemanly manner. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. GeoTge Taylor) wants to get home, but did not say anything unpleasant. But as to the hon. member for Vancouver, I would remind him that this Bill is for the purpose of incorporating certain gentlemen as a company for the transmission of electrical energy.
What electrical energy?
If the hon. member does not know what electrical energy is, it would be hardly worth while for me to explain.
I know -about electrical energy and could give an instructive lecture upon it. But whence is it to come in this case?
From water-power.
From what water-power?

From somewhere along the St. Lawrence river-I do not know where. Nor do I care. And I think the people along the St. Lawrence will not care very much either. If hon. members opposite, particularly the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Cowan), think they are making political capital out of this, they are welcome to all they can get out of it. There are other places in the Dominion than the province of Ontario, and we are not all bound, to the chariot wheels of the Hydro-Electric Commission, though the hon. member for Vancouver may be.
Or to the public interest.

I feel bound by the public interest and consider the course I am taking in the public interest. The hon. member did me the honour to intimate that I had some object in trying to force this Bill through. I have no interest at all. I am not a member of the Private Bills Committee. I advocate the Bill because I believe it to be in the public interest. I have stated before that I did not care how many transmission companies or other public utilities came into my constituency- the more the better. The hon. member for Vancouver, though he has spent an hour and a half in opposing this Bill had no qualms of conscience in putting through this House Bill (No. 118) to give his friends

in British Columbia the very rights he wishes to deny to others.
And over the head of the province.
What Bill-what is the title?

Bill 118. The hon. member knows what it is. He is not so innocent as he looks. Only two weeks ago he put this Bill through the House giving to his friends powers he now would deny to others. And he deliberately insinuates that the Minister of Public Works is hiding the facts, withholding the plans

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is only just to the member for Vaiieouver to say thkt he withdrew that.
But he repeated his statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think not.

I must bow to your ruling, but the hon. member did not withdraw it until he was forced by the chair to do so. He knows that the St. Lawrence Power Company's Bill, passed in 1901, is not now under discussion. If that company be alive to-day and have carried out the terms of its charter, it has the right to build these transmission lines without reference to this Bill. If that be so, what becomes of the argument that this company is only a subsidiary company?
It does not give them power of expropriation.
It does. Section 14 gives them that power.
It does not give them power to enter a municipality without that municipality's consent. '
No. But what has that Bill to do with the Bill now under discussion?
It is the same people.	..
Does the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Geo. Taylor) want to prevent the distribution of electrical energy in his county?
Certainly, if it means the destruction of the navigation of the St. Lawrence.

For three or four hours this Bill was opposed because it would interfere with the plans of the Hydro-Electric Commission. Now, we have an entirely new reason-the navigation of the St Lawrence. Does not the hon. member know that the plans must be approved by the Governor in Council? And has he not heard the Minister of Public Works say that when the plans are submitted to him
they were handed over to the Waterways Commission for investigation and that that body has not yet reported? Is it reasonable to hold up a Bill for an electric transmission company because it may theoretically have some effect upon matters of navigation which are in the hands of the Waterways Commission? If hon. members say: We do not want this Bill to go through and we have the physical power to sit hefe until Saturday night and commence agaia next Monday and sit until next Saturday night, of course, they are within their legal rights. But I think it would be much better if they take the ground that they are opposing this Bill because it interferes with the schemes of the Ontario government. It would be better for our hon. friends opposite to come out and frankly admit that they are opposing this Bill at the behest and by the orders of the province of Ontario. If they do that, we will know exactly what we have to face. But I pray my hon. friends not to take shelter behind this childish proposition that in some way or other they want the Minister of Public Works to bring down plans of a scheme which is on foot to dam the River St. Lawrence, and which has nothing whatever to do with the Bill under discussion, and which is entirely safe in the hands of the Waterways Commission and the government.

I would like to submit to the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Carvell) whether this discussion does not go deeper than the mere passage of this particular Bill. I think there is a question which goes deeper than any mere opposition, and deeper than the principle contained even in this measure. The question is, when a private member proposes a Bill and the leader of the opposition asks that the Bill may stand over until certain papers are produced, whether the Bill should not be laid over for further discussion. The leader of the opposition asks that further information be furnished, and surely as a mere matter of courtesy, if not of right, that request should be granted. The public have been led to believe that they would have access to these plans. We have Chairman Gibbons of the International Waterways Committee, stating at Toronto that the government and the commission have the plans, but they are withheld from the representatives of the Ontario government. Surely it is an extraordinary thing that where such vital interests are concerned, the representatives of the province of Ontario has not had an opportunity to see the plans upon which the committee are supposed to act. It is, I think, a grave discourtesy that one side if given information which is withheld from the other side. The representatives of the province of Ontario, of the great interests that are oppos-

ing this proposition, are not allowed to see the plans, while those in favour of the proposition are allowed to see them.

In glancing over the hon. members sitting on the government side of the House, I find there are 26, and only four of them come from the province of Ontario. One is the promoter of this Bill, the other is the redoutable member for Rainy River (Mr. Conmee), who always looks after the interests of the people of Ontario, one is asleep, and the other has not so far been heard from. So I think that if the interests of the province of Ontario are to be left in the hands of members from that province on the government side of the House, they are sadly neglected indeed. Now, reference has been made to the Bill passed the other day by the Railway Committee in reference to the Burrard channel. As I pointed out before, although the government did give that company the powers of expropriation, they were given to a company which produced documentary evidence showing that it was acting as trustee for five or six municipalities in the province of British Columbia, which municipalities contained one-half the population of the province. When we asked them if they were willing to carry on their undertaking without making any charges, they replied they were. Therefore that cannot be said to be a company incorporated for any other interest than the public interest of British Columbia.
If they said that, why was not that provision put in the Bill?

Because the Minister of Railways himself said it was not a reasonable proposition, and it was at the suggestion of the Minister of Railways himself that a clause was inserted giving them power to charge a toll. But the proceeds of that toll came to the people of British Columbia, because it was a public undertaking and represented half the people of the province. But let us consider the consistency of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell). He spent hours in this House arguing for the incorporation of the Nelson River Railway Company, basing his plea on the fact that* the Biil gave no power to expropriate water-powers. But now he argues that we should not oppose this transmission Bill although it gives powers of expropriation. In the Bill of 1901, we expressly provided that the company should not enter anv municipalit>
without the consent of that municipality. But the present Bill seeks to enlarge such powers and to give this transmission company entrance to a municipality regard less of the will of its people. In Bills that we have passed this session, we have specially inserted provisions denying the right of expropriation of water powers. In Mr. S. SHARPE.
the Nelson River Bill, in the London and Lake Erie Railway and Transportation Company and in others.
I rise to a point ut order. There is no minister of the Crown in the House. The debate should end.
This is a private Bill, and the presence of a minister is not necessary.
I do not think the point is well taken.
I ask the hon. member for Carleton where is his consistency in view of the facts I have submitted?

If the hon. member wants an answer, I would say that;, so far as the Ontario and Michigan Power Company is concerned, it was fought about as viciously as this Bill has been, and the promoter, to get it through, was willing to accept almost anything. But since 1901, the Railway Commission has been created and under section 247 of the Railway Act, which creates that commission, it is provided that if such a company as the one provided for in the Bill under discussion cannot get the consent of a municipality to establish works within it, it must get tin consent of the Railway Board. I think that, for the purposes of uniformity, all our Bills should be passed subject to that provision.
The hon. gentleman did not use that argument in support of the Nelson River Bill.
I do not think I opened my lips on that Bill.
Certainly, Last night, when he was
That is right. I thought the hon. gentleman was referring to the Vancouver Bill. .
The hon. member last night said we should pass the Nelson River Bill because it had no expropriation powers; now he says we should pass this with expropriation powers.
I am talking of transmission lines going through a municipality.
But we are granting exporpriation powers against private property.
A public utility Bill would be unworkable without it.

The hon. member (Mr. Carvell) does not agree with the Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Graham) who announced as the settled policy of the government that every Railway Bill should contain a clause denying the power to transmit electricity save by the consent of the parties interested.
Then I certainly differ with him.

If we strike out the powers of expropriation, the municipality that desires to have the service of the Hydro-electric Commission can have it. But if you give this company powers of expropriation under the Railway Act you open the way for the middleman.

The hon. member says the municipality should be free to choose the Hydro-Electric. But we on this side say that there should be the Hydro-Electric and as many others as want to come in. Let the competition be as free as possible. The Hydro-Electric Commission want a monopoly.
For the benefit of the people.

I hope this parliament will never grant a monopoly to the HydroElectric Commission or ' any other body. Does the hon. member (Mr. Middlebro) mean to say that if this Bill becomes law a_nd this company erect their transmission line to Brockville that will prevent, legally or otherwise, the Hydro-Electric Commission from entering Brockville?
It will mean that the poles will be erected, the wires strung, the houses wired and the connections made, and the Hydro-Electric Commission will be practically prevented from coming in.
Legally or from a business standpoint?
The other company would be installed, as the Bell Telephone Company is to-day so that nobody else can get in.

The logical conclusion of the hon. member's argument is that if the Hydro-Electric Commission get into a municipality they would be able to charge Lhe rates they want and make the people pay those rates even though they would be higher than if there was competition.
The hon. member (Mr. Carvell) seems to constitute himself an advisory board of one to tell the opposition how to argue their case.
The hon. member (Mr. Middlebro) asked my opinion.
I am surprised at the hon. member, the watchdog of the public interest allowed such a notorious Bill as he describes that of the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Cowan) to have been to pass the House.
I did not characterize it as notorious. I say it is a proper Bill.

Talking of monopoly, if you leave it to the people in the section
affected by the Bill now under discussion, whether they will have electrical energy-furnished by this company or by the . Hydro-Electric Commission, the people will soon decide irrespective of politics.
Then why not have both?
Because the Hydro-Electric Commission propose to give power to the municipalities at cost, and the smaller number that take it from them, the higher the cost will be to those who do take it.

If the Hydro-Electric Commission give the power at cost, surely there is no danger in incorporating this company, because, according to the hon. gentleman's argument, it will not be able to do any business.

The charges of the municipalities vary according to the cost of transmission, and my argument is that the fewer the municipalities that take the power, the higher the overhead charges will be, and consequently the higher cost of the power. But a stronger reason for my opposing this Bill is that it is simply a stepping-stone to the greater Bill which ii to come later to give a private company the control of the water-power on the St. Lawrence river. What will happen if we slow the current by the proposed dam?
You will have dead water.
Anchor ice will form and will cause the water to overflow the land.
Anchor ice only forms in running water. The dead water will freeze over.

Even if the water freezes over, the current from the river above will overflow it at the rate of several miles an hour. The hon. member for Stormont (Mr Smith) evaded the question of the height of the proposed dam. It was first proposed to be 54 feet. Now it is lessoned to 42 or 45 feet. The Cornwall canal is eleven miles long, and has a fall of 48 feet, with six locks. 'The hon. gentleman said that the proposed dam would be five miles from the head of the canal, so that it would be upwards of 40 feet high at six miles from the lower end of the canal. Involved in this question are the interests of the navigation of the St. Lawrence and the interests of the people. in_ that whole section of country. The American people are at present dependent upon our canals to get up the St. Lawrence river. The hon. member for Carle-ton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) is evidently willing that they should have a canal on the American side of the river. I am not willing to give them that privilege upon the St. Lawrence river, which is a great asset of this country. [DOT]

The question of damming the St. Lawrence is not involved in

this Bill. Moreover, the Minister of Public Works states that the proposition oi this company is to build a dam that will not affect the intake of the Cornwall canal. The hon. member for Dundas is wrong in his figures. If the dam is to be built seven or eight miles below the mouth of the canal, that will create a tract of level water eight or nine miles long, forming a lake, which will freeze over in the winter time, and be free of anchor ice. The only issue is whether this committee will give the company a right to build transmission lines to various points of Ontario and Quebec.

I regard it as an outrage that the members of this House should be kept here all night for the sake of private interests. It is all very well to say that this is only a transmission company, but it must obtain its power from somewhere, and, in view of the public interests in Montreal and along the St. Lawrence river opposed to this project, I think this Bill should be held over until the question of damming the St. Lawrence is before us, so that the two questions, which are involved in each other, can be taken up together.

We are not asking that this Bill should be destroyed. We are only asking that due consideration be given to the various questions that have arisen in connection with it. I think a feeling is growing in the minds of members on both sides of the House that we should begin more carefully to conserve our great natural resources such as are affected by this Bill. It has been admitted that the Bill is now before the Waterways Commission and all wo ask is that it be set aside until we have received the report of the Waterways Commission. This is not a government Bill, it is purely a private Bill in the interests of private parties, who are asking for large powers. And it is our duty to demand that we be furnished with all the information that is available before we consent to the passage of this measure. It has been said by the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) that what he stood for was the principle of open competition. I think he is aware that while there may be no actual legal opposition to two companies operating in a municipality for the production of power, yet it is well known that here are means of preventing an opposition company from coming into a municipality where another company is already installed. In our own western country when the telephone first came in, we were given a certain rate, afterwards another company came in and amalgamated with it, and immediately we were served with notices that the price was doubled for every telephone in the city. In regard to water-power we are paying many times the price that our neighbours are Mr. CARVELL.
paying in districts surrounding us, where a public company is serving the people. We realize that if these companies were established in the municipalities under this Bill, it would be impossible for the HydroElectric to come in. We have appointed a Conservation Commission, and it is proposed to vote them $60,000 for their work. We realize more than in former times the value of our great waterways with their water falls as sources of energy. Surely, the government should accede to the request of the opposition and allow a Bill such as this, which is said to have the effect of giving to private individuals one of the greatest water powers on our greatest river, to stand over for further information.

I see the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) has retired, but three ministers have come in. I desire to secure information which the Minister of Public Works did not give us. I would like to know the height of the dam shown in the plan that has been referred to. And. if it is to be 42 feet high, as has been stated, how can the present canal be used for Canadian traffic. The Minister of Public Works stated that it would not interfere with the passage upwards of Canadian boats, leaving us to infer that it would throw all the downward traffic on the American side. I see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) here. He is the senior of the ministers who have recently entered the chamber, and I will ask him for information on this subject.

I am rather surprised that the hon. member (Mr. Geo. Taylor) has singled me out for information on the subject of a dam. Knowing my mild and peace-loving disposition as he does, I should think that he would know that I am no authority on the subject of dams. But 1 know something of the wording of this Bill, and I do not understand that there is any reference in it to a dam.
The hon. minister was not present, but the Minister of Public Works said that this Bill was in conjunction with that passed in 1901-
That is hardly a correct interpretation.
That was the meaning.
No.
This is a power Bill.
No, a transmission Bill.
The Minister of Public Works admitted that the other company was to make the proposed works
No.
He said that this Bill and the other would work conjointly.

No.
5Jr. GEO. TAYLOR. That the same parties were concerned in both.
Oh, oh.
The minister did not say that.
He tried to get out of it, but he admitted it in his first statement.
No.

We will prove it by ' Hansard ' when it comes out this morning. I appeal to the Minister of Agriculture again. He is an old member of the House, as I am. I think he will agree with me that never before has he seen the House held up in debating a private Bill.
That proves that my hon. friend's friends are the most unreasonable men that have been here for many years.

The leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden), before leaving at two o'clock this morning, asked that the committee should rise, that plans that had been referred to in connection with this matter might be brought down. That was a reasonable request. The Minister of Public Works said the majority must rule. The majority is the government, and they are defending and supporting this Bill, a graft Bill of the worst kind. But they say the majority must rule and we will force the opposition down.
We do not know which is the majority until we vote.

The hon. member for Hants (Mr. Black) threw out the challenge that they would stay here until Saturday night at six .o'clock or pass the Bill. Hon. gentlemen on this side said they would stay with them and we purpose doing so. If the government are going to defend this Bill until Saturday night, it will be the first time I knew a government to back up a private Bill in this way. I think the government ought to accede to the reasonable request to allow the committee to rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again and in the meantime bring down the plans so we will see what we are doing, because there is no denying that it is all one company trying to dam the St. Lawrence and to use this charter to transmit power.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As a number of gentlemen have entered the House recently who have not had the great pleasure some of us have had of sitting all night until 9.30 o'clock, and for their benefit, I wish to again place on Hansard the exact position of this matter. I stated at an earlier stage
that every two hours I would put this point on record so there might be no misunderstanding. I wish it to be understood that there is no proposal on the part of anybody, still less on the part of the government, who have nothing to do with this Bill, to press this Bill through at this sitting of the House. I want that to go on Hansard in large letters. A proposal was made hours ago that this Bill might be treated like any other Bill, that the clauses that are unimportant might be passed and any contentious clauses might stand over, the Bill remaining in committee until a future day. We offered that hours ago, I offer it now.

The Finance Minister has. made that proposal time and again, but he must see the unreasonable part of it, that is that if we accept the Bill as it is at present, we will have to have the measure put through and it will be forced through by the government, no matter what the clauses are.. When we come to discuss it on the clauses, we will be confined to the clause before the committee. It cannot be too strongly impressed that this Bill is opposed by many important interests, such as boards of trade of our Canadian cities, and the Conservation Commission.

I wish to read a resolution that was moved in the Private Bills Committee for the addition of a clause to this Bill, and was voted down:
Nothing in this Act contained shall he construed to authorize the company to enter on, take or use any land or water, the property of any province, without having first obtained by order of the lieutenant governor in council the consent of the province to such entry, taker or user.
I wish to ask my hon. friend the Minister c.f Agriculture what objection he would have to a clause of this kind being inserted in the Bill.

My hon. friend is well aware that I am not a lawyer, and consequently would not like to commit myself on such a point without very careful legal advice. My own idea would be that the rights of the Dominion and the rights of the various provinces are pretty well defined in the British North America Act, and we could probably leave to those definitions to decide whether we were interfering with the rights of any province or not.
I suppose the next in order will be my hon. friend the Minister of Labour.

As I understand, the discussion of the committee is at present engaged on one section of the Bill. After I have an opportunity of listening to the debate as a whole, I shall perhaps be better able to appreciate whether the proposed amendment has any significance or not.
As these hon. gentlemen belong to this government, which is pressing the House to pass this Bill-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, no.

The Minister of Finance may suggest that the opposition all comes from this side of the House; but I may remind him that the strongest pronouncement against the Bill has come from the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson), and that it is also opposed by the hon member or Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff). If it is not proposed to take away any rights from any province, what objection can there be to this clause going into the Bill? I appeal to the Minister of the Interior, who before he entered this government was a champion of the rights of the people, to say if he sees any special objection to such a clause being inserted in the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would have to follow the discussion more closely than I have done in order to be able to give an answer to the question. Apparently this is a very involved matter. It has occupied the House during twelve or fourteen hours, and I certainly do not profess to have been able to follow the discussion during that time or to be able to make up my mind on the mere reading of the resolution.

I wish to point out that my hon. friend has brought forward this resolution on two or three occasions, and that the Minister of Public Works has pointed out that the question of dealing with the water power of the St. Lawrence river is not in the Bill before the House, but that if it were in issue, the declaration in the resolution proposes to settle a matter in dispute between the Dominion and the province by giving to the province wider powers than it has under the British North America Act. If this we,re a Bill involving the question of the construction of a dam, I would oppose that resolution on this ground. If the province controls the water-power, that control cannot be taken away by any declaration or legislation of this parliament. Why should we make a declaration which undertakes to give the province a more extended power than the constitution gives it?

The hon. gentleman who has just spoken is evidently an ardent opponent of this Bill, or at least will be when he comes to understand what it really means. We have had within the last ten minutes the lamentable exhibition of a minister of the Crown coming in at ten o'clock in the morning and frankly admitting that he is using all his power to force through the House this Bill without know ing what it is; and we find the hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) who should understand this Bill if any one does, distinctly stating that it does not and can
not take away from the province any rights it now has.
Does the hon. gentleman say it would?
I certainly say that it both can and does.
Does he say it deals with water powers at all?
I mean to say it does give water powers.
Will my hon. friend read the clause?

It has been read a dozen times, but I will explain it and perhaps then the hon. gentleman will see that it does give water powers and is intended to give them. Let us understand where we are. By jumping into the middle of the. discussion, my hon. friend fails to understand-
I have been here all night.

I have read that seed sown on stony ground just as carefully as on other ground did not take any root. That may be the case with my hon. friend. We had an Act passed in 1901 which no member of this House, if he will divest himself of his political prejudice, will say reflects any great credit on its judgment. By the Act a copy was incorporated, and it is a matter of notoriety that this House gave such powers to the gentlemen who obtained that charter that they were able to sell it at a handsome fortune. However, all that is past and gone, and the only argument I draw from that is this, that having made an outrageous blunder in 1901, is all the more reason why we should be doubly careful now not to give a little more and supply an omission which the promoters, by an oversight, failed to notice in the Act of 1901. In 1901 they are asking a little privilege which will make the government of 1901 absolutely complete. In the statute of 1901, the directors are given prettv broad powers. Under the Sth section thev can manufacture and dispose of electricity and build a transmission line. It is perfectly clear that under that Act this company has the power to construct its transmission line exactly where it asks to construct it by the Bill before it.
My hon. friend is mistaken in that. He will find that it does not give the company the power of expropriation for their transmission lines.

The hon. gentleman is perfectly right, and that is the reason the company come here to take the land belonging to the province of Ontario for the purposes of their enterprise. By this Bill, however, they ask that power. They

have the right to manufacture all the power they want in the Act of 1901, and they have the right to expropriate but not to expropriate provincial lands.
Where does my hon. friend find that?

I find nothing in the Act of 1901 which gives this company power to expropriate provincial lands. There is all the difference in the world between giving power to expropriate the land of individuals and the land belonging to the Crown. Under the statute of 1901 there is no power given the St. Lawrence Power Company to expropriate any land belonging to the province of Ontario. But this Bill of 1910 expressly gives the company all the powers conferred by the Railway Act.
For the purposes of its works.
Certainly.
That would give them power if necessary to expropriate provincial lands.

No, there is merely the general power given but not the rest to expropriate land vested in the Crown and provincial lands are vested in the Crown just the same as Dominion lands. The provincial claim held in the Attorney General of British Columbia against the Canadian Pacific Railway that section 108 of the British North America Act specially empowers the Dominion parliament to legislate regarding any lands including the foreshores proved to govern part of a public harbour. It empowers the Dominion to give the right to expropriate provincial crown land and, therefore, it has the right to expropriate the provincial foreshore for the purpose of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Taking this decision as our basis, we find in the powers conferred by the Railway Act that corporations have the right to expropriate provincial lands. Beyond question that follows from the decision in this case. Nothing can be clearer than the words in this Bill making the Railway Act applicable to this company. So it is obvious that this company, while professing to ask simply the power to extend their lines along the shore, are really asking something different.

I would ask the hon. gentleman whether that power, which he says is conferred under this Bill, of expropriating lands and waters belonging to a province, would apply to any waters or lands belonging to a province which they expropriate for the purpose of creating power. This Bill is one allowing the company to transmit power, and for that purpose the Railway Act and its expropriation
clauses apply to these people, but that would not make those clauses apply to powers granted another company under another Bill.
This company is given rather broad powers under section 6.
Under this Bill the company has no power to generate electricity.
What is the difference between a scheme carried on under one act of incorporation and a scheme carried on under two charters, if they are both controlled by the same people?
Any powers given under this Bill for the purposes of transmission do not apply to rights and privileges for the purpose of creating power.
That is a distinction without a difference if both companies are controlled by the same people.
I do not think so.
I do.

The Minister of Public Works said that in his opinion this company we are now asked to incorporate, is simply a transmission company. When asked where they expected to get their power, he said from a dam that will be constructed across the St. Lawrence, suggesting the charter of the St. Lawrence Power Company. It would not be worth while to pass a Bill of this kind unless the company were to get their power from some other company because there is no power in this Bill for the generation of electricity.
That is what I have been pointing out.
Would the hon. minister state where this company is going to get their power.
That is for .them to find out.

Will he explain in whose name and on whose behalf plans for damming this river were brought to the Minister of Public Works? I thought we had a pretty plain statement from that minister but perhaps my hon. friend will give a little new light.
Mr. FOSTT;''R I cannot see how this matters in the slightest degree to this Bill.

The promoters of this scheme, having secured that particular Act, possessing it and controlling it, propose under that to dam the St. Lawrence and already have their plans filed and submitted to the Minister of Public Works, who has had them considered by the engineers of three departments-does mv hon. friend claim, if that he the case, and the claims of these men that they can dam the river under

that Act be well founded, that this Bill, which gives certain powers to the very men who control that charter, is not part of a great general scheme for damming the St. Lawrence? This is an ingenious scheme for creating power and for conveying the ownership of that power by a very easy method to this company. By employing this company for the purpose of transmission, it is simply doing the work by two companies instead of by one. Can my hon. friend not see that? .

I cannot see why, if an Act of this parliament gives them power to generate electricity, they should not then be given the power .to transmit that electrical energy where this Bill allows them to do it. The question of a dam and the creation of power are not in this Bill. That is not conferred on the company by this Bill; but if my hon. friend is correct in his interpretation of another Bill and they have the right he says they enjoy, then I do not see why they should not be allowed to transmit the power to various localities in Canada which might benefit bv using it.

I will give the hon. gentleman some reasons. There was not the slightest suspicion in the minds of any man in this House when the Act of 1901 was passed, that any such scheme was intended. I have carefully looked over the debates of 1901 and find that the Bill went- through the House without a word of comment. Some very clever words were introduced into some of the paragraphs in the Act of 1901, and the contention of those who control that charter is that it enables them to build a dam across the St. Lawrence joining a dam on the American side, and thus generate that power. Having that authority, they ask that this parliament shall give them certain other powers which will only be useful for the purpose of carrying out the bigger scheme to which I have alluded, and I say that that is too big a scheme to receive the approval of this House under the conditions which prevail at present. We do not know enough about it. We have not even seen the plans which have been in the possession of the Minister of Public Works for eight months, and which we find, to our astonishment, he had submitted to three engineers of the government who made a report without any man in this House knowing anything about it. We were astounded "last evening to discover how far this project has advanced and how far the government is committed to it without making known its intentions to parliament, Under the circumstances, when this Bill is proposed as part of that great scheme, vitally and materially affecting the future interests of Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
this country, affecting the great waterway of the St. Lawrence, the products of the west, and when there is lack of information and the absence of any definite policy of the government in regard to that scheme, it is perfectly clear it should not receive the approval of the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman stated that- he was surprised to find how far the government were committed to this scheme. I think he will see that last night it was distinctly stated by my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works that the government were not committed at all to it.
I said I was surprised to see how far the government were committed to it. I did not say that the government were absolutely committed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If they are not committed, how can the hon. gentleman see how far they are committed?
I could not say. My hon. friend should know more about that than I do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, my knowledge is the same.

Perhaps so. Afterwards we discovered from the Minister of Public Works yesterday that he had gone so far as to send the engineers of three different departments to consider these plans, that they had been considered with certain objections which had been raised and that finally the engravers had come back with the plans which he said they had approved and which, as far as I can gather, had the approval of the government. They might not have had the formal approval of the government-I do not understand that they had-but if these three engineers had been sent to report upon the project and if they had reported favourably upon it with certain modifications it seems to me that they have made very great progress indeed towards winning the aporoval of the government. That impression is very greatly strengthened by the circumstance that the Minister of Public Works seemed to have committed himself to the project by attempting to drive this Bill through the com mittee before the committee should rise, although a respectful request was made to him at one o'clock this morning, wdien we had sat an hour and a half later than the House usually sits, and when the discussion had been absolutely relevant and instructive in every respect, that the committee should rise, the request was refused and we were told shortly afterwards by an hon member on the other side of the House that the government had determined to sit until Saturday night for the purpose of driving this Bill through. Thatr would seem to indicate that the government are pretty well committed to this Bill or they would not take a stand of that kind. I never knew a

statement of that kind to be made with regard to a private Bill or any other Bill under similar circumstances. There had not been one minute of debate in regard to this Bill that had not been relevant and instructive up to the time I made this request. A great deal of the debate had been raised by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) and by the hon member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), one of whom declared that this was evidently a .much larger scheme than the House was aware of at first, and the other of whom stated that this Bill had evidently been presented to the House under false pretenses. I say that the action of the Minister of Public Works under the circumstances indicates that whether the government's committed to this scheme or not the Minister of Public Works is very strongly committed to it; otherwise he would not have taken the action that he did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am obliged to take exception to the hon. gentleman's inaccuracies. If this matter is as important as the hon. gentleman thinks it is, he will agree with me that he should not be inaccurate in his statements.
I am very glad to be corrected.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I take exception to the statement that he made that some hon. gentleman on this side of the House stated that the government would sit here until Saturday evening. I say that no such statement was made.	[DOT]
What was the statement then?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend is making the statement he should not ask me to furnish him with the information.
Does the hon. gentleman say that the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Black) -did not state that? *

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member for Hants spoke for himself. The hon. member for Hants made no allusion to the government. No man undertook to speak in the name of the government in reference to this Bill. From the beginning to the end it was stated to be a private Bill in which the government had no concern and if my hon. friend was informed that a member on this side of the House said that the government would stay here until Saturday night and force this Bill through I can assure him that he was misinformed.
The hon. member for Hants is the chairman of the committee which had this Bill under consideration, is ha not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understand that he was acting chairman.
Well, he seemed to speak with some authority.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says that he ' seemed ' to speak with some authority. . A moment ago he said that the hon. member for Hants said that the government had determined to force this Bill through.
What did the hon. member for Hants say?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not called upon to answer for the hon. member for Hants; I am called upon to answer for the government when the government is misrepresented. My hon. friend was not so anxious to make a point against the hon. member for Hants as against the government. The essence of his statement was that he said that the government was going to force this Bill through.
Some lion. MEMBERS. So he did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that in that respect he has ()een misinformed. I have another objection to make to a statement of my hon. friend in which statement my hon. friend has also been inaccurate. He said that he was surprised to find how far the government have been committed to this scheme of damming the St- Lawrence. The English language is plain enough for my hon. friend to know that if he was surprised to find how far the government -was committed, then the government must have been committed, and yet the statement made by the Minister of Public Works was that the government was in no way committed, although it had caused some inquiry to be made by engineers. There are many projects presented to the government and to parliament as to which engineers are asked to make reports; but would any one contend that because the government sent out an engineer to inquire into a matter the government are committed to it?
