It is not a reasonable argument at all.

I would like to say in reply to what the Minister of Finance has advanced that I do not think all the inaccuracies are on this side of the House. What the hon. member for Hants said he said in the presence of the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Did my hon. friend hear him?
I heard him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I beg my hon. friend's pardon; I thought he was not present.

He said: We will stay here until Saturday night to put this Bill through. I am not quoting his exact words, but that is the substance of them, the Minister of Finance -was here at the time and he did not disclaim them. He

seemed, as far as I could judge, to assent t >
that declaration. The hon. member for Hants said that in his presence and said it after I had asked respectfully and courteously, at one o'clock, and after the hon. member for Westmorland had also asked that this committee should rise. Take the language of the hon. member for Hants, unrepudiated by the Minister of Finance, and take the action of the Minister of Finance in refusing to permit this committee to rise, put these two things together and let us see whether the inaccuracy is on my part or on the part of the Minister of Finance. My hon. friend says that I am inaccurate in stating that I did not know how far the government was committed to this project.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, that was not the hon. gentleman's statement. His statement was that he was surprised to find how far the government were committed.

Well, I am surprised to find how far the government are committed. Actions speak a great deal louder than words. When we find what has been going on without the knowledge of parliament, when we find that the Minister of Public Works informed us that these plans have been under consideration for eight months, when we find that they have been referred to engineers, that these engineers have reported favourably upon them, with some modifications, and when we find the Minister of Public Works evincing such a deep and abiding interest in having this Bill go through without the production of these plans upon the table of the House, I am surprised to find the government is committed to this project to that extent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To what extent?

To the extent of carrying on these negotiations with these gentlemen, having these plans referred to the engineers, receiving a favourable report about them, and making no communication whatever to this House in regard to the form of that report. It only come out last evening by accident. What does it mean? We had the Minister of Public Works endeavouring to convince this House at first-he was obliged to abandon the position afterwards-that these plans had been submitted to the government without the authority of any statute. Did any one ever hear of such a position? A body of men, without any statute, without any charter, without any legal sanction, come to this government and say: Here are certain pians for damming the St. Lawrence; will you be good enough to send the engineers of your department and have these plans considered? That was the position wdiich the Minister of Public Works took at first, but afterwards, under the Mr. R. L BORDEN.
effect of certain discussion, raised not from this side of the House, but from the other side by the hon. member for Westmorland, the Minister of Public Works was obliged to admit, and did admit in answer to myself that these plans were put forward to this government under the authority conferred by a Bill passed by this House in 1901. This House was absolutely in ignorance of the fact that the persons controlling that charter believed themselves to possess the power to dam the River St. Lawrence. I had no knowledge that any such claim had been made until that admission was drawn from the Minister of Public Works last night by the hon. member for Westmorland. This has been going on behind the back of parliament and behind the back of the country. Certain gentlemen acquired the charter of the St. Lawrence Power Company. These gentlemen had raised the claim that under that they have authority from parliament to build a dam across the St. Lawrence as far as the boundary line. The same gentlemen have procured legislation from the State of New-York authorizing them to build a dam from the American side to the same boundary line. These gentlemen, having these charters in their possession, came to the government, probably more than a year ago, presented their plans, and these plans have been under consideration by the government, knowing of the claim of these men, for at least eight months. The Bill now before the House is, according to the admission of the Minister of Public Works, a Bill which is designed to carry out part of this great scheme. That is the position, and under the circumstances and having regard to the action which this government have taken in endeavouring to force this Bill through against all custom and precedent, I am surprised that they have been so far committed to this project as they seem to have been.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has made an outcry, and many other hon. gentlemen have done the same thing, as to the government having in their possession certain plans which they did not present to the House, and which they say they are hiding from the House, which they are suppressing. There are hundreds of plans presented to the government in relation to public matters, and which are to be found in the various departments, which are never presented to parliament, and unless some hon. gentleman had asked for a plan and it had been refused, there would be no ground whatever, for complaint.
I asked for them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman asked for them last evening when he knew he could not get them.
I did not know that 1 could not get them. The Finance Minister and the Minister of Public Works stated here last night that these two Bills had a most important relation one to the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have said that plans are submitted to the government and unless there was some special request for them they would not be brought down to the House and so this bugaboo is extremely ridiculous.
Would the government send three engineers to see whethei plans prepared by persons having no authority to build a line of railway should be approved?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps not, but if they did send an engineer and plans were produced and filed in the archives of the department they would never be brought to this House unless they were asked for.
Were they not asked for at the Private Bills Committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know. The hon. member says he never knew anything about them until last night.
I am not on the Private Bills Committee, otherwise you bet they would have been asked for.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I find I was too charitable in supposing that the leader of the opposition was not here when the member for Hants spoke, he was here. He shifted his ground in his last speech, he first said that the member for Hants stated that the government would sit here. I took exception to that statement and when he was called to account he said that he heard the hon. member for Hants and that hon. member said: * We.'
Who is ' we.'
Who controls this House?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Nobody controls this House, this is the free and independent parliament of this country and it is not controlled I say in the name of the Liberals of this country there is no authority to control the parliament of Canada.
To whom did the member for Hants refer when he used the word 'we '?
The friends of the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I suppose the member for Hants spoke foT himself, perhaps he is in the editorial chair sometimes.
If the government are not committed to this proposition is that not all the more reason to call a halt.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend does not know, we called a halt long ago when he was sleeping.

If they are not committed to the project and it is known that this is part of a much wider project, why commit the House to this minor proposition when there is still a major proposition to be dealt with? The government will surely take time to discuss this with the International Waterways Commission, the Conservation Commission and other bodies of that kind. The Minister of Finance is engaged in a great issue in regard to the tariff. It is said that the United States government may have to put in force their maximum tariff against this country on account of some action of this government, and at this very time we propose to pass legislation which means that the greatest power we have left on the St. Lawrence may be so developed that the bulk of the power will be transmitted to the United States for the development of their resources. We ought to keep in our hands the absolute control of that power which may be an important factor in this tariff discussion with the United States. This power is to be used, as far as I can judge, to electrify the New York Central Railway, one of the greatest rivals of our Canadian system. That power ought to be reserved to electrify the Canadian roads. The Bill could well stand over for another year. An international claim may be based on what is done now and so we should move slowly. The province of Ontario and the people of Toronto are trying to work out a great political principle known as public ownership. For some reason this principle is being assailed by many interests, and a determined effort is being made here to prevent the progress of that movement in relation to electrical energy. There is no urgency except the urgency of private as against national interest. Is the national interest to be jeopardized in order that private interests may be advanced? Where is the national urgency? The matter should at least rest for a time to allow the fullest discussion and amplification of the facts.

The leader of the opposition and some other members may not have heard the offer from the Minister of Finance early in the evening, that in order to prevent a deadlock he would be willing that the committee should pass the noncontentious clauses of this Bill?
There are none.
Oh, no.

That is what I understood him to say. The course of hon. members opposite is a pure question of obstruction on their part, and in all fairness and having regard to the rules of this House and to the general conduct of public affairs in any legislative assembly, a minority ought

not to undertake to dictate or to control the House either in regard to the legislation of the mode of procedure with any particular legislation. I cannot see any difference between, a private Bill and any other kind of Bill. It is just a question of the majority ruling. This Bill has nothing to do with the navigation of the St. Lawrence river. It does not disturb the lock, which is on the Canadian side, and not on the American side. The reason for the proposal of a lock on the American side is that there is a channel there which steamers coming down the river run without going through the lock.
Large steamers cannot go through the south channel.

But certain steamers do use it. It is not this government that is insisting on a lock on the American side, but the United States congress. In that there is no menace to Canadian interests, but an improvement. The Minister of Public Works has stated time and again during the debate that the government were not committed to any improvements of the river, and that no plan would be approved of by them until it was first submitted to and approved by parliament. The hon. member says this Bill is linked with another Bill. I do not know that it is so.
The Minister of Public Works said so.
The Minister of Public Works was asked where they were going to get their power, and he said he expected they would get it from the St. Lawrence Power Company.
Where does my hon. friend expect they will get it?

I do not know, and I do know that my hon. friend knows; but 1 do know that they could get more than 100,000 horse-power without dealing with the St. Lawrence Power Company at all. I know that there is power at the Lachine rapids, at Cornwall and at other points on the St. Lawrence where they could get power. Hon. gentlemen have referred to the Bill passed in 1901 giving a charter to a company to build a dam and generate and utilize electrical power. It is doubtful if they have exercised that power sufficiently to hold their charter. But assuming that they have that power, hon. gentlemen do not take it away by holding up this Bill. Moreover, at that time we did not make the rights of the company subordinate to the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners. Under this Bill, we protect the public interests by putting machinery in force that will insure to the people cheap power and reasonable service. I do not care whether it is Canadian capital, or American capital, or English capital that develops this dr any other water-Mr. CONMEE
power so long as the people of Canada have that power under their control. This company cannot, under the law, export any power unless the government allows them to do so, and I have sufficient confidence in this government to believe that it will not alow them to do that. I may have objections to some of the clauses of this Bill, but the time has not come to discuss them. Hon. gentlemen who are opposing the Bill are determined that, as they are in the minority, they will not allow a vote to take place. I do not think any good purpose can be served by- that attitude. I submit that the hon. minister has made a reasonable proposition which hon. gentlemen should accept.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to call your attention to the fact that the Railway Committee, of which you are the chairman, is called to meet at eleven o'clock this morning, that it is now that hour, and that there are engagements to meet to-day by that committee, and parties are here attending on those engagements who would like to go on; and I submit to the leader of the House, in order that the work of the House may not be disarranged, especially in view of the statement that the government is not committed to this Bill, that the committee should rise and report progress, and that those who are members of the Railway Committee should have an opportunity to go and attend to its business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I quite appreciate the desire of my hon. friend to put an end to this protracted sitting and to go to the business of the Railway Committee; but after all we must meet the situation as we find it. He is not aware of the proposals made on this matter when he supposes that the government is attempting to force this Bill through the committee. That is due to a misapprehension of the facts. At an early stage of the discussion I asked that this Bill be treated as any other private Bill. Most of the clauses are unimportant and non-contentious, and I proposed that we pass them clause by clause, and that whenever a clause was reached that any hon. member wished to have stand over, I would raise rny voice to have it stand over, and the Bill would remain in committee to give hon. members a reasonable time to prepare their amendments or do anything else that was necessary. That is a fair and reasonable proposition, and is entirely at variance with the suggestion that the government aTe trying to force this Bill through.

Let the Minister of Finance recall the situation last night. Until the Minister of Public Works made the formal statement that he did regarding the connection between the company controlling this Bill and the St. Lawrence Water Power Company, the feeling on this side was to

accede to the suggestion made by the Minister of Finance. But how were we met up to that time? Five ministers of the Crown sat in a row, and, I say it advisedly, never during the twenty sessions that I have been in this House have I seen them fight more ardently for any government measure than they fought for this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the only other minister who spoke on the matter besides myself was the Minister of Public Works. If there were five ministers of the Crown sitting here, they were only doing their duty.

If more of them sat here while the government measures were being discussed, we would be less surprised; but when a government measure is before the House, there are usually only two or three ministers present. But on this private measure, the mandate was sent out by the leader of the House to the chief whip from the province of Ontario, the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee), who is in charge of this Bill, that not one concession was to be made, and the Minister of Finance told me that we had to let the Bill pass last night. That was early in the evening. We have discovered' by our fighting that the company promoting this Bill is intimately asociated with the St. Lawrence Power Company, and I give the minister notice that we are going to get to the bottom of this thing before this Bill goes through.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hope you will, and I will help you.

It might be well to find just how far we are in accord. We have a Bill before the House to confer certain rights on a company in connection with transmitting power throughout a district on the St. Lawrence river not very far from here, and for some reason no member from that district, and knowing the feelings of the people there, would father such a Bill, and its promoters had to go to the western limits of the province to find any one to father it, and selected the chief government whip for that purpose. That is a piece of evidence which certainly points in one direction, though it does not necessarily prove what is behind the Bill. Then the Bill comes before the House and we do not find the hon. gentleman who fathers the Bill or any of the hon. gentlemen from the part of the country more particularly concerned taking any active part in supporting it.
I beg my hon. friend's pardon. I have been strongly supporting it all through the debate.

I apologize to the hon. member for Rainy River. I admit that I was wrong. I admit that he is the father of all waterworks legislation save this and he is the step-father of this. We find that this Bill was introduced by the chief gov-173*
ernment whip and that it is supported by the members of the cabinet, and when an hon. gentleman, sitting beside the minister' who is now leading the House (Mr. Fielding), says that they will sit until Saturday night if necessary to force the Bill through, that is certainly further evidence -to excite suspicion. The hon. gentleman-who leads the House found fault with the' leader of the opposition because he did not exactly quote the words used by the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Black). But the hon. gentleman himself did not quote his words.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why should I?
I think he should have done so or not have contradicted the leader of the opposition. As a man of honour, he could not contradict him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no right to answer for the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Black). I understand that the hon. gentleman, feeling displeased at the conduct of hon. gentlemen opposite, expressed his own views. He did not profess to speak for the government, he had not the right to do so, and he would be the last man to attempt to do so.

In order to be perfectly fair to the Minister of Finance and afford him the opportunity to make the explanation, I am sure he is anxious to make, I ask him now whether it is the intention of the government to force the Bill through?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The government have no intention in the matter. This is a private Bill, and I have expressed the view that this Bill shall not be forced through and that hon. gentlemen opposite, if they will only take a reasonable course, will have ample opportunity to consider what they deem the contentious clauses. If they will only consent to our making some progress, the Bill may remain in committee, and they will be riven ample time to consider it. Can anything be fairer?

The proposition would be perfectly reasonable and proper if it be admitted that this is a government measure, because what the hon. minister suggests is the practice whfch is followed in. connection with government measures. In 1903 I had the honour of affecting a settlement along similar lines with the Minister of Justice in connection with a government measure. The principle admitted" as settled is that when this House meets: to transact government business, some government business must be transacted or that is an admission that, the government has lost control of the House. Therefore, in connection with the Grand Trunk Paci-' fic Bill, hon. members on this side, al-

though bitterly opposed to it, consented to some objectionable clauses, assuming that the Bill must eventually pass because it was a government measure. But h.ere the case is different. If the hon. minister says that no pressure will be brought on members of the House

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have certainly said a dozen times at least that as this is not a government Bill, I would not presume to recommend it to any member of the House. How any member of the House may vote, I do not know or care. All I desire is to make some progress with business.

Inasmuch then as it is not a government measure, and hon. members are not bound by political allegiance to support it, there may be some chance that, by discussing it, we may possibly succeed in protecting the interests of the country against the promotors of this Bill. Whatever the facts may be, it is unquestionable that the province of Ontario is bitterly opposing this Bill as encroaching on its rights. Whether the province be right or wrong is another question. In my opinion, it is right. But here we have these cabinet ministers, who formerly used to boast that they were the special defenders of provincial rights, using their influence to put through a private Bill which the Ontario government says is an interference with its rights. Here we have the singular spectacle of a government intervening in the case of a private Bill to force it through, which the Ontario government says is an interference with its rights.

I have not made up my mind on this Bill entirely, but would like to consider it clause by clause. The only point affecting provincial rignts is clause one, which gives some gentlemen the right to form themselves into a company.

I am opposed to this Bill, and ony a few minutes ago I told the hon. the Finance Minister that I would vote against it. He said to me: Do as you like, because it is not a government measure. I am against it, because the Board of Trade and the municipality of Montreal oppose it, but I want to be understood that in any vote any hon. member may give on this side, he is not influenced by the government. and no one on this side is voting in a certain way because of ministerial dictation.

We are getting more and more light as the debate progresses, and probably by Friday evening or Saturday morning the House may unanimously agree to throw the measure out. In the first place, we have the Bill introduced in this House by the chief government whip, who lives 100 miles away from the locus in quo, and in the second place, the Bill is Mr. NORTHRUP.
being pushed through the house by the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

It is by the efforts of the hon. gentleman who is leading the government that the Bill is thrust upon the House. Then we have this other fact. If we look into the Act of 1901, we find that that Act would apparently require the construction of works on this side of the St. Lawrence, and it seems to me impossible for the St. Lawrence Power Company, under their Act, to carry on their business without constructing works on this side of the St. Lawrence. But the company now being incorporated is asking the power to make contracts for the purchase of electricity from any other company. So that this company could lease their electricity from the American side. In every way therefore the in terests of Canada would be overlooked and the interests of the state of New York protected. We all know the wonderful strength of vested rights. If these enormous power plants were established on the American side and the electricity distributed along the Canadian shore to various industries, then the time might come when the supply of electricity from the United States might be shut off unless our Canadian industries w'ould give way to some threat from the other side. As was held by my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) this is a most inopportune time for Canada to do anything which would in any way jeopardize its supply of electric power. We have recklessly given away an immense amount of national wealth in timber, coal and minerals, and here it is proposed that we should part with the last and greatest of all our assets, the water-power of the St. Lawrence, which is equal to almost all the water-powers on this continent taken together; and we are doing this in absolute ignorance because there is not a member in this House competent to discuss and estimate the consequence of such an act.

I want to try and give an intelligent vote on this Bill. I have listened for some hours to the discussion, and as I understand the rules of the House, we are simply called upon to consider clause 1 of the Bill. Clause I provides that certain gentlemen of Ontario, with the exception of one who is a resident of the town of Messina, N.Y., shall be incorporated into a Company. The question of provincial rights I understand may be discussed under clause 6. When we come to the other clauses, if we find that the rights of any province are jeopardized, it would then be proper to reject any proposal which will have this effect. But by rule 53, I take it that this Bill must be considered clause by clause. I think it is a very fair proposal on the part of the government to ask hon. members to consider clause 1, against which there can be absolutely no objection and

then, after the clause is passed, it will be in order to consider whether we should go on with another clause.

I do not understand what my hon. friend means by saying there can be no objection to clause 1. Why should we incorporate a number of men, a lot of them unknown, to transmit power? Where are they going to transmit it to?
We will come to that in considering the other clauses.
The hon. gentleman says we must stick to clause 1. I would point out that he is prepared to vote for something without knowing what it may amount to. Where is this power to be transmitted to?
That will come up for consideration in a subsequent clause.

Not necessarily. This clause undertakes to say what the name of this company shall be. It is the St.. Lawrence Power Transmission Company, Limited. The St. Lawrence river is a boundary stream, and if you are going to transmit power from the St, Lawrence you are just as liable to transmit it southerly as northerly, and I do not think this clause should pass without more limitation.	.
I am not now discussing the merits of the Bill. I may wish to vote against clause 6, but that is no reason why I should vote against clause 1.

I do not think we should pass clause 1. I do not agree with the point raised by the hon. gentleman who has just spoken, that there is no harm in passing clause 1 even if I did admit that there was nothing but the name of the company in it. When we are incorporating this compaaiy as the St. Lawrence Power Transmission Company, Limited. I want to know what sort of transmission they are going on with.

If the hon. gentleman could point out anything against the honour or ability of the gentlemen seeking this incorporation, I could understand that there must be an objection to it, But, if they are honourable gentlemen, the usual practice of parliament is to allow them to be incorporated and then decide afterwards what shall be the powers to be given to them.
Mr. LANCASTER, The hon. gentleman might be quite willing to give them all the powers that they ask, but I am not willing and I do not say that this is any slur upon their honour or ability. The government is not prepared to tell us what these gentlemen are going to do. The government apnarently knew months ago but they have not seen fit to place these plans before parliament, and parliament does not know.
The company are in this position, that they cannot legally get this legislation by any secret arrangement with the government, although they must have made one. They ask parliament to endorse it, but they will not show the plans to the endorser. Yet my hon. friend thinks we should go on and consent to clause 1 of the Bill If my hon. friend knows that there is no harm in clause 1 will he give us the information that he possesses and undertake to get these plans that we have asked for so that parliament may vote intelligently upon this question.
That is just what I want to do. I want to give an intelligent vote upon the Bill after due consideration of it.
By whom?
By the House.
Well, let us have the plans.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have no plans affecting this clause.

By rule 53 I find that ' in proceedings of the committee of the whole House upon bills, the preamble is first postponed and then every clause considered by the committee in its proper order, the preamble and title to be last considered.' We are now at clause 1 and there is absolutely no question of plans in clause 1. When we come to subsequent clauses it may be open to any hon. gentleman to ask for the production of plans in order that we may see just exactly what power they seek, but it is certainly not under clause 1.

Is it not unusual that plans are withheld until we reach a clause in the Bill which requires a discussion of the plans? Would it not be fair to submit the plans when the subject was introduced for discussion in the committee?

I perfectly agree that it will be proper for the promoters of this Bill to produce the plans of the powers which they may be seeking to exercise when we come to the consideration of those particular clauses, but under clause 1 of the Bill I fail to see how any plans which might be produced would enlighten us upon the character, the quality or the honour or ability of the few gentlemen of the province of Ontario who are seeking incorporation under the name of the St. Lawrence Power Transmission Company, Limited.

Clause 1 seeks to incorporate these gentlemen under the name of the St, Lawrence Power Transmission Company, Limited. Before we allow them to be incorporated under that name surely

we ought to know what sort of power they are going to transmit and where they are going to transmit it to. The hon. gentleman says that when we get to certain clauses these plans should be produced. Are we going to bring the promoters before the bar of the House when we get to these clauses and call upon them to produce these plans? I say that they should have been produced when the Bill was called, but the hon. gentlemen admits that when we get to certain operative clauses these plans should be produced.
What plans is the hon. gentleman referring to?
To the plans that you were referring to that you stated the promoters should be called upon to produce?
I was not referring to any clause, but I said that if there were any plans to be produced, I presumed they would be produced. I did not know what they referred to.

We should have had these plans put on the table of the House before the Bill was called at all, why should we be prevented from examining them? These plans might be produced at a subsequent stage of this Bill, but the clause applicable to them would be called carried while hon. gentlemen were looking at the plans to see what they contain. There must be some reason in all this. I suspect this is a huge attempt being made by some persons-some of whom are mentioned and some of whom are not-to get possession of these water-powers on the St. Lawrence and avoid all our legislation about the exportation of electrical power, &c. These plans would settle the question. 'The people want to get that information, and they will have it.
What information?

The information that the government have, but that parliament has not. The engineers have made these plans, the government have seen them and -still they withhold them from parliament. Why do they want to keep that information from the country? What is wrong about it? Some hon. gentlemen propose to stay here until Saturday night to put this Bill through. I am prepared to stay until Saturday night, if the Lord allows me to live that long, before I shall vote for any such legislation.
If the hon. gentleman is sincere in his position-
Did the hon. gentleman ever know me not to be sincere in any position I took?

I am asking if he is sincere

	*
You can bet your life on that.

The rules of the House compel us to accept any hon. gentleman's statement as to his sincerity and I am not questioning the hon. gentleman's sincerity. If he wants to question it he has a perfect right to do so. The proposition that this Bill should be considered clause by clause seems to me to be very reasonable. The hon. rnember knows that passing a clause in this committee does not finally pass it. If the hon. member is sincere in his desire not to give these gentlemen any undue powers, why can he not wait until we arrive at the clauses in the Bill which are objectionable to him as giving undue powers? He talks about plans, i find no reference to any powers granted to the incorporators in this Bill that call for any plans. That has been said over and over again. Hon. members are simply trying to^ connect up this Bill with some other Bill, some other proposition, that has no relationship to the Bill before us.

The Prime Minister is now here and perhaps he would use the influence of that sweet smile of his to induce the hon. members behind him to permit the committee to rise and report progress, and ask leave to sit again, as it is about twelve o'clock. The Prime Minister has not heard the argument on this Bill. It is a private Bill and the government should not take sides on it. When the Bill was introduced the opposition and others asked that it should stand over, Rut the Minister of Public Works could not agree that the minister -said last night that the majority must rule. This being a private Bill there is no majority unless the government force their majority to back it up. Hon. gentlemen on this side took a different view of it and we have been talking since five o'clock las! evening. The question which was asked of an hon. member a few minutes ago was not answered as the Minister of Public Works answered it last night. The discussion that then took place was as follows:
Where does the minister think they would get their power?

My own idea is that they will get their power from a company which may develop it along the St. Lawrence. I do not know that to be the case but I suspect it. This Bill simply incorporates a transmission company which would have to make an arrangement with another company for its power. The development of power upon the St. Lawrence must be provided for by another statute, but this Bill does not give the slightest authority to dam the St. Lawrence or construct any works in the St. Lawrence or anywhere else except such works as are essential for a transmission line. As head of the department which has been investigating this subject, the matter has come before
Mr. LANCASTER,

me and hon. gentlemen are doubtless aware that the plans of the company were submitted to the government for the development of water-powers on the St. Lawrence. It was directed that these plans should be referred to the chief engineer of the Department of Railways, the chief engineer of Public Works, and the chief engineer of Marine and .Fisheries.
Under what statute did the company profess to be acting when it submitted these plans?

They did not state, but I understood it to be under the St. Lawrence Power Company charter granted by this parliament some years ago. I also understood from them that they expected to have to come back to parliament to get authority to dam the St. Lawrence.

They have it under the other statute.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. So my hon. friend (Mr. Emmerson) thinks, but they did not lead us to understand that they had. The three engineers to whom the plans were referred reported adversely to the plans as originally proposed, and they suggested certain _ modifications which were accepted. The engineers, reported that the project was feasible, that the dam could be erected without interference with navigation, and the matter is now before the International Waterways Commission.
I was going to assure the committee that no plans would be approved of, no arrangement would be approved of, no agreement would be ratified by the government which does not amply protect Canadian interests. So far as the Department of Public Works is concerned, I can assure the committee that the plans will not be approved of unless upon the express stipulation, which will be thoroughly safeguarded, that one-half of the water-power which will be developed will be reserved absolutely for the use of the people on the Canadian side of the line.
Are these the dam plans?
Yes.

The thing is under consideration then?
Mr. PUGSLEY". That is the view my department has arrived at, and that will be made a sine qua non of any action the department will take.
Has your department power to do that without the consent of parliament?

I think not. Parliament will have to consent to the matter in the end, and my recollection is that some time ago, in answer to a question put by the hon. member (Mr. Hughes) the Prime Minister stated that before the plans were approved - of, the whole matter would be submitted to parliament for consideration, and before definite action would be taken, parliament must be satisfied that the work will be in the interest of Canada.

Were these plans which were submitted by the St. Lawrence Power Company to your department for approval, plans for the construction of a work to connect with another work that would come out from the American shore?

Yes, the plans were for damming the river across from the Canadian
side to the American side, and also for the building of a lock for the purpose of improving navigation, the idea being to give an additional lock to the one that is already there, and which was constructed, and is owned by the Canadian government.	.
Does the plan provide for a lock on the American side ?
Yes, and that is strongly objected to by the engineers of the department. They urge that the lock should be built on the Canadian side.

Why build a lock on the Canadian side unless the water is to be raised? The minister approves of it, the engineers say that lock has to be built, but they insist on it being on the Canadian side and the minister corroborates every word the opposition has contended for, that this company is a part and parcel of the company which got a charter in 1901. He says so here in plain language. I think the Prime Minister should allow the members of the committee to take recess and have dinner. The opposition have made a strong claim that they do not want to go on with the Bill until they see the plans in the minister's possession. I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
There is already an amendment to the motion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As I understand it, clause 1 is before the committee. There was a motion that the committee rise and report progress but that was defeated and it cannot be repeated until some further business is done.
No vote was taken.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I declared a motion of that kind lost at an earlier stage and it cannot be repeated until some further step has been taken.
I think it is unfair for honourable gentlemen opposite to keep us here against our will and prevent the public business from going on.
Private business.

We want to get at the public business. I am as keen as any other hon. member to maintain provincial rights, but I hardly see how that question comes in here. We are dealing with the St. Lawrence river, which is a navigable river, and is therefore under the exclusive jurisdiction of this parliament. But we are now considering simply clause 1 of this Bill, and the question before us is, shall a number of gentlemen of the (province of Ontario be allowed to form themselves into a company for some purpose to be here after considered? I ask the leader of the opposition whether he considers that we are wrong.

Let me enlighten the hon. gentleman with regard to clause 1, which he evidently does not understand. The St. Lawrence River Power Company, which was incorporated in 1901, and this company, are practically one and the same company, incorporated to do the same thing. [DOT]
They are two different companies, composed of altogether different gentlemen.
I do not say they are the same people; but the hon. gentleman proposes to incorporate two companies to do the same thing on the same river.
Will the hon. gentleman state whether, if we vote for clause 1, we must of necessity give this company power-that may conflict with those of another company?	.
It follows that we must give them some powers, and it follows from the name of the company that wre must give them powers for the transmission of power from the St. Law'rence river.

My hon. friend from Wright (Mr. Devlin) asks for some expression from this side of the House as to wrhy this Bill should not pass. May I direct his attention to his neighbour sitting besides him, the hon. member for St. Mary's division, Montreal (Mr. Martin). That hon. gentleman will say that in his opinion, in the interests of the largest city in Canada, this Bill should not become law because it gives this company the right to enter on the streets of Montreal without the consent of the municipality.

That statement is not correct, as the Bill stands before the committee. This company will have no power to enter on the streets of Montreal or those of any municipality without the consent of that municipality. If permitted, I would like to make clear one or two points which are evidently not known to some hon. gentlemen opposite. I had not an opportunity to be here early in the discussion, as I arrived in Ottawa only at midnight. According to my interpretation of the Bill as it has been reported on by the Private Bills Committee, the rights of the city of Montreal are absolutely safeguarded.
May I ask the hon. minister if the hon. member for St. Mary's division agrees with that?
I do not think my hon. friend would dispute it for a moment, if he reads the Bill and also section 247 of the Railway Act.
I may say that the hon. member for St. Mary's division (Mr. Martin, and the hon. member for St. James di-
vision^ (Mr. Gervais) appeared before the committee and contended that this Bill did invade the rigths of the city of Montreal.

That was before the Bill was changed. I was in the committee at the sitting when this Bill was finally passed upon and reported to the House. It was only in that sitting that the provision I have referred to was inserted. Consequently any disputes in regard to that point must have been at previous sittings.
Which provision does the hon. minister mean?

The section providing that clause 247 of the Railway Act shall apply to the works and undertakings of the company. _ That is subsection 3 of section 6 of the Bill as reported. That section was inserted for the express purpose of protecting the rights of municipalities and was accepted by the promoters of the Bill. The section provides that when any company is empowered by special Acts of the parliament of Canada, to construct or operate lines for the conveyance of light, heat, power or electricity it may, with the consent of the municipal council, or other authorities having jurisdiction over any highway, &c., enter thereon. And subsection 8 says:
Nothing contained in this section shall be deemed to authorize the company to exercise the powers therein mentioned for the purpose of selling or distributing light, heat, power or electricity in cities, towns or villages without the company having first obtained consent therefore by a by-law of the municipality.
That being the case, the rights and privileges of Montreal and all the other municipalities are absolutely safeguarded. Another word or two with regard to tome of the provisions. When the Bill first came in, there was nothing to control the rates, but we added a clause which gives the control to the Board of Railway Commissioners. The Bill, as it left the Private Bills Committee, is entirely different from the original measure.
My hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) has spoken about the opinion of the Commission for the Conservation of Natural Resources and he read a portion of a letter addressed by the Hon. Mr. Sifton, chairman of that commission, to the chairman of the Private Bills Committee. I propose to read that letter of which my hon. friend gave a part.
The letter had been previously read by the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe).

I was not aware of that:
Referring to the letter of your clerk on tha subject of Bill (No. 115), I -beg to state that the Bill has been examined as carefully %s time and information permits.

The St. Lawrence Power Company is at present seeking authority to develop a power scheme hy damming the St. Lawrence river at Long Sault. This project is being opposed by the Commission of Conservation for reasons, some of which have already been made public.
I want to point out that the company referred to is the St. Lawrence Power Company and not the St. Lawrence Transmission Ccfmpany.
An examination of Bill (No. 1151 indicates clearly that the introduction of this Bill is a portion of the St. Lawrence Power Company's plans. It is to be noted that the president of the power company and one of its engineers are the first named among the proposed incorporators, and the powers asked for are of an unusual and very sweeping charaeter.
The passage of the Bill as it stands would give parliamentary sanction to an important portion of the St. Lawrence Power Company's proposals, and would complicate the situation unnecessarily.
Was this modified Bill submitted to Mr. Sifton for his opinion?

I do not know, but I was going to point out that his suggestions, with hardly an exception, have been embodied in the Bill, and, consequently, there was no need of submitting it to him. The Bill as reported from the Private Bills Committee is exactly in the lines of the recommendation of the chairman of the Commission for the Conservation of our Natural Resourc.es. Mr. Sifton goes on to say:
On the other hand it is urged that some of the towns affected, particularly Prescott and Brockville, are without a supply of power, and that a transmission line is necessary in their interest. There does not appear to be any reason why authority for the construction of a transmission line, simply, should not be given, and if Bill (No. 115) were for such a purpose alone there could be no serious objection to it.
This letter has been quoted to prove that the chairman of the Conservation Committee is opposed to this Bill. But the words I have just read in this letter show that on the contrary Mr. Sifton does not see any reason why there should be any objection to the Bill if it were for the construction of a transmission line simply.
Your particular attention is drawn to sections 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14 as being objectionable, on account of the large and unnecessary powers asked for.
These clauses are practically all struck out of the Bill and other clauses giying the safeguards asked for are inserted in their places:-
These clauses apparently contemplate monopolization of powers on a very large scale. It is to be noted also that there are no provisions in the Bill protecting the municipalities in regard to the use of streets or roads, nor
anything requiring the company to acquire or pay for a right of way. Difficulty has already arisen in regard to this latter point in other cases, and it requires to be specifically provided for.	.
Under these circumstances it is recommended-
First, That sections 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14 be struck out and that, in lieu thereof, there be substituted proper provisions giving authority for the construction of a transmission line, and for power to buy, transmit and sell power within Canada.
The Bill provides for that.
Second, that a clause be added declaring that the Act shall come into force only 911 proclamation of the Governor General in Council and upon such conditions as tho Governor General in Council may by order provide, such conditions to be read as forming part of the Act.
At the "end of the Bill reported is clause 15, which provides that this Act shall come into force on a day to be named by proclamation of the Governor in Council. That is an acceptance of Mr. Sifton's recommendation, but does not go quite so far. He asked that such conditions as the Governor m Council may by order provide, shall be read as forming part of the Act. When that came before the committee, I rather took exception to that last part of the recommendation, and I did so on this ground: I believe it to he the duty of parliament to insert the conditions under which the Act shall have effect and force, and not the duty of the Governor in Council to provide those conditions and add them to the Act. If my hon. friend opposite see tit to entrust that duty to the hands of the present government, that would be a mark of their confidence, but that should not warrant this parliament in shirking its duty and putting that responsibility	on	the	shoulders	of	theGovernor in Council. If hon. gentlemen opposite, however, wish to impose it on the Governor in Council they may move to that effect. Under these circumstances, I did not support that proposition	of	the	chairman	of	the
Conservation Commission, but all the other propositions which he advised are embodied in this Bill, and the clauses to which lie objected are eliminated. Had that not been done, I would have protested against the Bill being reported and I would have opposed its adoption in the House. Now that the Bill is safeguarded in the way that I have indicated, first that they can only transmit power, that they cannot export any power to the United States, that they can take no action in case of any municipality without obtaining the permission of that municipality, that their expropriating powers are subject to the clause in the Railway Act and that the Bill shall only come into

force by proclamation of the Governor General, I cannot see why it should pot pass. Personally, I am not interested in the Bill any more than any other member of the House. As a member of the Private Bills Committee, it was my duty to examine the Bill to listen to and take part in the discussion and see to it that the Bill fulfilled the conditions necessary to proper legislation on the part of this parliament. As to whether this Bill overrides the jurisdiction of the local legislatures I do not presume to give an opinion, but the contention of.the hon. gentleman for East Hastings (Mr. Northrup) does not seem to me to be an accurate one. He seemed to' imply that this Bill would extend the power to expropriate the property of a provincial government, obtained under section 247 of the Railway Act, to what is called the original company. I am not a lawyer and I do not profess to give a legal opinion, but it does not seem to be possible that the power which is given to one company under one Act of a certain character can be thereby given to another company under another Act.
The same people may acquire stock in both companies.

The same people may be in the two companies, but the powers given to one incorporation under the statute could only apply to the works exercised by that corporation and not to the works which they exercise under another statute.
I think I observed in the letter of the Chairman of the Conservation Commission an expression of opinion that this was merely part of the larger scheme.

No, not a part of the larger scheme. He says that:
The introduction of this Bill is a portion of the St. Lawrence Power Company's plan.
That may be so. I am not aware of what their intention is.
We know that from the declaration of the Minister of Public Works.

Whether it is or is not, the powers given under this Bill have reference to works connected with the transmission of electricity, and they cannot apply to the powers given under the original incorporation for the erection of a dam, &c. I cannot understand how powers created by this Bill for a certain work defined in this Bill can be transferred to work which is to be done under another and different statute. My understanding is that only this has the Railway Act applied to it and consequently the power which under the Railway Act is given to companies incorporated by this parliament Mr. FISHER
to expropriate the property of provincial governments is not included in the charter of the original corporation. It is only by reason of the fact that the powers of expropriation under the Railway Act are given to this company that they get power to expropriate property of the provinces, and the reason that was given was that if they were not given that power, under the involved construction of provincial rights in regard to land under streams and on river beds, they might be prevented from crossing any river bed in Ontario, which would mean practically that they would be obstructed absolutely and forever in any work which -this parliament authorized them to carry on.
Does not that take away some rights of the province of Ontario?

I am not going to give a legal opinion on that, but if there is a right on the part of Ontario to obstruct a company's works which are in the interest of the people of Canada, then I say that the _ property of the province ought to be subjected, as private property is, to expropriation to enable the works of the company to be carried on. If the works are not in the public interest this parliament ought not to give a charter at all, but if it does give a charter it should give facilities to the company to carry on the works which this parliament has authorized.
Would the minister advocate a measure which would override the rights of the municipality or the province?
If this parliament sees fit to incorporate a company for certain purposes, it ought to give that company the power to carry on its purposes.

The minister is saying today the very opposite of that which he said last session. Last session when he introduced the Bill to establish the Conservation Commission he explained that the interests of the provinces and municipalities as well as the interests of the Dominion would be safeguarded by this commission. We had presented the argument that this House had created certain committees on conservation, and that, therefore, there was no necessity of going to the expense of creating a Conservation Commission. Asked by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) what the Conservation Commission would do, he said on May 12, page 6369 of 'Hansard':
They will hold a meeting and discuss what recommendations they may he able to lay down for the treatment of the natural resources of Canada in the future on such lines as may rightly appeal to the administrative bodies, all through Canada, whether municipal, provincial or Dominion who have con trol over natural resources.

A committee of the House is purely federal in its character. It does not enlist the sympathy or co-operation of the provincial or municipal authorities.
When the question was raised that there was a committee of this House on natural resources the minister said:
A committee of the House is purely federal in its character. It does not enlist the sympathy or co-operation of the provincial or municipal authorities.
Now, the hon. gentleman says that he would vote in support of measures which would absolutely override and take away rights municipal and provincial, notwithstanding what these rights may be, and in favour of federal legislation. My hon. friend must see the inconsistency of that position. I have a word to say to the hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Con-mee). He takes a rather extraordinary stand in reference to this Bill. He has said that we should override by this Bill the rights of the provinces. The hon. gentleman has not always spoken along that line. When he was a member of the provincial house in Ontario, supporting the provincial government, he took a different position, and in the first year that he was a member of this House he also took a different position.
No, there has been no inconsistency in my position.

Having regard to the principles which are involved as regards the rights of provinces and municipalities through which this proposed transmission line would pass, I feel that this Bill should be allowed to stand over. With regard to the principles of this Bill, the time has to come, and it might as well come now, when a policy must be laid down for dealing with these questions. It is the duty of the government to lay before this House such a policy as will prevent such a discussion as this being precipitated and will prevent private rights, municipal rights and provincial rights being so continually invaded as they are at the present time.
I would like to ask the Minister of Agriculture what he makes of section II subsection 4.

I take that to mean that the company has the right to acquire in fee simple such lands as it may need for the construction of its transmission line. The words, fee simple, were put in so as to require the company to buy the lands and not simply obtain a lease of them.

Section 247 of the Railway Act, to which my hon. friend referred, and the general provisions of the Railway Act on which he relies, do not seem to cure the situation created by this subsection, which apparently gives the company
the right to enter on and expropriate any land without acquiring a title in fee simple. This might give the company the right to obtain an easement in any municipality without acquiring the right in fee simple. Subsection 6 of section 11 says:
In. the event of the company exercising the rights of expropriation hereby given for the purpose of acquiring land for its right of way, such land must be acquired in fee simple.
I do not know what the. effect of these two provisions read together is. I would think it extremely probable that under subsection 4 the provisions of section 247 of the Railway Act might not be of very much avail.

If that is the case, the clause, when we reach it, ought to be amended, because the Private Bills Committee fully understood that all questions of expropriation should be subject to the permission of the municipality, and I would be prepared to support any amendment which would make it clear that no such power would be left in the hands of the company.

The difference between the two subsections is this: that in every case of expropriation the company would be obliged to acquire a title in fee simple; but they would not be required to do so in obtaining an easement or a privilege.

If that is the intention, it has been very badly expressed. The Railway Act gives a company power to expropriate land. This Bill proceeds to say that ' the word land, so far as it applies to this Act shall include any privilege or easement required by the company for constructing or operating the works authorized by this Act without the necessity of acquiring a title in fee simple.' Therefore it seems to me that this result would follow, that this company would have the right to acquire a right of way without the necessity of - acquiring a title in fee simple. If this clause gives it the Tight by expropriation to obtain an easement for the purpose of erecting one pole, it has an equal right to acquire an [DOT]easement by similar proceedings for the purpose of erecting all its poles.
I would suggest to my hon. friend that that can be very easily remedied when we reach that clause in the Bill. Therefore I would suggest that we facilitate our reaching it.

I have listened with a good deal of interest to what the Minister of Agriculture said in regard to the innocent character of this Bill as it now stands, and his explanation of the letter of the hon. Chairman of the Conservation Commission. I do not read this Bill as of the innocent character that the Minister of Agriculture does, and I think he must give more consideration to it before he comes to that

conclusion. As I understand the letter, Mr. Sifton, the Chairman of the Conservation Commission, wanted the Bill to be limited to transmission, and I do not understand the minister to say that Mr. Sifton has seen the Bill in its amended form. If it be intended that this Bill is to accomplish nothing but transmission, that is not its effect even as amended. By clause 6 the company may purchase or lease electric power, and acquire such lands, easements and privileges as are necessary for the purpose of it3 undertakings. Now, it must be admitted that the Act of 1901, incorporating the St. Lawrence Power Company, though it may be a different Act, gives that company the right to sell those powers, and that Act contains no clause such as we insert in railway charters, preventing any amalgamation with any other company except with the approval of the Governor in Council or the Railway Commission. So that the two companies, being under the one control, could be so manipulated as to give them the joint power of generating and transmitting electricity. Clause (6) provides that the company may:-
(a) construct, maintain , operate, use and manage conduits, tunnels, transmission lines, structures, buildings, machinery, plant, appliances, instruments and devices, and erect and maintain poles and towers, and lay and maintain pipes, cables, wires or other conductors and connect them with similar lines in other provinces and with similar lines in the United States for the purpose of importation only.
It does not say for transmission only, and I cannot presume that would be the result
That is the whole object.
Why not limit this clause so as to provide for transmission only in Canada?
When we reach that clause we can put that in.
Let my hon. friend read clause 12.	.

That clausa provides that nothing in this Act shall be construed to empower the company'to export electricity or electric or other power to the United States. But there is nothing here that limits in any way their rights to transmission. Wa have this statute of 1901 which gives powers far beyond transmission to another company, almost identical in name and composed of the same parties, and we then are asked to pass this Bill in which care is taken not to limit the powers of the company to transmission. An attempt has been made to show that municipal rights will not be invaded and a clause was put in to that effect. Whether operative or not shall be found out later. The Bill declares [DOT] Mr. LANCASTER,
what the works and powers of the company are to be, but it does not limit them to a transmission company or to anything that could be so construed. On the contrary, we do S|ay that they can acquire, lease or obtain current, power or force, and may supply, sell, &c. They can buy or sell from any other company that can give them current. We are giving them this power and we are not putting in any such safeguard as that they should be subject to the Railway Board or to the Governor in Council. The chairman of the Conservation Commission who is not merely as an individual for whom we might have respect objected to this measure. He is not a gentleman who is simply appointed and who is desirous of protecting this country, but he is, under statute, made the policeman or guardian of these things, and it is his duty to watch and keep tab on such legislation. That gentleman has condemned this Bill as far as we know. I would like a letter from the chairman of the commission saying that, having seen the amended Bill, he is satisfied that it is all right. I understand the Bill does not remove his objection. If it were limited to transmission only, the chairman saw much objection to it, but he made the distinct statement that it should be limited to transmission only. This Bill is not limited to transmission. Does not the Minister of Agriculture think that if it is to be limited to transmission only, it would be well to put into this Bill a statement to that effect, either at the end of clause 6 or in some other part of the Bill, so that it would be quite clear?
When we reach the clause in question I am ready to support any wording which will make clear the intention I have already described.

We are asked to pass clause 1 saying what the name of this company shall be, but we have not yet determined that the name is the proper one. I am not prepared to vote that this company shall be a transmission company if it is to be something else, and the Bill indicates that it is to be something else. It is to be a great deal more than a transmission company.

I think that the corporation ought to be made to agree with the title of the Bill, which is that of a transmission company. It is a transmission company that I am prepared to incorporate and grant powers to.
Mr. LANCASTER, There is nothing that limits it to a transmission company.
I think there is. If there is not I am ready to put it there.

Was I correct in understanding the Minister of Agriculture

to say that everything objected to by the chairman of the commission had been struck out?

As far as I can see the Bill has been reframed in exact accordance with the recommendations of the chairman of the Conservation Commission except what lie proposed in regard to conditions being- put in the order in council.
I observe that the chairman recommends that clauses 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14 should be struck out of the original Bill. Clause 10 has not been struck out as it appears here as clause 7.

I see that the clause is exactly the same but it seems to me that other clauses having been put in to prevent the power there provided for being exercised except under certain restrictions that clause is not objectionable.

He seemed to think that it was and he continues the objection to it as it stands at present. There are rather peculiar words in clause 7:
The company may construct or acquire by lease, purchase or otherwise, and operate in connection with the works, lines and business of the company and for the purposes thereof, lines of telegraph or telephone or other works and means of communication.

The word^ 'and for the purposes thereof' mean that these lines of telegraph and telephone are only to be used for the purposes of the company in the same way that a railway company is allowed to use telegraph and telephone lines for its own purposes.

Is the minister quite sure of his statement when he says that all the recommendations of the chairman of the Conservation Commission have been embodied in this Bill? The hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) produced a letter from the chairman of the Conservation Commission and I gathered from his statement that there were very material differences between the recommendations and the Bill as presented to the House. I notice that the Minister of Agriculture seems to have the impression that the Bill carries out all that the chairman recommended.
With one exception.
Is the minister sure that all the recommendations made by the chairman of the commission purported to be carried out-that the committee decided to adopt them all?
That was the intention of the Private Bills Committee.
Would the minister be good enough to state again what the exception was?

It was that the chairman of the commission thought that in the proclamation of the Governor General bringing the Act into force there should be additional conditions imposed which I objected to on principle.
I do not recall whether the chairman is apjxnnted by order in council or selected by the commission itself.
He is specially appointed as chairman.

The practice is growing up in the committees of referring matters to what is called the Conservation Commission; that is referring them practically to the chairman of the Conservation Commission. I recognize that the chairman is a man of very exceptional ability, but that alone does not constitute a Teason why we should leave-matters of important legislation to him. The question of ability is not the sole question. I have a very serious objection to that method. It works exceedingly well at all times. It may work well on this occasion, but the time will come when it will work in the reverse order, and I think that if we once adopt that method of referring matters nominally to the Conservation Commission, but to be actually decided by the chairman or even directly referring them to the chairman, we will come to a very dangerous condition of things before long. For a time the chairman may recommend things that seem to be in the line of conserving the public interest, and the opposition will say it is very willing on these occasions to adopt them, but we have no guarantee that on other occasions the chairman will not recommend the adoption of a Bill which is a very dangerous Bill, and the fact that we have referred it to him will get us into the practice of being careless in investigating matters ourselves, and it will not be very long before a serious blunder will result from this practice. I do not wish to attack either the Conservation Commission or the chairman of that commission, but I say that in principle it is wrong. We are delegating our duties to a commission which has no responsibility, because we cannot consider that Mr. Sifton as chairman of the commission is filling a responsible position in the Sense of being a member of this House, although he happens to be a member. By referring Bills to that commission or its chairman, we are delegating duties which we should perform ourselves, and we will yet bring censure upon ourselves for doing that. The most valuable work of the commission will be to deal with general cases, not on refer-

ence of a particular instance or particular Bill. They take a general survey of the country, its interests and resources, and form an opinion on these matters, when no one is interested in influencing them in a certain way, but I feel it is a dangerous principle to relegate our duties to the chairman of that commission or even to the Conservation Commission itself.
Was this Bill not referred to the Conservation Commission?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: The original Bill was, but this Bill was not referred to them. The Conservation Commission went over the first Bill and cut out what they thought were objectionable clauses, and returned the Bill to the Private Bills Committee. They had no objection to the Bill going through in its amended form,

The Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of the Interior and the Minister of Mines are ex-officio, by the Act, members of the Conservation Commission, to which this Bill was referred
I ask the Minister of Agriculture whether any meeting of the Conservation Commission was called for the purpose of considering the Bill that was referred to that commission? It must be clear that it has never sat and deliberated upon this Bill, and we have no recommendation from the commission as to the best method of dealing with this matter. This Bill was referred to a body composed of 35 members, and we have received, not the opinion of the commission, but the opinion of one member of it who is called the chairman, and whose duties, as defined by the Act, are purely administrative, to carry out the decisions of the commission. Therefore, unless we are to make a farce of the proceedings of that commission, we should refer to it this Bill and obtain the recommendations of the commission, and not merely those of the chairman. I would like to know the opinion of the Minister of Agriculture, himself ex-officio a member of that commission, and the minister who introduced the measure creating the Conservation Commission, as to the chairman of the commission, without calling the commission together, himself disposing of questions referred to that commission?

The only reason, so far as I know, that this question of the Conservation Commission has come up at all, is that hon. gentlemen who oppose this Bill, quoted the letter of the chairman of the commission, and used it for the purpose of obstructing the Bill.
The hon. gentleman is wrong in saying that the letter was used for the purpose of obstructing the Bill.

I apologize. I meant to say for the purpose of opposing the Bill,
Mr. LENNOX
the argument being advanced that this Bill was opposed by the Conservation Commission. That is why I referred to the matter. As to referring this question to the Conservation Commission, that suggestion is open to objection and also to commendation. There are reasons on both sides. But it is obvious that the commission, composed of thirty gentlemen scattered over Canada, cannot be got together to discuss every question that may be referred to them. If a question of that kind is referred to the commission, either the whole commission will have to be called together to deliberate and pronounce upon it, or the chairman may call together the executive committee for that purpose. I am not aware whether or not in this case he called together the executive committee.
You are a member of it.

No, I am not. One of its members is one of the hon. members for Toronto, another is the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), another is Dr. Robertson, another is the Attorney General of Nova Scotia, another is Senator Edwards, and there are two or three others. What the chairman wrote may be his own personal opinion as chairman, or it may be the opinion formed in consultation.	Hon. gentlemen opposite,
supposing that the letter of the chairman supported their opposition to this Bill, brought it up; but now that they find that it does not oppose the Bill in its present form, they are rather tired of the subject and are objecting to the opinion of the chairman of the commission being quoted against them.
The hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe), in reading the letter last night, distinctly stated that some of the requests of the commission were granted in the Bill, and some were not.
I think they all are practically.
My hon. friend will not say they all are.	'
With one exception.
A very important exception.

I will repeat my question. Does the Minister of Agriculture, as the minister having charge of the Conservation Commission, consider that a reference to that commission is conformed to by a reply from the chairman of the commission, and is that the way the Conservation Commission is going to do its work?

I would say that if the chairman of the commission is not authorized by the commission to act in that way, his reply would be of very little value except as an expression of his own personal opinion; but if the organization of

the commission authorizes the chairman to act for the commission in certain circumstances, then his reply would have the force of the commission behind it.
My hon. friend knows that there is no authority for the chairman to act in that way.
Not by statute.

Then, upon the minister's own statement, there is no renort of the Conservation Commission on this Bill; and if we accept this letter from the chairman as the judgment of the Conservation Com mission, the hon. minister must see how dangerous a precedent we are etsablishing in dealing with the natural resources of this country. This is a precedent which the hon. Minister of Agriculture himself (Mr. Fisher) is supporting by his attitude in the House. It was he who explained last session the great value of this commission for the conservation of our nat ural resources in dealing with just such cases as this affecting federal, provincial and municipal matters, and I appeal to him, as a responsible minister of the Crown, not to allow this matter to be dealt with simply by one member of that commission. I ask him to see that where there has been a reference to the commission, that commission shall pass upon it as a body and not have it simply dealt with by one of its members, no matter how distinguished that member may be. It is the report of the commission as a whole that the parliament of Canada is entitled to, and that report the minister should see that parliament obtains.

We have had from the Minister of Agriculture the rather startling and novel statement that this parliament has the right to empower a private company to expropriate the public domain of any province. That is a claim which has never before been put forward in this House by any hon. gentleman much less by a minister of the Crown.
Is it not true that undei 'the provisions of the Railway Act, this company may get that power, and was not that Railway Act passed by this parliament and agreed to unanimously?

That is one reason why I object to this Bill. It is declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada and the company are given very extensive powers under the Railway Act. We are indebted to the minister for this very frank statement of the policy of the government. It has never before been contended in this House that the Crown, as represented by the Dominion parliament, has the right to authorize the expropriation of the territory or domain of the Crown as
represented by any one province, because a province is just as much entitled to its Crown rights and the entirety of its Crown privileges. as is the Dominion. The provinces have just as much right to the preservation of their exclusive ownership to whatever property they possess. But the statement is now made for the first time that one Crown has the right to authorize a corporation to expropriate the right of another Crown. No court has held that doctrine in this country at any time. There was a case in British Columbia in which a company was given the right to expropriate the Crown domain for the purpose of carrying out an undertaking authorized by this parliament, but that had reference to Dominion lands in that province. The Minister of Agriculture went further and practically supported every clause in this Bill.
