What would be the use, therefore, of our acceding to the apparently moderate request of certain hon. gentlemen opposite that the first clause of this Bill should be passed? At the end of the final clause, the hon. gentleman was somewhat doubtful as to whether he would not add a line to it, but apart from that he is perfectly satisfied with the Bill. Apparently the government is going to force the Bill through, no matter what objections there may be to it. The hon. minister attempted to quiet the well founded apprehensions of hon. members representing the constituency of Montreal and he read the Railway Act to prove that this company has no power to enter upon the highways and byways of that city without its consent. Surely that is elementary. Every one knows section 247 of the Railway Act, and that section simply protects the municipalities to the extent that no one shall enter upon their highways without their consent. The Railway Act does not say that this company shall be bound by section 247 and. that it shall not enter the city of Montreal without the consent of the city.

The Minister of Agriculture was not successful in using the words of the hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's (Mr. Martin), because he resented and did not endorse the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture.

Quite true, I was not in the House at the time, but I understand that to be the fact. This Bill gives this company the right to expropriate indiscriminately throughout the entire territory from Kingston to Montreal, inclusive. They have to buy their way, but they are given not only powers of expropriation, but the Bill gives the company the right to expropriate as far as they require expropriation powers.
With the authorization of the municipality.

No, without. I make the statement, and I challenge contradiction of it, that this Bill gives the right to this company to expropriate without the consent of the municipality. A company operating under the Kailway Act was bound to acquire in fee simple and pay the value of property expropriated, but this company have the additional right of being able to acquire any privilege or easement. It means that they can run their lines anywhere in the city of Montreal, upon the side of a building or over a building, and they can acquire a privilege or easement wherever they please. They do not have to expropriate a right of way. That costs a lot of money. They do not need to spend that money. They can simply acquire an easement or right or privilege and run their lines wherever they please; the company gets this power under subsection 4 of section II of the Bill. I hope that bon. gentlemen representing the city of Montreal will see the effect of this thing and join with those who are trying to protect provincial rights. The Minister of Agriculture said that he saw no peril in the amalgamation of this company with its predecessor, the St. Lawrence Power Company incorporated in 1901, that whatever rights the old company had they would retain, and that this company would retain its rights, but that they could not in any way by making a combination form one company, merge their powers and operate for the joint advantage of both companies. The minister is entirely mistaken, because if he will read the statute incorporating the St. Lawrence Power Company in 1901, he will see that by clause 11 this company have the power to amalgamate with the company which is now being formed, and that the rights possessed by each company will be owned by the joint company. The company which we are incorporating will possess the entire rights of the old company, the old company of 1901 will possess the entire rights of this company, and they will jointly have the enormous powers that are provided for in both cases. With the power given to the old company to amalgamate with this company, these two companies will become one and there will be one gigantic corporation enjoying the powers of the old power company, together with the very large privileges sought in this Bill by the distributing company.
Why was that information not communicated to the Private Bills Committee?
I do not know. Possibly it was.
No, my hon. friend from North Ontario says it was not.

Well, it is here in the Act. They bear on their face the evi-Mr. J. I*. TURCOTTE.
dence that they are one and the same. They have practically the same name, the old company being called the St. Lawrence Power Company, and this company being called the St. Lawrence Power Transmission Company. If this company that is applying to-day was not in substance the old company, would not the old company object to the similarity of names? The minister sees no danger in the exportation of power to the States. I contend that it is extremely doubtful, under- both Bills, whether or not the company can be prohibited from exporting power, because the old Act contains no restriction whatever on the exportation of power. The company can sell its power.
No, the Exportation Act would cover that.

Chapter 16 of the Exportation of Fluid Act of 1907 provides for licenses to export power and unless this company is prohibited from exporting its power it has the right to apply for a license to the Governor in Council under the Act of 1907, and if there is no good reason why it should not get a license it will doubtless get one. There is no attempt made to say that this company shall be prohibited from exporting this power, and if it applies for a license no doubt it will be given the right to export its surplus. Let me point out the unwisdom of allowing our power to be exported. Let me refer to the condition that existed at Niagara Falls many years ago, a condition of affairs that we are now repeating on the St. Lawrence river. The International Waterways Commission found that they had developed power on the American side largely in excess of their right according to the flow of water, but having regard to the establishment of industries and vested rights they divided the power over the whole river by giving to Canada some 36,000 horse-power, and giving about 20,000 horse-power to the American side, whereas, if it had been dealt with on a proper basis, the American side would not have been entitled to more than one-sixth of the total power that could be developed as less than one-sixth of the water flowed over the American side. What has happened there will happen here, and history will repeat itself. You will have the water and power diverted to the American side, or you will have the power exported to the American side, and the Americans will get a great deal more than they are entitled to. Ultimately when the question comes up to be dealt with as an international question our rights will be sacrificed, and we will get the small end of the horn, and not what we are entitled to. It is claimed that we are obstructing because we are going on record as being in favour of protecting the interests of the people as against this

corporation which is seeking to be incorporated at the public expense for its own private interest and advantage. The Minister of Agriculture has made the startling statement that this House has a perfect right to incorporate a company, and give that company the right to expropriate the domain of any province. He justifies that by saying that the company may have to run across the bed of some provincial stream, and they should have the right to expropriate there. Does that justify the sweeping power given to this company to expropriate the public domain of Ontario throughout nine counties along the St. Lawrence from Kingston to Montreal? Ii the Bill is only intended to give the right to expropriate the river bed here and there whv not say so?

I musi discuss this Bill on the assumption that there is an intention to dam the St. Lawrence. That may not appear in this Bill, but it does in the Bill of 1901. I think it is clear that in time a dam will be erected across the St. Lawrence; that will be found to be the joker, the little elusive pea that is under the shell. We all agree that the St. Lawrence is one of our great national assets. It drains the, Great Lakes and'forms the only natural outlet for the trade of the best part of the north American continent. The Americans would give untold wealth if they could acquire the exclusive right to navigate the St. Lawrence from the lakes to the ocean. That is our great privilege, and we ought not to consent to put the slightest hindrance to the free flow of the trade that properly belongs to our great water route. So jealous are the American authorities on the subject that a proposal to build a bridge across the Detroit river was rejected at Washington, and the railways had to spend $12,000,000 to tunnel the river. The proposal to build a dam at the foot of Lake Erie, near Buffalo, to maintain the waters of the lake at standard level, has been rejected for fear of causing an ice jam with consequent flooding of the land bordering the lake and the checking of the flow of the Niagara river.
The building of such a dam as this on the SJ. Lawrence river would put a stop to the carriage of rafts of timber down the St. Lawrence, and it would destroy one of the great scenic attractions of the St. Lawrence river, the shooting of the rapids, which would be a very serious loss from a sentimental point of view.
The Welland canal is admittedly one of our greatest national assets. It has been enlarged three times, and the Minister of Railway and Canals proposes a still further enlargement. That would mean an enlargement and deepening of the St. Lawrence canals, but it is more likely that if this
dam is erected it will be found a serious obstruction in the enlargement of those canals, as the water supply might be affected and currents caused that did not before exist. The whole condition will be changed by this scheme of spoliation. By means of our great water routes we have it within our power to draw the trade of half of the north American continent, a trade which now taxes the American shipping interests and railroads. All that is open to us with a proper system of water transportation. Moreover, it is within the range of possibilities that ocean vessels will soon find their way up the lakes. We are face to face with the possibility of difficulties in connection with our coal supply from the United States. In connection with the discussion of tariff matters now pending there may be a difficulty in adjusting the question of duties. We are all looking forward to utilizing our own coal supply in Nova Scotia so as to make it serve the lake ports and the northwest. To do all this we require the unobstructed navigation of the St. Lawrence. This is a larger question than one of a week's discussion. It is much larger than the question of the transmission of power to a number of large towns. It should be considered from a national point of view. Hon. gentlemen should not consent to the alienation of this most valuable asset of the nation which we have in the St. Lawrence river. From every point of view we should not consider for a moment the possibility of an obstruction being placed in that waterway. If we agree in all this, can we not get together on this question? I am willing, in conclusion, to propose that we call this debate off and get out and have an old-fashioned game of snow-ball before the snow disappears-and I invite my friend Mr. Loggie to be my opponent in a friendly game-and we will come back on another day and dispose of this matter quickly.
Mr. HUGHES This morning three ministers were appealed to in succession by one of the hon. members on this side of the House, and each of them gave the clearest possible reason why this Bill should be postponed immediately. The Minister of Agriculture, in answer to the query what he thought of the Bill, stated that before he could answer he required to consider the Bill; the Minister of Labour stated that before he could express an opinion, he would require to consider the whole discussion ; and the Minister of the Interior stated that the question involved matters which had taken up twelve or fourteen hours of discussion, and he wanted more light. I appeal to the Minister of Militia, who is now leading the House, to comply with the very proper request of the leader of the opposition, that this Bill be laid over until fire plans can be looked into.

When this Bill first came before the Private Bills Committee, it attracted very little attention. Very few on this side of the House suspected that there was anything behind it. Our suspicions were first aroused by seeing the great interest taken in it by certain gentlemen who were never known to attend the meetings of the Private Bills Committee at all. They were there early and late; they drummed up their friends and urged all sorts of arguments for the passing of the Bill. On one occasion thirty or forty men deserted one power scheme in the Railway Committee to float another through in the Private Bills Committee. The spectacle naturally excited the attention even of honest plodding Conservatives, and we-thought it our duty to commence an inquiry Then suspicion grew, based on the rumour that behind this scheme was the plan to dam the St. Lawrence river, and hand over the entire water-power to this- grasping corporation of American trusts. I was amazed to see the determined interest taken in that Bill by the government. I strolled in, not expecting anything special on, but when I saw the activity of five or six ministers of the Crown in pushing through this private Bill, I began to suspect, to use an Americanism, that there was a nigger in the wood pile. The Minister of Public Works in a moment of excitement gave the whole story away. He frankly admitted that there was a connection between the two Bills, the St. Lawrence Power Company, and the St. Lawrence Power and Transmission Company. He admitted that he had been waited upon repeatedly during the la3t two years in the interest of that Bill, that this company had come to him and had shown him the plans for damming the St. Lawrence, and had talked the whole matter over with him, and he admitted that the two Bills were one and the same thing. Up to that time we had confined our efforts to preserving the rights of the province of Ontario. We asked the Minister of Public Works to let the Bill stand over until we could obtain information on certain matters, and that we might look more carefully into it. That was refused, they point blank refused to take, anything short of the passage of the entire Bill. Well, the Minister of Public Works saw that he could not carry his point. Then, as the night wore on, these gentlemen agreed to compromise the matter if we would pass the preamble, and all the clauses, leaving one to be reserved for discussion. We very properly rejected that proposition. We were determined then that before this Bill should go through the plans of that dam should be brought down, and we would see what was behind it all. I am sure that there is nothing that any Mr. HUGHES.
fair minded man on the government side could object to in the position we took. Then what was the next step on the programme? Two of these gentlemen from Ontario, the province that was being robbed of her natural resources, commenced in their usual manner to try and shove this matter through. They found that did not work. So in the small hours of the morning the government came to their senses, and another proposition was made that section 1 should be passed, and all the rest should stand over for consideration. But since we had been denied an opportunity to see the plans, we decided to reject that proposition. Our duty to our constituents demanded that we should get to the bottom of this whole matter. I see before me now three ministers who were not here during the night, the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Labour, and the Minister of the Interior. Have they heard the reasons why this matter should be adjourned? I am sure the Secretary of State will join them in a desire for more light on this matter. I regard this as a most dangerous measure in the interests of the peace and good relationship which should exist between this country and the United States. I feel satisfied that if the Minister of Militia will only give my hon. friend the leader of the opposition a definite statement that these plans will be brought down we will be prepared to end this matter by the passage of section 1.

I would ask the government if the rumour is true that a deputation from Montreal waited on the government yesterday to ask that they be granted the privilege of placing a dam across the St. Lawrence river? If so, has any decision been arrived at?

No, it was understood that they would present a modified plan to the International Waterways Commission, and that commission would give an opportunity to the navigation interests and those who might naturally be opposed to any obstructions to navigation, to be heard. That is the plan which I would propose to lay upon the table, together with the joint- report of the three engineers in reference to that plan.
When my hon. friend made this statement, I presume that there were two sets of plans submitted by the company to the members of the Privy Council. Will he submit both?

What I mean is that I will submit the modified plans, which were approved of by the engineers. I desire with some reluctance to point out to the House, some features in connection with this Bill. Doubtless, most of the members have read the evidence. It does seem to me that the committee before whom the witnesses were examined must have proceeded upon a very extraordinary method of dealing with the evidence. There are two matters which contain the substance of the evidence on which the relief was based. One was the

co-habitation of the respondent with another woman and the other was the production of evidence tending to show that the respondent was afflicted with a venereal disease. I present to the House this proposition that upon a perusal of the evidence given before the Senate Committee and sent over to this House there is not one fact from which even a presumption, if a presumption were proper, could be drawn as to the affirmative of either of those two facts. What-is the evidence with regard to co-habitation with another woman? There is the evidence of only one witness, a medical clergyman, and the whole statement by that one witness consists of his having met this man in a shanty in the Yukon or in Alaska territory out of which shanty, before he went there, he had met a woman coming. That is the whole evidence with the exception of what he states himself was evidence of a notorious fact with regard to co-habitation which as all lion, gentlemen know is no evidence at all where the direct fact has to 'be proved. The evidence with regard to the other part of it, from which fact if proved might be drawn a presumption of infidelity, is absolutely wanting. It is the evidence of a medical man, a man used to the care of the sick. He at first stated that it was his opinion that this respondent was afflicted with that disease, but when he is asked, not on crossexamination but in examination in chief, whether he is sure of that fact he says: No, he is not, it had the appearance of that, but it might be something else. I do not desire to interfere in a private Bill or to prevent relief which doubtless is, apart from the weighty considerations attached to it, very much to be desired between two people evidently not mated to one another. I do not desire to interfere, but I feel it my duty to submit to you and to the House the fact that it appears to me that there are absolutely wanting any elements and all elements on which this House can safely proceed to give the relief asked for by this Bill.

Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 102) respecting immigration. He said: In view of the fact that some explanation was given on the inrodnction of the Biil. and in view of the further fact that the Bill was before the House during a great deal of last session, it will not be necessary to make any very lengthy introductory remarks. The main reason for the introduction of the Bill is not so much the desire to change the policy of the government

as to facilitate the administration of that policy to a degree that is not provided for under the present Act, and to bring out, as clearly and as fully as possible in the form of the Act, what the policy of the government is, so that all parties interested may understand it.
There have been, of course, changes of conditions since the Act of 1906 was passed. One important change, and one that leads to a number of amendments in detail which appear in this Bill, is the necessity which has arisen for the exclusion of immigrants at international boundary ports. Up to the time of the passing of the Bill of 1906, there had not arisen, so far as we then understood the matter, any necessity for special efforts toward the exclusion of immigrants at these points. It was understood that there was such necessity at ocean ports, but in the framing the details were not made so Clearly applicable. Since then, cause has arisen for quite as strict exclusion provisions at international boundary ports as at ocean ports, .and necessarily, in the application of .the policy of the government, there are points arising from day to day which make it desirable that they should be made as far as possible in legislation, so that, as I said, all parties interested shall have due notice of the intention of the government in administering its policy. There are many changes in detail throughout the Bill-all these changes in the Bill are changes of detail and not of policy. Some of them are important-in fact, we believe them all important or they would not have been proposed-but they are made for the purpose of carrying out mere thoroughly and with more notice of the public the policy of the government, rather than to secure any change in the policy or in methods of administration.
One or two of the more important details I may mention. One is to define the word ' domicile.' As matters stand at present, the person who has once lived in Canada is entitled to come back, whether he is desirable or not. We agree that after a man has established his domicile in Canada, whether he has become a citizen or not, he should be entitled to re-entry into Canada. But there has been an indefiniteness on that point which should be cleared up as far as it can be cleared up. We are aware that a definition of ' domicile ' is very difficult, but, for the purposes of this Act, for the better administration of the government's policy and for the better information of the public-both immigrants and those interested in transportation-we think it well that this word ' domicile ' should be defined as clearly as possible. There is another very important provision, one which may not meet with the approval of the House. I drew attention to it when. I brought the Bill before the House in the first piace, and I again draw attention to Mr. OLIVER.
it. This is a provision which, while guaranteeing to the immigrant every opportunity to establish his right to enter the country-guaranteeing to him the full opportunity of giving evidence and of having that evidence recorded, with the right of appeal -yet does not permit the immigrant to take advantage of the protection of the courts until he has passed the administrative authority of the government at the port of landing. We believe that it is desirable, in the interest of proper exclusion of undesirable immigrants, that this provision should be made. We understand that it is a somewhat radical provision, and as I have said, it may not meet the approval of the House. But, as I have said also, we believe that it would be in the best interest of immigrants, transportation companies and the country generally if that provision were adopted. As I have suggested, there being no change in policy or administration intended, it will be more convenient to deal with the changes of detail as we come to them in the different clauses of the Bill, and with the opportunities of explanation and discussion that are afforded when the House is in committee.

I want to tell the hon. Minister of the Interior that, if he is going to class me with the Doukhobors, he is like Paddy's dog, making a mistake. I want to tell the hon. gentleman that while they are perhaps pets, the so-called Sifton pets of this government, they are no pets of mine, and I will tell the hon. gentleman the reason. They have been a detriment to the civilization of the west in every possible manner. They have been a people so immorally indecent-innocent perhaps- that they have been a disgrace to the people of the west, and to the administration that brought them here. I want to ask the Minister of the Interior, if he will come down from the lofty position of levity he is assuming, how many of these people he expects, and how he is going to take care of them? I want to ask him what the cost has been to the Dominion in the past in bringing that class of immigrants into this country; and further, what cost it has been tc the decent self-respecting people of Canada in taking care of them, and keeping them in some way of decency since they

came. I want to ask him what the cost has been to compel these people to comply with the laws of Canada, that all other immigrants are obliged to comply with.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps it would be as well to defer question and answer of this nature until we are in committee. I am unable to give my hon. friend at the moment the information he asks for. He has asked for considerable information in thg way of figures and facts, of course he does not expect me to have them in hand. But I will be glad to furnish all the information we have that he has asked for. The intention of the Bill, and the policy of the government, is .that all immigration shall be treated on exactly the same footing, on the same basis, according to their merits, irrespective of their race or religion. Our purpose in the Bill is to put before the public as plainly as we can what the policy of the government is, so that there may be no misapprehension in regard to it.
I would ask the minister if, after the experience of this government with regard to that particular class of people, he considers them desirable as immigrants?

I can tell my hon. friend what it cost us to move the Doukhobors out here. The transportation of the Doukhobors by the government from their native country to their settlement in the Northwest, cost $48,000. That was the answer given several days ago in the House by the government when asked upon that >
point. But it must not be forgotten that since they are in this country they have cost us large sums of money every time there has been amongst them a breaking out which is familiar to most of the members of this House. One is naturally led to inquire whether we have not advanced far enough to take precautionary measures before we import into this country in large
numbers certain classes of people. That is a question that naturally arises at this stage of the legislation. Nor is it, I think, for the minister to say that we have not state-aided immigration. We have not state-aided immigration in the sense that we do not take the immigrant at our own expense on foreign shores and bring him here. There are not many nations that do that, in fact I do not know of any. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) alluded to the system we have followed of bonus-ing immigrants in the first place, and in the next place of keeping a large number1 of immigration agents in different parts of the world, many of them at great expense, and to very little purpose. Should we continue that system? Is it wise, for instance, to keep in the United States so many immigration agents, who are merely nominees of the government for political purposes, and who do very little there, when we see, as we do at this moment, such large numbers of immigrants coming into this country, according to my mind, without any particular action on the part of these agents that cost us so dear? They came in last year, I think over 60,000 from the United States. We are not in a position to say how many of these men were brought in through the action of these very expensive immigration agents, I think none at all. We have no trace of any one that was brought in by our agents from Michigan or Minnesota. Look at the expense of those agents, the paucity of their reports. Indeed, we have no reports from them in the departmental report. There is a general report from the chief, but surely when an agent in Michigan, or some other state, costs us between $6,000 and $8,000 a year, we ought to get from him a detailed statement, some document that would give us information showing what use he is to the country and what results he has obtained. Hon. members of the House know that we have also in England and in many parts of the continent immigration agents, and even there I question if they are of much use to us. I think the time has arrived for Canada, as for the United States, to adopt a different policy, not catering for immigrants, but making a suitable advertisement of this country by a grant when exhibitions occur, keeping an office in London in a general way, but not paying men to remain over there for the purpose of soliciting immigrants. I think the time has come when such an effort on our part is superfluous. So I think I am right in saying that we have an absolutely different policy from that of the United States, who receive over a million immigrants a year, and sometimes more than that. They are overcrowded with immigrants, without paying a single cent for soliciting them. On the contrary, they charge a head tax which leaves a

handsome surplus and enables them to defray entirely a system of inspection.
Does not my hon. friend think that the policy of this government is in reality a policy of assisted immigration?

Certainly, I call it assisted immigration, as much so as in any country that adopts it. My hon. friend thinks that assisted immigration means defraying part of the expense of immigrants who come out here.
I have no such thought in my mind.

Then we assist immigration in that we provide considerable help for the immigrant when he arrives. That, I think, to a certain extent, might continue. We have spent a great deal of money on hospitals and inspection. I heard from a medical man that the disease of trachoma, which is a great pest in eastern Europe, has spread very considerably, and that it now exists in different parts of Canada. For a time we had it in Montreal, and I believe they have had it in certain parts of the west. The minister speaks of this Bill as being a continuation of the policy of the government. I do not think he is altogether correct in that. This Bill is getting away from the policy of the time when we spent $50,000, and more in importing Douk-hobors, and making special conditions for them, one of which was that they would be entirely exempt from one of the duties of every citizen of this country -military duty. That would not be done to-day by my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior. This Bill is an improvement and I regret that we did not adopt it last year. But, that improvement-let us be fair-is due to two causes particularly. In the first place, it is due to the criticism which for several years we have offered in this House of the system of immigration as it is being continued. It was more or less the system which brought the Doukhobors in. The inspection was insufficient and faulty in many respects. The principle of the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton), who then occupied the position of my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior, was to fill the country up at any cost with anybody, provided we crowded up the country, and could report to the people that the immense prosperity of Canada was producing this result. We criticised that system. We pointed out that every man admitted to the Canadian family should only be admitted after careful examination. We were .seconded by the immigration officers of the United States who made representations to this government that they were not exercising due severity in the examination of the immigrants that we bonused to come Mr. MONK.
here, and who then went over to the United States, because that course had been followed for a long time. Bonused immigrants passed over to the United States. The Americans got the cream of them, and those that they refused remained in this country with their diseases and short-comings. That criticism brought about an improvement in the regulations. The representations of the American officers in their yearly reports on immigration in which they blamed very severely what we were doing brought about this change, and I think we can claim some of the credit for having brought about the improvement in this line. But, let the House bear in mind that even to-day we keep no trace of the immigrants who came here. Where do they go? About 60,000 Americans came into Canada last year. I think a larger number went from Canada to the United States.

Who were they? You must, under your immigration system, trace those who come in, and those who go out. We do not trace those who go out, and until we have a provision to that effect in our law, our law would be failing in that respect. We have spent millions a year in securing immigration, we should know that we have it here, and I think we are getting the full benefit of this expenditure. We ought to know who are going out too. We ought to know if our own people are going out. There was a time when there was a large exodus from Quebec, and the maritime provinces, and when the best in those provinces left . us. We should know that, and we should rather spend our money to find that out than to take it to pay our cousins, our friends and our defeated candidates, large salaries to do, we do not know what, in the United States, and elsewhere. There is an improvement in that policy, and some of the credit for that improvement is due to us, but as the minister is not always willing to give it, it is better to call the attention of the House to it. I notice some points in connection with this new legislation to which I desire to particularly call the attention of the House. This Bill fails entirely, as every other Bill has failed, to provide for moral guarantees with respect to immigration. We continue to receive somewhere about a quarter of a million people every year without any inquiry whatever as to who they are or as to what are their moral qualifications. Who are the men who compose this vast herd that is going to make up the nation here, and that is going to enter into our families? I contend that we should endeavour to secure some certainty as to who these people are. I do not pretend to solve absolutely the problem that presents itself as

to how that can be done, but no effort is attempted in that direction. Could we not secure some certainty as to his moral qualifications from the immigrant before his embarkation? It seems that that could be done since we have a staff of immigration agents in foreign countries. At any rate, could the immigrant, when he arrives, bring something to show where he comes from, and who he is? This is just as important as the physical examination. Members of this House who have given this matter any attention know that when the immigrant arrives in a batch of 1,200, and sometimes 2,000 on a ship, he passes the physical examination very quickly. The inspector general told us once at the Immigration Committee that as many as four a minute passed the inspecting medical officer. It is somewhat difficult even to ascertain the physical condition. He is detained, of course, if there is some suspicion as to his condition. What about his moral qualification? Would it not be necessary that a man should be required to bring, when he comes to this country, some reference, something from the mayor of his municipality, from some responsible officer, from somebody, to show that he is not a criminal, and that he ought to be welcomed into this country? You do not admit a man into your family without letters of introduction. When these people come in large numbers we ought to have some means of ascertaining who they are, because it is needless to say that a vast number of those found in our jails in Montreal, and in Toronto, and in the jails, penitentiaries, and houses of refuge of Ontario, and -of my^own province, and probably in others there is an undue proportion of foreign criminals. I think that we might, before the immigrant starts out, or at any rate when he arrives here, have some means to get from him guarantees as to his moral qualifications. A very serious question arises as to whether it would not be an act of humanity to the immigrant himself, a great economy for ourselves, and generally a better course to secure the examination physically before he leaves foreign shores.
I am sure that is possible. It is done in the United States to a very large extent. They have an examination at the port of destination, no doubt; but I understand that in the great ports of embarkation in Europe there is an officer who examines the emigrants. I think that last year the cost of our deportations considerably exceeded $25,000, because even though the transportation companies are obliged to take a man back if he is rejected at the port of debarkation, or after a certain delay, still he sometimes wanders into the country and causes great expense to the municipalities and to the government before he is
brought back under guard to the place of embarkation and handed back to the country from which he came. Anyway it is a great expense and a fearful hardship. You have to separate families; you return |a man to Europe and land him there penniless and hopeless. Instances appear from time to time in the papers. This is a matter which I think ought to engage the attention of the government. I repeat what has already formed the subject of a question by my hon. friend from Peel: ought we not now to abolish state aid in any form? Canada is becoming well known; we advertise it, and should continue to make it known everywhere in the proper way; but should we pay more bonuses? The answer given to the question of the hen. member for Peel was that there was now no state aid properly so called. But it must be borne in mind that the labouring classes in the country, through the Trades Congress and other societies, have from time to time called on the government to abolish bonuses, giving reasons therefor, and coming and urging these reasons verbally on the government. There is, therefore, a large class, and a class exposed to suffer from bonused immigrants, who have repeatedly asked for the abolition of bonuses. I think that the Bill, even in its incomplete and imperfect state, is a considerable improvement on past legislation. There is a point which I wish to make in favour of the immigrants, and it is the result of representations made to me in the city of Montreal and elsewhere, not by government officials as a rule, but by men who are familiar with immigration and who take a large part in assisting worthy immigrants. Is it right to fix the amount of money which an immigrant on landing should have? I have often raised an objection to that. It very often happens that an immigrant who lands without a cent, is just the man to fall to work at once; he may be an excellent immigrant, eager to work, and yet because he has not that fixed sum in his hand, he is sent back. There is no discretion in the office. Lately my attention has been called to Syrians, who are to be found in Montreal and elsewhere. They came to this country very poor, but I am not aware that there has ever been a Syrian who has required public aid. Why should we not admit into this country men of that race, or of any other race, if they are willing to work, and' are qualified in every other respect to become excellent settlers? A man who arrives here with more than the requisite sum of money may be a very unfit man, who intends to live on that money and afterwards to rove. This is the testimony I have heard from men who follow closely the movement of immigrants. When I first raised this question, I was told by my hon. friend that it was a dangerous discretion to leave to the officer

who inspects. Surely an officer who is obliged in a few moments to judge of the moral, physical and general qualifications of an immigrant ought to be able to say whether he has sufficient resources upon him or whether he is disposed to become a public charge. If he is a suitable officer for this important function, he ought to be able to exercise that discretion. On the whole, I think the Bill is a good one, because it constitutes a progress on the laxity of previous legislation; but I shall never be satisfied, so far as I am concerned, until we advance a step further-until we consider that the admission of an immigrant into this country is not a goal to be sought for at all costs. The country is rich, we are called on to make a great country of it, and we ought not to admit any but the most suitable into it. We should go further even than the Americans have gone in the selection of those who are to constitute so large a section of the Canadian people.

We swapped off 34,000 Canadians, our own people, the best citizens we yould have, for aliens from Europe, or some other country. This is a condition of things that should be more thoroughly looked into. The figures are carefully collated, and there is no doubt that they are correct. We hear so much about the outflow being stopped, about no more Canadians leaving Canada. There never were so many leaving in our history as there are now. I can quite understand the 15,000 Americans who go back home. They come here and buy land, and go home, they are speculating in our lands. They have not got their coats off, they come over here with their pocket books. We hear so much about $92,000,000 coming into the country with these people. If a man comes into our country with $92,000,000 and invests it and makes the price double in ten years, if he is not doing so much, for this country, especially, if he goes home with his coat on to wait until those lands become valuable. Fifteen thousand people have done that.
Another astounding thing to me is that coming and going by our different transportation lines into the United States, and

back again last year 8,000,000 passengers passed to and fro between this country and the United States according to thi3 book. These are rather astonishing figures to contemplate, that is more than the whole population of this country. That is a large outflow compared with what we thought there was and some record should be kept of the fluctuation of population. If we cannot fasten them down somewhere, we ought to be more careful about bringing them in.
I can understand the effort made a few years ago to bring all kinds of people into this country. Why? Because a good many men influential with the government wanted to see the prices of land go up because they were holders, and therefore wanted to fill the country with any class of immigrants who would come in order to make lands in the Northwest more valuable.
Another serious question is the outflow of people from the older provinces to the west. I do not find fault with that, the western country is the heritage of the older provinces; but there should be some attempt on the part of the government to counteract that in some sense by bringing other people into the older provinces to take the places of those who leave. There are no better pioneers than our own Canadian born young men who grow up full of energy and strength and purpose, no better men, but while they go out to the west, to build up that great country, and make it what it will be, a good country, some reasonable attempt should be made to fill their places by suitable immigrants from some part of Europe. I suggest these things to the House, thinking they will look more thoroughly into them. It is a condition of things that should not exist, and we ought to make some attempt to counteract these things.	*

While the Immigration Bill is under discussion I wish to draw to the attention of the government, and parliament the fact that immigration so far as the Atlantic provinces of Canada are concerned, has in the past, been neglected. The efforts which the government have been putting out for many years past have been entirely directed to the filling up of our western country. With the peopling of that country, and with its development, we in the east have no quarrel whatever. On tbp contrary it is our pride, and it would be a very great source of satisfaction to us to see that country filled up with a desirable class of people, to see it developed and to see it prosper.
At the same time we cannot but recognize that the government have overlooked almost entirely, if not entirely, the needs of the maritime provinces so far as immigration is concerned. Only some few weeks ago, the question of the representation of these provinces in parliament was
discussed in this House. It was then very clearly pointed out that there has been serious loss in the population of the three maritime provinces during the past few years, and the next redistribution will probably result in the loss of two or three, possibly more seats in this House to the maritime provinces. The question i3 one of very vital interest to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. The government should make some effort to see that these provinces, which have been described as the long wharfs of this Dominion, should not merely serve the purpose of a wharf, but should retain a certain percentage of the people brought to this country as the result of the government propaganda. We have in the past lost tens, of thousands of people who have gone to the United States. Some of our best and most capable people who have gone there have secured in that country eminent positions. They as a whole have been a credit to the country from which they went and were gladly received by the American nation. But when this government, some time ago placed immigration agents in the eastern states for the purpose of inducing the return of some of those people from the maritime provinces back to Canada, the instructions, so far as I am informed-and I am led to believe by the answer which the Minister of the Interior gave to a question put last year that my information is correct-were given those agents to endeavour to secure the return of those people not to the maritime provinces, but to direct them to western Canada. I do not think that is right. In view of the fact that the maritime provinces have lost very seriously in population, and that their representation is likely to be seriously impaired after the next redistribution owing to the fact it would be, only right and proper that the government should make a special effort, and direct its energies particularly, towards the preserving to the maritime provinces of a percentage at least of the immigrants of the agricultural class brought into Canada through those provinces. For many years the literature which this government has been circulating in Europe has been almost entirely that descriptive of our western country. As I said a few moments ago, we of 5the east have no quarrels with the west, on the contrary the west is a source of great pride to us, but I say that the government have unfairly discriminated against the east in their immigration policy. I trust that in the future a more equitable and proper view of the matter will be taken by the government and that some of the energy of their various representatives in Europe will be directed toward sending immigrants to the maritime provinces and

towards informing them of the advantages offered by those provinces. This in a measure will redeem the injury they have sustained through the serious emigration from our provinces which took place some years ago and which let me add is still continuing, to the eastern states of the American union. I hope also that the government will change the instructions to their agents in the eastern states and instruct them, when they seek to return to this country the people who have left it in years past, not to alone direct their attention to the Canadian west, but make at least an effort, and a fair effort, first of all, to see that these people are reminded of the advantages which the maritime provinces offer them, and endeavour to return to the land of their birth those who left it. In this connection I may refer to the condition which has developed as the result of some regulations recently issued by the Postmaster General with regard to postage upon newspapers published in Canada and going to the United States. Some time ago I put a question on the order paper respecting this matter and the answer I received I confess was somewhat confusing. I placed the question on the order paper at the request of the editor of a local paper in the town where I reside. He told me that up to the time that increased postage was imposed his paper had a large circulation in the United States, and that these papers were taken very largely by people who had formerly been residents of the county of Digby and also by subscribers among American summer tourists who spent part of their time in Digby. The result of the increase in the postage necessitated an advance of 50 per cent in the subscription for the paper, an advance from one dollar to one dollar and fifty cents. The consequence was that he found the circulation of his paper in the United States declined very materially. This, he said, did not represent all the loss. The greatest loss was to the country, through losing touch with the former residents. This applies to all weekly newspapers in the east. The local paper is the best repatriation agent. So long as we are able to place in the hands of people who have left this country our weekly newspapers and they can see what, transpires from week to week in their old home, so long do we retain their interest in the place and we have always a prospect of bringing them back. I have known of many instances where, because of some development reported in the weekly newspapers, people have returned to the country and taken up their abode there again. I consider that the imposition upon the weekly newspapers of that increased postal rate is a very serious detriment and is in no Mr, JAMESON.
way compensated by the paltry increase in postal revenue. I trust that the Postmaster General will remove the charge, as I think it would be for the general benefit of the country, by keeping our people who have gone to the United States in touch with their old homes. The severing of that tie involves the risk of losing them for ever, as residents of the maritime provinces.

I confess that I have not made any preparation for this debate, but there are a few observations I should like to offer in view of the fact that I have given some attention to this question of immigration. I think I am correct in saying that this Bill is similar in principle to the existing Act. This Bill elaborates certain features of the existing law. My opinion is that, so far as the operation of the law is concerned, we can accomplish the same results under it as under this Bill. The principle of this Bill is to keep undesirables out of the country. Therefore, the Bill is good. Any weaknesses are not a question of law, but in the operation of the law. There is a law, ordained some centuries ago, commanding men not to steal. That law has been elaborated from time to time down through the ages, yet it has not wholly restrained people from walking off with their neighbours' goods. If we had only one entrance to this country and instructed the doorkeeper to allow none to enter but the morally and physically sound, we might elaborate the order into pages of law, but unless the man had the discriminating faculty to sift the good from the bad, the law would not be of much effect. I make no criticism of the immigration officials, for those I know appear to be very good men. But I suggest to the minister that he cannot get results under the present system of selecting the outside service. This applies whichever government may be in power. You cannot get the same results as if you placed the selection of these officers under a commission and allowed the superintendent of immigration to pick out men speciallv suitable for that character of woTk. We hear much about the greatness of Canada and of the vast number of people we are going to receive into this country. We certainly are haying some prosperous years. Lean years will come, and the movement, some day, will be from the cities back to the land. If we have confidence in our own statements as to the riches of this country, we must believe that there will be a vast movement of people towards our borders. We ought not to wait until that time comes before beginning to train our immigration service. There is no portion of our public service so necessary or important as this immigration service. The commissioner general of the United States,

in reporting on his men in his report tor the year ending June 30 last, states:
The bureau never fails in its annual reports to call attention to the high estimate it places upon the character and capacity of employees, as a whole and taken individually, and to its appreciation of their loyality, zeal and industry. The work upon which they are engaged is quite different from that performed by many other classes of government employees. They handle human beings, and must, in order to be successful in the highest sense, exhibit the qualities of mind and heart that have no particular place in the handling of books, papers or commodities.
Our present system of securing an outside service, by patronage committees, the recommendation of members of .parliament -I speak regardless of wliat party is in power-must certainly result in putting some men into this immigration service who are better fitted for something else. We must get away from that system if we wish to properly guard our borders. I am making no complaints about the officials; I believe our men are doing good service. But there will be a greater service for them to render when later on they will be called on to inspect vast masses of people who turn towards Canada. When that movement comes it will carry with it the flushings of vice out from the large centres of population. Upon our immigration officials depends our ability to maintain the moral and physical standard of our people. Let that go down, and it is unnecessary for me to say what will happen to this country.
So far, I assume, the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) will largely agree with what I have said. If there should be a question of difference between us, it may be on what I am about to say. I believe, that it is the duty of the government to appoint a royal commission to investigate immigration matters. It will cost a little money, of course, but great results will accrue. We are largely creatures of habit; the ordinary business institution gets into a rut; departmental officials are apt to get into a rut. It is desirable to bring in fresh thoughts and ideas and have these matters thoroughly investigated. That idea is not original with me, as the minister knows. The United States government, in 1907, appointed a commission of nine-the President, the Senate and the House of Representatives each appointing three. That commission is doing a most valuable work for the United States. If it has not already done so, it will shortly present its report to congress. I believe the time has arrived when there should be a royal commission to investigate immigration matters in this country, and I certainly think there should be a representative of the labour interest on such a commission.
Another question is that of naturalization. I believe that we make ourselves too
cheap in the making of Canadian ciitzens. Everybody knows that we pay no heed or attention to the matter. If citizenship implies anything in Canada, it must mean ownership. In some European countries, citizenship means burdens. In this country it carries responsibility, but it means also the ownership of something very valu-* able. Are we not offering this citizenship too freely? We all know that the idea of making citizens never occurs to any one until there is an election. And we know,' in the west, at least, the method is this: A foreign-born man is met somewhere; he takes an affidavit before a notary public; this is posted up for a few days; and the man is shortly afterwards certified by the judge as a citizen of this country. The United States have realized that this is a very serious question. In the past few years they have changed the Naturalization Act, and the three-year period no longer exists. At present no man can become a citizen of the United States without being approved by two other citizens who will guarantee his fitness to become a citizen. Perhaps the minister might not agree with me in this matter, but I think it is one that might be profitably looked into by a royal commission, certainly it is of great importance to this country, and I am sure that every hon. gentleman in the House realizes that I am correct in that statement.
The Bill before us has no bearing on the policy of the government. There are some features in connection with the immigration administration that I will refer to in committee, when the minister will be better able to. discuss it with me. We have a branch of our government supplying us with statements as to the estimated population. I am afraid we will discover, when our next census is taken, that the population w'ill not be as great as we have hoped. A short time ago, I put a question on the order paper, and learned that those estimates are based upon the increase of births over deaths as determined at the last census, which increase was 12-7. To that is to be added yearly the increase by immigration as shown by the returns. Well, this country is not like Siberia, where people who come in cannot get out. There is freedom to come in and to go out, and there is a movement of population back and forth. Population is more or less in a fluid state, and there are many people who come in and who go out, of whom no account has been taken in these estimates of population. In the United States, while they have not much information to work upon, they estimate the population that remains at 68 per cent of the entire immigration. I mention this because, if I am correct in the interpretation of the answer that wTas given me, I repeat wre will probably be disappointed when the next census is taken.

Before you leave the Chair I would like to make a few remarks on this question of immigration The minister has increased the time for deportation from two to three years. Dr. Clark, of the insane hospital in Toronto, is strongly in favour of increasing the period to four years. For myself I can see no reason why there should be any limit fixed to the time within which deportation may take place. If people come into this country who are not able to take care of themselves, who have to be sent to an insane asylum, or other places, to be supported by the public, I do not see why we should retain them at all. There is another provision that I am sorry the minister has not put into his Bill. In the law of the United States they have a clause that when transportation companies bring aliens into the country having a loathsome or dangerous disease, or of weak mind, if the diseases are such as might have been discovered at the port of embarkation, those companies are liable to a fine for each case of $100; and last year, for that offence, the fines amounted to $27,400. In his last report the commissioner recommends that the fine be increased to $200. I think that such a provision should be put into our law also, because there is a temptation on the part of transportation companies to bring people into this country for the purpose of getting the price of their fare across the Atlantic. Then there is another matter which has been mentioned by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), and that is the advisability of doing away with commissions. I am in favour of cutting out these commissions altogether and of Appropriating the money now spent on that purpose, or as much money as is necessary, to the employment of a doctor on each immigration ship, who shall thoroughly examine every immigrant on the voyage across the Atlantic from whatever country he may come. I think in that way we would be able to exclude people coming to this country who are diseased, or weak minded, or otherwise unfit to become permanent and useful citizens of our country. The question of weaklings and undesirables is troubling the United States a3 well as Canada. There are people in the United States, as stated by the report of the _ Commissioner General, who advocate an increase in the head tax. Some are advocating a literary test, and some are in favour of both. Now, whether that would be advisable,. I am not prepared to say. But one thing is certain, and that is that we ought to get at the best possible means of discovering those undesirables before they embark, and keeping them out. That is a question in which not only we are personally interested, but in which our children and our grandchildren will be still Mr. MAGRATH.
more interested, because they will have to live side by side with these undesirable people who succeed in entering our country. We ought to take every precaution to keep the physical standard of Canadians as high as possible. There are people in the United States who even think that thbre should be a physical test applied to immigrants, and that all males from 16 to 50 should be submitted to a physical examination as severe as the military test. A good many people are sent to. this country by relatives who are anxious to get rid of them. I notice in the reports from the asylum that people have been sent out here, and after they have been deported, their friends in the old country have admitted that they sent them out here for the purpose of getting rid of. them. I could mention a number of such cases. I have here the report issued by the Ontario government for the last year, in which is pointed out quite a number of cases that are very interesting. Here is what it says about deportations:
The work of deporting undesirables has been effectively carried on throughout the year, and with the result that 263 persons were deported.
That is from Ontario alone. There is here a comparative table showing the number of persons deported in the years 1906, 1907 and 1908. In 1908 there were 263 persons deported. In November of that year, 18 insane persons were deported as not coming within the provisions of the Immigration Act. Arrangements have been made by the Ontario government agent at Liverpool for the reception of deported people in their respective homes upon their arrival. So that these eighteen were not deported in the regular way. Private arrangements were made by the government of Ontario whereby these people were sent back to their friends in the old country.
Of these 18, nine were acknowledged as being mentally defective before coming to Canada and two others were acknowledged epileptics, the relatives having no hesitancy in stating that they were sent to this country for the purpose of getting rid of them. . . . Of the 65 insane deported, their average residence in the hospitals for the insane wTas one year and two and a half months. Of 81 criminals deported 15 were committed to the Central prison and 66 to the jails of the province. Of the 117 deported ' as likely to become a public charged 26 had been living on public charity since their arrival in Canada, It were young children of undesirables who wrere deported, and the remainder were deported owing to disease, physical infirmities and immorality. The pecuniary advantage to the provinces by the deportation of the insane persons alone amounts to over $325,000. In addition to the deportations which were mentioned above, the chief of frontier police at Niagara Falls, acting on instructions received from the Attorney General's department, de-

ported to the United States, during the three months ending December 31, 1908, 303 undesirables.
These were people in regard to which nothing was done by the Dominion government. I have a good deal of that kind of information, but perhaps it would not be worth while to go into it at this stage. It was mentioned here to-day that we have a very imperfect way of ascertaining the number, of people that are living in this country. I recollect that the Minister of Finance, in his budget speech, made the statement that there were in this country at the present time 7,450,000 people. I quite understand how he got that information. He, in all probability, got Mr. Blue to prepare the statement for him. That statement was made up from the census of 1901, and every person then in Canada was enumerated in that census. Then the natural increase was added. We all know that large numbers of people from the older provinces went to the Northwest. Train loads of them went. Only the other day
4,000	left Toronto. We know that in 1906 a census was taken in the northwest. Every person who went to that country from the older provinces between 1901 and 1906 was enumerated there as if he had been a newcomer. Then, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance took the reports of the Immigration Department and added the figures which were there given to make the total amount. According to the figures in the United States reports for 1907-8, 58,000 people left Canada and went to the United States. For the year 1908-9, we have the report that 81,000 people left Canada and went to the United States. We also know that the United States keep track of their immigration, and I have some figures here taken from their report. In 1908 there were arrivals in the United States to the number of 924,695. Of these, it was reported that 714,874 left the United States again, leaving a net increase in population of 209,867. Then, in 1908-9, the total arrivals in the United States numbered 944,235 and the departures 400,392, leaving a net increase of 543,843. They do not claim in the United States that more than 68 per cent of the immigrants that go to that country stay there, and I do not see how we can reasonably expect that we will retain any-w'here near the whole of our immigrants because there are attractions in the United States. There are people who come to this country to work during the summer time many of whom go to_ their own countries in -*the fall. Possibly there are a great many reasons why men should stay here and there are a great many why they should not, I presume. However, I am very strong upon the point that we should be very particular about the inspection of immigrants coming to this country, and I think the best way to do that is to have a doc175
tor upon every ship that brings immigrants and have them thoroughly examined on the voyage. Those that are not up to the mark should not be allowed to land. I think that is the best from the humanitarian point of view, because it is cruel to allow people to be brought to this country when we know they will have to be deported and sent back to their own country, after having spent perhaps all the money they have in their attempt to get to this country. We should keep in mind the reports from the asylums and jails. In the province of Ontario we have not quite 20 per cent of a foreign-born population. It is about 17-1 or 17-2 per cent. I mean people born outside of Canada, but in our jails, prisons and insane hospitals, according to the report of Dr. Clark, 40 or 50 per cent of the inmates are foreign-born. That is a state of things that ought not to be, and it did not exist before 1900. The whole trouble has been that we have been too careless in our inspection. Just imagine 7,000 people being landed at one port in one day to be examined. I do not care how many officials you have at such a place, there is no room to examine them properly and do justice. At Ellis Island, New York, they will not allow the number to be examined to exceed 5,000 in any one day, and the equipment that they have there must be better than ours, because their immigration is so much larger than that which we have, and it is necessary for them to have a better equipment. I do not know that I shall continue this dhbate any longer, because as the Bill proceeds we will have an opportunity of speaking on the different clauses. I think it is an improvement on what we have had heretofore, and I think that the government has to some extent listened to the suggestions that have come from time to time from the opposition. If we cannot get quality and quantity it is essential that we shall have quality anyway. I think the minister himself has come to that conclusion and that the immigration work should be carried on upon that principle. I think that Mr. Scott is a real good official. He wrote a letter in 1908 to his assistant over in London, saying that the only kind of people we wanted in this country were experienced farm labourers, farmers who Sre able to take up land, farmers who had money to buy land, or female domestic servants. These were the three kinds that he specified as being desirable, but I notice that the government are very anxious to take credit when they get before a popular audience, excepting it be an audience of workingmen or a trades union, to show the great number that they have brought to this country. But, when they are talking to the trades unions that view of it does not get very much prominence. They



then give more prominence to the class of people that they are paying bonuses for, that is farmers, farm labourers and female domestic servants. I hope that this Bill will be made as perfect as possible, and that a clause will be inserted providing that the transportation companies that bring undesirable people to this country shall be fined and made to take them back, and if necessary made to take a caretaker with them so that they will not suffer.

I would be very pleased if _ efforts were made to improve the immigration into this country. I have in my hands the report of the Superintendent General of Immigration of the United States, and as it has been freely quoted from I shall not cite many figures. In the opening pages of the report, the commissioner deals with the accuracy of the work done by his department and states that it is as nearly perfect as possible. He refers to the fact that further legislation will be required to keep the undesirable immigrants out of the United States. With all the perfection they have obtained they still find it necessary to recommend that further steps be taken in the way of legislation in order to keep out this class of people. I shall quote his-words:
It is not intended and should not be regarded as a declaration that the bureau is-satisfied that the law, even if made at every point effective of its present intent, would be all-sufficient to control immigration. On the contrary, the bureau believes that the time-has come for the adoption of some measures-more restrictive than any so far enacted That such is the case has been demonstrated' by the evils that have grown out of immigration, particularly in the large cities of the east and middle west, which evils have been accentuated during the past few years of industrial depression. The point at which, perhaps, the

law is especially inadequate is in the class of excluded aliens termed * persons likely to become a public charge/ This standard is not high enough. The alien who becomes a burden on the taxpayers is ultimately undesirable principally for financial reasons. The alien who is barely able, perhaps even with the assistance of private charity, to eke out an existence is continuously undesirable for economic reasons. The presence of such persons in the community tends always to lower the standard of living, of work, and of wages; must have, in an economic sense, a degrading effect. Each community can in time elevate a few such persons to its own level, but its -capacity in this respect is limited, and many >of our communities have been degraded, and many others will be unless some means are found of preventing the immigration of the alien who is barely able to maintain himself.
We will all recognize the difficulty _ of drawing the line with regard to alien immigration. The figures have been given in this report of the total immigration into the United States during the last financial year as 944,235 and I would like to Doint out that of that total immigration three-quarters is what they term immigrant and one-quarter non-immigrant immigration.
They found it necessary to stop a large number at the borders, and of that amount of 944,000, over 400,000 went out of the country almost immediately during the year. Where did they go? We can arrive at no other conclusion than that a large number are trying to make their way across the border into Canada. I have it from the Immigration Department that over 6,700 of these people were stopped at the border last year, and only some 1,300 from all other countries. That would point to the fact that there must be a large number of an undesirable class who manage to get into the United States in some way, and either the American authorities are trying to squeeze them out of the United States, or these undesirables are trying to get into our borders.
I am pleased that a step has been taken to make the regulations more stringent, and I hope the minister will be able to keep out a larger number of these undesirable Immigrants. A year or two ago I said 1 [DOT]did not believe that Canada was getting an excess of immigration from the United States over and above the emigration going there from this country. There is a balance in favour of the United States. AVhether that could be overcome by efforts on our part I do not know, but it is more important that we should get the best class than have a larger immigration, it is especially important that we should keep our young people at home. We ought to direct *our attention to getting the diversified employment necessary to keep our young people* in the country rather than run the chance of getting foreign immigration to replace those who leave us for the United Mr. WEIGHT.
States. If there be no way of preventing that large emigration from this country to the United States, we must do the best we can to get the best class of immigrants to fill their places. What has been the gain of our Northwest Territories has been in a large measure the loss of our provinces in the east. In Ontario we have been losing our best young men. There has been a depreciation in the value of farms in the east, and they are worth less to-day than they were worth twenty years ago. Go into any of the outlying settlements in Ontario a little distance from the larve cities, and you can buy a farm cheaper than you could "at any previous time in my memory. That is caused by the drain to the United States on the one hand, and to our Northwest Territories on the other. We ought to make that up to the eastern provinces; but if 1 understand rightly, the hon. minister is directing his sole attention to filling up the west. I do not object to his giving his attention to the west, but without any effort on the part of this government, the people of the east are flocking out there to get these free lands. In my humble judgment every quarter-section homestead in that country is worth, when the patent is issued,- $1,000, and our government are offering that as a bonus to people from the United States. A large number of these people, when they get their homesteads, sell them as soon as possible. They simply settle in our country as a sneculation, and return to the United States as soon as they can. Some 15,000 of them returned last year and 18,000 of them the year before. That being the case, it would be well to look into the question, and see whether the reeulations misrht not be changed so a3 not to allow these settlers to get their patents so quickly, and in that way keep them in the country.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

It seems to me that this government has made the same mistake that was made by the Conservative government; it has been entirely too anxious to bring immigrants into this country. We all recognize that we have a great heritage in the west. But I think what we do not recognize is that that heritage belongs to the people of Canada rather than to the people of any other country. It seems to me that the people of the older provinces. Ontario, Quebec, and the maritime provinces, should have been more considered than they have been in times past in settling the Northwest. There are many parts of Ontario and Quebec, for instance, that, in the days of the lumber kings, gave employment to hundreds of people and that were far more capable of yielding a liveli-

hood to the people than they are to day. In my own county, for instance, there are sections which have been denuded of their timber, yet which are entirely unfit for agriculture. I believe that if 'some of . the money expended in times past in inducing immigrants to come to Canada had been expended in assisting some of these people to take up homes in the Northwest, that money would have been well expended. One of these settlers from the older portions of Ontario, acquainted as they are with our laws, our language and ouit-cus-toms, would be worth more to this country than a whole colony of Doukhobors. I think it would be worth the government's while to take into consideration the people of the older provinces in settling the Northwest, We know that there are people in older Canada who would be only too glad to take up homes in the west and would do so if they had a little encouragement and assistance. But they find, if they make their way to the Northwest with a view to taking up lands, that the lands have been apportioned to peoples from other countries. Their means are limited, and they find themselves unable to cope with the conditions. I am heartily in accordance with the expressions of the hon. member for Lennox (Uriah Wilson). The statistics of our jails and asylums afford ample evidence that not sufficient attention has been paid to the quality of our immigrants. In our anxiety to people the Northwest we have thought rather of quantity, and have paid too little attention to quality. I agree with the hon. member for Lennox in advising that the government should use the utmost care in examining immigrants, not only as to their financial standing and the amount of money they have, but, also, and even more carefully, as to their mental, moral and physical qualities. I reserve any further remarks I may have to make on the subject of immigrate another occasion.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
